name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia probes House candidate for allegedly voting in two states
description: Georgia’s secretary of state is investigating allegations that David Dillie, a Democratic candidate for state House District 161, may have voted in two state primaries this year in a violation of state law. Dillie, a 24-year-old mechanic for Gulfstream who lives near Pooler Parkway, has denied the accusation, first reported by The Atlanta Journal-Constitutio[...]
text:
David Dillie addresses 300 people gathered outside the Effingham College & Career Academy to protest the proposed OpenAI data center in Rincon on July 23, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaGeorgia’s secretary of state is investigating allegations that David Dillie, a Democratic candidate for state House District 161, may have voted in two state primaries this year in a violation of state law.
Dillie, a 24-year-old mechanic for Gulfstream who lives near Pooler Parkway, has denied the accusation, first reported by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, that he voted in both Georgia’s May primary and a month later in a primary in Nevada. Dillie lived in Nevada before returning to Coastal Georgia in 2024.
Dillie, a third-generation Georgian, blamed youth and inexperience for the potential legal trouble. Under Georgia law, double-voting is a felony punishable with imprisonment and fine.
“I thought when you moved, your stuff gets canceled. That is not what happens,” Dillie told The Current GA. “No one mentioned” that the process is not automatic and that I would have to cancel my voter registration in Nevada, he said. “I’m young and, frankly, wasn’t knowledgeable,” he added.
Dillie is challenging Republican state lawmaker Bill Hitchens for the seat he has held since 2012 representing parts of Effingham, Bryan and Chatham counties. Statewide, Democrats have voiced optimism that they can flip the state House of Representatives in November and win control of the chamber for the first time in more than two decades.
Dillie’s outsider status helped him gain traction among voters amid widespread anger at established Republican leaders over the planned $20 billion OpenAI data center near Rincon.
As he jumped into the rigors of campaigning, Dillie said he did not look closely at his own voter registration details before the accusations cropped up.
He was a registered voter in Nevada, where he spent years working in construction in the Las Vegas area, he said. When he moved back to Georgia in September 2024, he registered to vote in the Peach State. But he did not proactively cancel his other registration, he said.
Under a state law passed in 2021, Nevada sends mail-in ballots to every registered voter — and Dillie cited that as the reason why a ballot there with his name on it would have been sent to his old address in the Los Vegas area.
A ballot bearing his name was returned and apparently counted in Nevada’s Republican primary, according to documents obtained by The Current. Dillie, however, says he did not fill out that Nevada ballot and does not know who did. His former residence is a home owned by his godfather.
Dillie said he does not know who submitted his Nevada ballot. “As soon as I know you’ll know,” Dillie said. “I’m glad there is an investigation. I wish it would have been flagged sooner.”
The secretary of state’s office announced its investigation last week, but the press release did not indicate how long it would take to look into the matter.
“Voting in another state’s primary while claiming to be a legal Georgia resident is a very serious allegation,” Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said in a news release. “My office has opened an investigation to gather all the evidence, determine the facts and take appropriate legal action.”
Raffensperger gave no timeline for the completion of the investigation.
Hitchens, 79, is a retired U.S. Marine and Georgia State Patrol officer, and lives in Rincon, a few miles away from the planned OpenAI data center. He is also a close ally of House Speaker Jon Burns, who is also from Effingham County, something that has attracted ire of local voters mad about the proliferation of data centers in Georgia.
The Republican-led state legislature has failed in two successive years to pass regulation of data centers, despite more than two dozen bills seeking to put guard rails around the industry.
Dillie says he is confident of being cleared of any voter wrongdoing, and won’t be dropping out of the race to represent the district.
“I’m taking this one day at a time,” he said. “I’m not hiding. My opponent wants me to be disqualified. I want the voters to decide.”

title: The pro-Amendment 3 campaign is outspending the opposition by a 33-1 ratio
description: A report shows that the campaign working to see Amendment 3 on the statewide ballot win approval in November is vastly outspending opponents of the measure. The campaign to fund the measure raised $18 million through Sept. 25. All of that financial support came from the Florida Association of Realtors. The two political committees opposing […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis announces his proposal to provide property tax relief in Tampa on May 27, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)A report shows that the campaign working to see Amendment 3 on the statewide ballot win approval in November is vastly outspending opponents of the measure.
The campaign to fund the measure raised $18 million through Sept. 25. All of that financial support came from the Florida Association of Realtors.
The two political committees opposing Amendment 3, Floridians for Shared Prosperity and Vote No on 3 Florida, have raised a combined $537,357. That’s a ratio of more than 33:1 that the pro-Amendment 3 forces have raised so far over the opposition.
That compilation was originally provided by OpenSecrets, the Washington, D.C., independent research group that tracks money in U.S. politics.
The proposal would raise the homestead exemption on non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would lower the annual assessment growth cap from 10% to 5% for non-homestead properties such as commercial buildings and rental units, and would require people moving to Florida after Dec. 31 to wait 5 years in continuous residency before qualifying for the full increased exemption.
State economists have projected that those changes would reduce local government property tax collections by up to $12 billion annually by its fifth year.
Public polling has been split on whether the measure can generate the 60% yes vote required for approval. While a recent St. Pete Polls survey shows the measure losing by getting only 45% support, it also showed that a quarter of the 913 surveyed said they were undecided.
However, a new survey  of 504 registered Florida voters shows Amendment 3 drawing 74% support, according to a Pioneer Institute poll on the housing market released Tuesday. The Pioneer Institute is a Boston think tank that has just launched a research initiative in Florida aimed at studying housing and education.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Passing Medicaid ballot measure would reduce services and spike insurance costs, opponents say
description: SIOUX FALLS — Opponents of a Nov. 3 ballot measure to end Medicaid expansion if federal funding is cut said Monday that the measure would reduce access to care and shift more health care costs onto people with private insurance. South Dakota’s Republican attorney general and its opponents say Amendment I would automatically repeal Medicaid […]
text:
South Dakota Nurses Association President Deb Fischer-Clemens (left) and Republican Jean Hunhoff, a longtime nurse and former state lawmaker, chat after their coalition encouraging people to vote "No on I" host it's first press conference in Sioux Falls, South Dakota on Aug. 9, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — Opponents of a Nov. 3 ballot measure to end Medicaid expansion if federal funding is cut said Monday that the measure would reduce access to care and shift more health care costs onto people with private insurance.
South Dakota’s Republican attorney general and its opponents say Amendment I would automatically repeal Medicaid expansion if federal funding falls and no longer covers 90% of the program’s costs. Proponents say the measure allows lawmakers to consider repealing, altering or maintaining it if federal funding falls below that level.
The ‘No on I’ coalition is led in part by Republican Jean Hunhoff, a longtime nurse and former state lawmaker who served 24 years in Pierre, including as chair of the state’s budget committee. 
Hospitals can’t turn people away because they are uninsured, she said. If people lose Medicaid and their ability to pay for care along with it, Hunhoff said, hospitals will need to charge other people more to make up their losses.
“They have to serve those patients, and they’re going to do it,” Hunhoff said. “But they are a business, too, and like any other business, they have to have the finances to be able to continue those services.” 
Medicaid is a federal-state health insurance program for low income people. In 2022, South Dakota voters approved a citizen-initiated state constitutional amendment to extend Medicaid eligibility to adults with incomes up to 138% of the poverty level. The expansion capitalized on a federal law passed during the President Barack Obama administration that covers 90% of states’ expansion costs.
Because the expansion is part of the state constitution, only voters can alter it.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At a coalition press conference in Sioux Falls, Hunhoff and South Dakota Nurses Association President Deb Fischer-Clemens said Medicaid expansion provides health coverage to more than 31,000 South Dakotans and helps patients get preventive care and treatment before medical conditions become more costly emergencies. 
“It is health insurance coverage for real people, real families and real communities across South Dakota,” Fischer-Clemens said. 
Fischer-Clemens said the financial burden on hospitals would only grow as more preventive care and minor treatments become emergency room visits and surgeries.
Ballot measure could auto-repeal Medicaid expansion, attorney general says in contrast to lawmakers

Expanded Medicaid provides about $400 million annually to hospitals that would otherwise go unreimbursed, South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations President Tim Rave said. Without Medicaid reimbursement, more of that care would become charity or unreimbursed care, Fischer-Clemens and Hunhoff said, leaving hospitals to find other revenue sources or cut services. 
“If you take that away, think about the future,” Hunhoff said.
The consequences of undoing Medicaid expansion would be particularly serious in rural communities, Hunhoff said, because those hospitals and clinics often operate on thin margins.
Those costs could ultimately be spread through higher private insurance premiums, too.
“The public will pay for these people’s health care, whether you cut Medicaid or not,” Fischer-Clemens told South Dakota Searchlight. 
The federal government could warn states if it planned to cut the federal match rate, the measure’s opponents argued, giving lawmakers and voters time to address a hypothetical cut. But if they didn’t, Hunhoff said. programs would need to be cut or new taxes would be needed to pay for them.
Republican former Rep. Will Mortenson, of Fort Pierre, sponsored the bill to put Amendment I to a public vote. The issue is fundamentally about budget priorities, he said. If federal funding declines, lawmakers should have the flexibility to decide whether Medicaid expansion should continue, rather than protecting it ahead of other budget priorities, he said.
“This is about whether able-bodied people receiving welfare is a higher priority than, say, K-12 education,” Mortenson said.

name: VTDigger
title: A bear broke into my kitchen. Then I watched him die.
description:
As bear encounters rise across Vermont, how do we share the woods and the yard without harm to either side?
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A bear broke into my kitchen. Then I watched him die..
text:
This commentary is by Rachel Lee Stoll, an antiquarian bookseller.
There is much conversation right now about bears in Vermont, about their increasing numbers and how and when we hunt them down. I have a dog in this bear fight, because my son and I came home a few weeks ago to find that our house had been visited in our absence by a hungry bear.  
The bear — terrifically nimble — opened a window I had not firmly latched, fell into my son’s room, clambered all about the house and found the glory hallelujah that is the kitchen. His paw hit a knob on our electric stove and turned on a burner. A sturdy old teapot took the heat. The bear opened our fridge and, in what I hope were the best damn hours of his life, slashed and spilled and feasted. He came in and out more than once, started taking food outside, to-go bags; why not? The house was, to put it mildly, a mess. At least the bear was gone when we arrived. But he came back the next morning.  
I hollered at him, airhorn bleating, old dog barking. I did not want him dead; I wanted him gone. He left, but slowly, so forlornly. And he came back again, unafraid of us. I called the wardens, who were excellent, kind and professional. While they set up a huge bear trap, I saw him coming back yet again, moving in that thick, silent manner, slipping through trees, and I pointed him out and said, “Do what you need to do.” They shot him. I started shaking. I think about that bear every day. He has entered my dreams. I have not cleaned his not-so-big prints off our walls.  
I do not want what happened at our house to be used as an argument for shooting more bears out of trees or while asleep in their dens. But there will be more dangerous encounters. Before the bear reached our house, he had been at neighbors’ houses — battering one family’s door and windows while they were inside baking cookies. He was not afraid of people. A few years back, a woman in Winhall was mauled by a bear. I fear we will hear more such stories.  
I had a close encounter with a grizzly while hiking in Montana long ago. I have had two brain surgeries and an adrenal crash alone in a car. I know what to fear in life, and, generally speaking, black bears are not high on that list. But that is a far cry from saying they are not dangerous at all, nor that I want a bear in my kitchen, gobbling up the cheese and peanut butter and buttermilk and 17 Clif Bars — though not the shimmering jar of honey left on the counter. 
What can we do? What should we not do? I am not against hunting when it is done properly. Hunting can be honorable: an animal living its life wild and free until the moment it is killed. But unlike other states such as Colorado and California, Vermont allows hounding: Many dogs are let loose against a bear that runs up a tree and then, terrified, is shot out of the tree, and often shot again when he falls if he is still alive. I despise bear hounding, as do many I know who are hunters. There is no honor in it. We owe the bears more than that.  

READ MORE

If bear season is extended, we need absolute clarity: Killing denned bears should be clearly prohibited. No fuzzy, vague language. What Vermonter wants a bear shot while sleeping in its den? Who are we? What are we made of?  
We do have a problem with too many bears. Everyone in our area who has lived here for decades, as we have, has noticed the uptick. Mother bears leave cubs up trees along our driveway. One cub this summer would sit on a sturdy branch and dangle his legs and chatter on, adorable as all babies are, and I wished he were not there. I told his mother not to trust us so much. Told her I am a bear killer, to no avail. We bark, we holler. I do not want that little bear shot next year. Or going into anyone’s house.  
So what do we do besides kill more of them? Resorts and restaurants should use bear-proof garbage containers properly, with serious fines and regulations with teeth. Why can’t resorts keep garbage inside, or build special garbage sheds? What if more Vermonters kept garbage inside?  
And we can use common sense. I used to keep our kitchen windows closed all summer. This summer was too hot, and I opened one. It was open the day a bear walked right by, inches away. I’ll try to keep those windows closed all summer. But what are we to do on hot summer nights when more bears start realizing, as it becomes part of their culture, that so much tasty food is inside every house?  
We can love bears and still know that their numbers, absurdly good sense of smell, strength and dexterity have become an honest-to-God problem without easy answers. 
Rosh Hashana just passed by. I found myself deep in the woods by a stream, with an old piece of Clif Bar in my pocket. Oh, I thought, as the old dog stumbled happily through the cool water, I could do tashlich, the ritual of symbolically tossing our sins into water as the new year begins, a fresh start. 
I thought of those I needed to ask forgiveness. Faces swam into view, but then the bear rushed in, his beautiful face taking up every inch of my mind. I tossed tiny bits of the stale bar into the stream, sunshine glinting off the water and the rocks all around, and I asked for his forgiveness, again and again.  
I’ll keep walking in their woods, slipping between the trees, searching for beechnuts, calling out with that loud sound that is neither friendly nor alarming, the one that says, I am here, and I know you are too, so let’s be careful, please, mindful of each other.

name: WyoFile
title: Mental evaluation sought for Wyoming journalist accused of forgery
description:
An attorney for April Morganroth told a judge there is reasonable cause to believe that she has a mental illness or deficiency.
The post Mental evaluation sought for Wyoming journalist accused of forgery appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The criminal cases against a former Wyoming journalist accused of perjury and forging documents should be suspended while she undergoes a mental evaluation, her attorney wrote in new court filings.
The attorney asked a judge in Platte County to order that April Marie Morganroth undergo an outpatient evaluation by the Wyoming State Hospital’s Criminal Justice Service.
“There is reasonable cause to believe that [Morganroth] has a mental illness or deficiency, and it is necessary that an examination of Defendant’s mental condition be performed” to determine her fitness to proceed with the criminal case against her, wrote Assistant Public Defender Denny Harts in a motion filed Monday.
Platte County prosecutors this spring filed 20 charges against Morganroth in two cases. The first involves allegations that Morganroth, who went by the name Marie Hamilton in Wyoming, forged documents and lied under oath while fighting a proposed Chugwater area wind farm. 
In the second case, prosecutors allege that Morganroth forged documents as part of a homebuying scheme. Those documents falsely indicated she had received a loan and grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture for a Chugwater home that she rented for a time, court filings show.
The 41-year-old has pleaded not guilty to all charges. Neither Harts nor the county prosecutor returned messages left Tuesday seeking comment. Morganroth, who is free on bond, declined comment when approached by a WyoFile reporter at an April hearing.
Morganroth worked as a journalist in multiple states including Nebraska, Colorado and Wyoming. The Denver Post reported she was fired by the Boulder Daily Camera in 2021 after editors there acknowledged in a lengthy retraction that she fabricated multiple quotes in a story about local residents reflecting on the Sept. 11 terrorism attacks.
She later moved to Wyoming and worked as a reporter, under the Marie Hamilton name, for the Platte County Record-Times, the Guernsey Gazette, the Torrington Telegram and the Newcastle News Letter Journal. Morganroth later launched her own publication, 307 Wyoming Sentinel, and also freelanced for Oil City News. 
Her bio on 307 Wyoming Sentinel claimed she was pursuing a “Juris Doctorate” in media law at the University of Wyoming, even though the school doesn’t offer one. She also claimed she had 26 years in the journalism industry, which would have meant her career started around the age of 15.
In his request for a mental evaluation for Morganroth, Harts cited a Wyoming law that requires legal proceedings to be halted if there is reasonable cause to believe a defendant has a mental illness or deficiency that makes him or her unfit to proceed. The public defender did not offer details about what prompted him to believe such an evaluation was needed for his client.
After the evaluation is performed, the examiners are tasked by state law with providing a report to the court related to the defendant’s competency. The judge then holds a hearing to determine whether the accused person is mentally fit to proceed, though the prosecution and defense sometimes stipulate to someone’s fitness.
Harts, in his motion, asked for the report within 60 days of the judge’s order. 
In addition to the Platte County charges, Morganroth also faces a criminal case in Laramie County alleging she forged documents to enroll her child in a school district there and obtain special education services. Investigators say she submitted a letter from a doctor who told them he didn’t write the document.
Although a Laramie County Circuit Court judge issued a warrant for Morganroth’s arrest in late April, she has yet to make a court appearance in connection with that felony charge.
Writer CJ Baker contributed to this story.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Colom challenges Hyde-Smith to debates, calls her ‘chicken’
description: Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, challenges Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to participate in three debates before the November election on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026 in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom said Tuesday he accepted invitations from two TV stations to debate and challenged Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to join him.
Flanked by a staffer in an inflatable chicken outfit, Colom told reporters he sent Hyde-Smith’s campaign an invitation to debate before the Nov. 3 general election. In a letter sent to the Republican’s campaign, Colom asked her to respond by Friday. 
“She’s chicken!” Colom said of Hyde-Smith at the press conference. 
Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, said in a statement that “losing candidates always want to debate about debates” and that there was “no point in debating someone so out of touch with Mississippi that he advocates for the sex change surgeries for children.” 
“Mississippians are not confused about this race,” Monssen said. “Cindy Hyde-Smith has spent years delivering real results and defending our values. Scott Colom is bankrolled by billionaire George Soros, ActBlue, and the Southern Poverty Law Center, and he is beholden to their far-left agenda.”
Monssen’s statement about children refers to a letter Colom, a district attorney in northern Mississippi, signed in 2021 where he condemned the criminalization of gender-affirming care and said families of trans youth should not be prosecuted.

Colom has said that he has never supported gender-affirming surgeries for children and that he does not believe trans athletes should compete in women’s’ sports.
If Hyde-Smith doesn’t agree to debate Colom, it’s unclear if the TV stations would proceed with Colom talking about his platform. It’s also unclear if Ty Pinkins, an independent candidate, was invited to participate in the debate. 
Hyde-Smith participated in a 2018 debate during a special election runoff with opponent Mike Espy. She did not debate Espy two years later when she ran for her first full six-year term, and it appears she doesn’t plan to debate this year. 
Hyde-Smith has a long history of not doing off-the-cuff events or open town hall meetings and rarely does interviews with the media. Some constituents have complained about a lack of access to her or response from her.
Last year, Mississippi Today tried to interview Hyde-Smith at the Capitol to ask her about budget cuts President Donald Trump’s administration was making and how they would impact her home state and about Mississippi’s infamous welfare scandal. 
When asked if she had time to answer a few questions, she curtly responded, “No.” 
After the Washington trip, Mississippi Today emailed her spokesperson asking if she was satisfied with the investigation into the federal welfare scandal that has rocked Mississippi’s politics and caused several people to plead guilty to federal crimes.
Her office did not respond to the question, which made her the only member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation to either not respond to the question or not grant Mississippi Today an interview. 
Colom, Hyde-Smith and Pinkins will compete in the general election on Nov. 3. The last day citizens can register to vote is Oct. 9.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Ferguson launches council to boost WA’s commercial space industry
description: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson hopes the state’s space entrepreneurs can pilot their industry to infinity and beyond. To that end, Ferguson signed an executive order Monday night launching the 23-person Washington Space Council. Its mission is to come up with bold ideas to propel Washington’s commercial space industry to new heights — and possibly development[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson hopes the state’s space entrepreneurs can pilot their industry to infinity and beyond.
To that end, Ferguson signed an executive order Monday night launching the 23-person Washington Space Council. Its mission is to come up with bold ideas to propel Washington’s commercial space industry to new heights — and possibly development of a launch facility somewhere in the state.
“Washington has deep roots in the space industry,” Ferguson said in a release issued Tuesday. “But the industry moves at an incredible pace. To remain a national leader, we cannot be complacent. My council will help us innovate and adapt as this sector rapidly grows.”
Ferguson signed the executive order at the Museum of Flight in Seattle at an event to kick-off  Seattle Space Week.
Washington is home to more than 90 space companies employing more than 13,000 workers, according to the governor’s office. Collectively, these businesses generate about $4.6 billion in annual economic activity and $1.6 billion in annual payroll. Approximately two-thirds of the world’s operational satellites are built in Washington, the press release noted.
The state’s ties to space exploration are deep. For example, Boeing workers in Kent built the lunar roving vehicles used on the moon during the Apollo missions in the 1970s. 
More recently, several Washington firms contributed critical components for the Artemis II mission in which a crew of four astronauts traveled around the far side of the moon and back to Earth.
Members of the Washington Space Council include Michael Edmonds, senior vice president of Blue Origin, the company founded by Jeff Bezos and Cornelia Rosu, senior director with SpaceX, the firm created by Elon Musk. This week, a SpaceX Starship reached orbit and deployed Starlink satellites before returning. Starlink, a SpaceX subsidiary, is headquartered in Redmond.
Philip Johnston, co-founder and CEO of Starcloud, which envisions establishing data centers in space, and Colin Doughlan, co-founder and CEO of Gravitics, which designs and makes space structures including orbital carriers, are serving on it, as well. 
And there are representatives from aerospace labor unions, the University of Washington and Washington State University, as well as state lawmakers and elected city officials.
This group is tasked with assessing workforce development and research needs as well as identifying barriers and opportunities for growth. It also will evaluate requirements for a Washington-based commercial launch site and other space-related infrastructure.
“It is going to elevate the industry,” said Kelly Maloney, founder and CEO of Pacific Aerospace Launch and Spaceport, who is on the council. 
“We have a diverse council made up of gig players and leaders of startups and they have their ideas on how to make Washington state more friendly to the space industry,” Maloney said in an interview Tuesday.
The group will compile its findings and recommendations into advisory reports for Ferguson but there is no time frame for delivery of the first report. The state Department of Commerce will provide staff to the council.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Dionne would use ‘bully pulpit’ to press for more local aid
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: Elizabeth Dionne appeared on GBH Radio on Tuesday and detailed how she sees the state Treasury addressing "affordability via local aid."
text:
IF SHE IS ELECTED treasurer, Elizabeth Dionne would be “the voice for local aid” on Beacon Hill and would champion it “in the same way that Diana DiZoglio has raised the profile of the audit,” Dionne said Tuesday.
The Republican angling to unseat Democrat Deborah Goldberg in November appeared on GBH Radio on Tuesday and detailed how she sees the state Treasury addressing “affordability via local aid.”
“The reason that the treasurer has a voice here is because of the Lottery. The Lottery is the fourth-largest single source of state revenue and the single-largest source of local aid. Now, the treasurer has significant power. … She doesn’t appropriate, and that is true,” Dionne, a former corporate attorney who served 10 years in Belmont town government, said. She added, “But what I do have is a bully pulpit and a bullhorn.”
Invoking the Democratic state auditor, she added, “And in the same way that Diana DiZoglio has raised the profile of the audit, I would have the ability to raise the profile of local aid.”
Traditional Lottery revenue makes up part of the unrestricted general government aid the state provides to its 351 cities and towns, and online Lottery revenues fund child care grants. The current budget provides $1.363 billion in so-called UGGA, along with local education funding and more. An October 2025 report from the Massachusetts Municipal Association said that, when adjusted for inflation, UGGA funding has fallen 25 percent since 2010.
Dionne said she is “not even necessarily talking about increasing Lottery revenues, because we already have the highest per capita spending on lottery in the nation.” So to give more Lottery money back to communities without increasing overall revenues, the Lottery would have to pay out less to winners, co-host Jim Braude stated.
“No, actually, what I’m saying is because of the Lottery, I want to argue that the state needs to take more of the rest of the budget and return it to local aid,” Dionne said. “So I am not arguing change of payouts.”
The Mass. Lottery generated $5.904 billion in fiscal year 2026 revenue, down about $59 million or 1 percent from a year before, and turned an estimated profit of $1.045 billion for use as local aid, $22 million than the prior year. Players won an estimated $4.379 billion during fiscal 2026, which featured a 50-year record high prize payout percentage of 74.19 percent. Administrative costs totaled an estimated 2.4 percent of overall revenues.
This year’s state budget provided about $7.65 billion in state Chapter 70 aid that is used to augment property taxes and fund local schools. The school aid is one of the biggest single pots of money in the annual state budget.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill looks to expand housing production on state land
description: The state will expand a program that saw NJ Transit sell land for development, this time with the aim of keeping ownership while producing units.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill said the state will expand a program that saw NJ Transit sell land for development, this time with the aim of keeping ownership while producing units. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey will expand a program intended to leverage public land for the creation of affordable housing, raising its goals to nearly 43,000 new units over the coming decades.
The plan, announced in a report released Tuesday, calls for the state to examine 2,300 acres of state property for the creation of affordable housing.
“We’re doubling the number of new homes on state land. We’re investing tens of millions in affordable and workforce housing, and we’re getting shovels in the ground faster,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, said at the Governor’s Conference on Housing and Economic Development in Atlantic City Tuesday.
The program, which the report says could see between 37,200 and 42,800 new homes developed on state property, is an expansion of a 2024 program in which the Economic Development Authority purchased NJ Transit properties for development with the goal of remitting some proceeds from their sale or lease back to the transportation agency.
NJ Transit’s program was expected to generate $1.9 billion for the agency over three decades, while roughly 800 acres of its property were expected to host up to 20,000 housing units.
An inventory of state property across New Jersey’s government found an additional 2,300 acres that might be suitable for housing development, according to the report. The program at present includes a mixed-use development near Metropark Station in Woodbridge.
“The Governor’s announcement provides a much-needed, whole-of-government approach to addressing New Jersey’s housing crisis,” said Adam Gordon, executive director of the Fair Share Housing Center, which monitors compliance with housing laws. “We look forward to working with Governor Sherrill and her administration to turn that vision into lasting results.”
New Jersey’s housing shortage is dire, and the Housing Governing Council, which drafted the report, has previously said the Garden State would need to add as many as 406,500 new units over the next decades to meet demand.
A report released Tuesday by the Pew Charitable Trusts found 28% of poverty in New Jersey could be attributed to high housing costs.
Alex Horowitz, project director of Pew’s housing policy initiative, said expanding housing supply in New Jersey could put downward pressure on rents, as expanded supply did in Austin and Minneapolis, which have seen historic housing booms and a decrease in inflation-adjusted rents.
“Housing costs can push families into poverty even when their paychecks are growing. Building more homes helps bring rents down, leaving families with more money for the basics and helping lift people out of poverty,” Horowitz said.

title: US Supreme Court allows Trump to resume deportations outside immigrants’ home countries
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday granted, for now, the Trump administration’s request to continue rapid third-country deportation of immigrants to countries not their own. The decision will allow the Trump administration to carry out its aggressive deportation method of quickly removing immigrants to one of the countries — some with human rights concerns — the administration that has agreements with to take third-country removals from the United States. The high court will hear oral arguments in December, and directed the parties to answer several questions including if the district court has jurisdiction over the issue, if the lower court can deliver classwide relief and whether the Trump administration's rapid third-country removal policy is lawful. Tuesday’s order will remain in effect until the justices reach a decision in the case.The three liberal justices, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, noted they would have denied the emergency request.The lower court’s order did not bar third-country removals, but prevented the deportation from occurring unless adequate time was given for a noncitizen to verify that they would not face harm in the third country.Third-country removals are when a noncitizen is deported from the U.S. to a nation other than that person’s home country. It occurs when the home country of a person with a removal order from the U.S. does not accept the person’s repatriation. A district court and appeals court found that immigrants must have an opportunity to challenge their removal to a country where they do not have citizenship if they fear for their safety or if they might be returned to their home country where they could experience harm.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Citizens Research Council outlines impacts of Mop Up Michigan initiative
description: As absentee ballots make their way to voters, Michigan residents this election season are faced with another question beyond just candidates running for various offices.  Among the final questions on the ballot is Proposal 2, also known as the Mop Up Michigan Initiative. The committee backing the ballot effort, Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, […]
text:
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics submitted its signatures in Lansing to make the November 2026 ballot. May 27, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. As absentee ballots make their way to voters, Michigan residents this election season are faced with another question beyond just candidates running for various offices. 
Among the final questions on the ballot is Proposal 2, also known as the Mop Up Michigan Initiative. The committee backing the ballot effort, Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, says the proposal would help hold politicians accountable to the people rather than corporations by banning government contractors and regulated utility companies from making political contributions to candidates for state and local office.
On Tuesday, members of the Citizens Research Council of Michigan, a nonpartisan, nonprofit public affairs research firm focused on providing factual information about state and local government, released a report breaking down what the proposal does, how it could affect the state’s political environment and potential challenges the proposal would face, if it is approved by voters.
Speaking with reporters, Research Associate Karley Abramson explained that the proposal addresses three key issues by amending the Michigan Campaign Finance Act. It would require “paid for by” disclosures on certain political ads distributed on the internet; expand donor and spending disclosure for certain types of political ads; and would restrict certain campaign contributions from regulated utilities, government contractors and their principals.
If enacted, a three-fourths vote from the Michigan House and Senate would be needed in order to amend the law. Abramson also noted that the proposal includes a severability clause, meaning that if any part of the proposal is found unconstitutional, the unaffected pieces would remain in effect. 
DTE Energy Headquarters in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)
Potential impact
The proposal’s opponents argue that the effort impinges on free speech, with Abramson telling reporters the proposal will likely face challenges over its restrictions on government contractors’ and utility companies’ political donations.
In Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in 2010 that political spending is considered speech, and that the only permissible justification for most restrictions would be to prevent quid pro quo corruption.
“Generally the public favors stricter controls on money in politics, but this is an area where there aren’t a lot of more robust laws because of the high bar that SCOTUS has set for restricting political speech,” Abramson said. “So there’s only so much that any state can do to really tackle this issue under the current framework.”
As such, the proposal limits its scope to a few specific targets Abramson said, before explaining its first, closing loopholes in campaign finance disclosure loopholes. 
Michigan’s existing law doesn’t explicitly require internet ads to include a disclosure of who pays for them, Abramson explained, noting that the proposal tweaks the language to try and address that. 
The proposal also aims to ensure issue ads that effectively function as campaign ads are required to disclose their donors, Abramson said, emphasizing that changes should not impact true issue-centered ads.
“Ultimately, this will lead to more transparency about the spending and the donors,” Abramson said. 
She noted that the disclosure requirements could deter some groups from running political ads. There could also be some additional cost to both the groups and the state to make sure they comply with the law, Abramson said.
While Abramson raised concerns that some language within the proposal could restrict disclosure requirements to a 100-day window ahead of the general election, she told reporters this is something that could be a potentially easy fix.
Constitutional questions
Looking at the restrictions on political spending, the proposal focuses on two groups: state and local contractors with more than $250,000 in annual contracts, and rate-regulated gas and electric utilities. Owners with a 5% or higher stake in the utility or the contractor, board members, individuals in the executive suite and their family members, lobbyists and groups controlled by these individuals would also be barred from making political contributions.
There would be an 18-month implementation period for the ban on contractor donations. If a contractor knowingly and willingly makes a donation prohibited by the proposal, the contract can be canceled and the contractor will be banned from receiving contracts for a year. However, there is a 30-day window where an unlawful contribution can be returned.
As far as the impacts, Abramson noted that this change would affect thousands of contracts valued at $250,000 or more at the state level and could come with a high cost to ensure the law is enforced.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The change could also deter contractors from wanting to do business with the government, Abramson said, creating a smaller pool of contractors. 
As far as utilities, it’s hard to know the total amount of contributions that will be impacted, Abramson said, noting that utility companies give a lot of money as campaign contributions. 
However, the proposal does not bar utilities from shifting that money into outside spending independent from political campaigns.
“Even if the political influence is affecting the regulatory process, campaign contributions are only one part of the political spending,” Abramson said, noting that utilities could just spend their money on ads.
Additionally, while Michigan residents have raised frustration with poor energy reliability and high energy bills, demanding better accountability from their electrical providers, the economic reality is that utility performance and energy rates are working in opposite directions, Abramson said.
The report also notes that regulatory capture, where agencies intended to protect the public are dominated by the groups they are tasked with overseeing, can occur with or without political contributions.
Looking at the potential for a constitutional challenge, Abramson noted that restrictions on political contributions must be closely drawn.
While the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit has upheld restrictions on federal contractors making political contributions, Abramson said the ban included in the ballot proposal is broader, and could see a challenge on those grounds.
In order for the ban on utility contributions to survive a constitutional challenge, proponents would have to articulate a way in which the energy utility industry holds a particularly high risk for quid pro quo behavior and why this risk applies to utilities and not other industries impacted by government action, Abramson explained.
Even if the court finds that there is a quid pro quo risk, the proposal could still be subject to narrowing, Abramson said.
Ultimately, the report concludes that Proposal 2 could bring additional disclosure requirements and new restrictions on political contributions, but the extent of its impact would depend in part on how the law is implemented and whether its provisions withstand legal challenges.

title: Congressional watchdog says Trump administration can’t defy lawmakers to revoke $810M
text: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration must spend the $810 million that it said last week it planned to cancel, according to a report released Tuesday by the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office. The congressional watchdog’s decision contends the White House budget office doesn’t hold the ability to claw back that funding without approval from Congress. “Any withholding of appropriated funds beyond their date of expiration, regardless of size, subverts both the constitutional process for enacting federal law and Congress’s constitutional power of the purse,” wrote GAO General Counsel Edda Emmanuelli Perez.Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought disagreed with the decision, though he wrote in a social media post it was not “a surprise.”“GAO has become hyper partisan and Congress recently attempted to cut their spending because of it,” Vought wrote. “GAO changed its long-time opinion on this very issue from the 1970s when they specifically noted the tool was available to the president. They make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.”‘Pocket rescission’A federal law known as the Impoundment Control Act allows the White House to ask Congress to cancel funding that lawmakers previously approved and the president signed into law.  Lawmakers have 45 days after the rescission request is sent to decide whether they want to approve it in full or modify the proposal. Congress declining to take any action means lawmakers have rejected the plans and the administration must spend the money. A request sent during the last 45 days of the federal fiscal year, which ends on Sept. 30, is known as a pocket rescission. The Trump administration believes that sending a rescissions request during that timeframe allows it to cancel the funding regardless of whether lawmakers sign off on the plan. The GAO has disagreed with that opinion before and reiterated it Tuesday in its five-page decision.“The Constitution vests in Congress the power of the purse, and Congress did not cede this important power through the ICA,” Perez wrote.  “Instead, the terms of the ICA are strictly limited,” she added. “The ICA permits only the temporary withholding of budget authority and provides that unless Congress rescinds the amounts at issue, they must be made available for obligation. The President cannot rely on the authority in the ICA to withhold amounts from obligation, while simultaneously disregarding the ICA’s limitations.”Refugee aid programsThe rescissions request the Trump administration sent Congress on Friday proposed lawmakers cancel funding for several line items, including refugee assistance programs at the Department of Health and Human Services, a Treasury Department program that provided “debt forgiveness to foreign countries that make climate change-related investments for coral reefs and tropical forests” and a grant program at the Minority Business Development Agency.The administration submitted its first pocket rescissions request in August 2025 and cancelled $4.9 billion without congressional action. That came a few months after the White House budget office successfully worked with Republican lawmakers to rescind $9 billion in funding for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and certain foreign aid accounts.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser sues to stop ICE detention center in Hudson
description: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser sued the federal government on Tuesday in an effort to stop or delay the opening of a new immigration detention facility in Hudson, alleging that the agencies in charge failed to perform a statutorily-required environmental review or provide information to the public before finalizing the plan. The lawsuit is very […]
text:
Protesters demonstrate against Immigration and Customs Enforcement outside the empty Hudson Correctional Center on Sept. 13, 2025. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser sued the federal government on Tuesday in an effort to stop or delay the opening of a new immigration detention facility in Hudson, alleging that the agencies in charge failed to perform a statutorily-required environmental review or provide information to the public before finalizing the plan.
The lawsuit is very similar to one filed last week by two advocacy organizations over concerns that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement ignored requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act before entering into a contract with The GEO Group to open and operate the new detention center. The state also alleges that the agencies violated the Administrative Procedure Act and the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Weiser’s office wants a judge to cancel the contract and stop any ongoing preparations for the detention center’s opening until the Trump administration completes the required analysis.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Neither DHS nor ICE engaged in the required public review process involving the necessary analysis of potential environmental impacts from any of the construction, renovation or operation of this facility,” Weiser said Tuesday. He called the lack of transparency by the federal government “stunning.”
Weiser, a Democrat, is running for governor and has led or joined dozens of lawsuits challenging actions by the Trump administration over the last two years.
“Even though this proposed facility would nearly double the town’s population, the federal government is ignoring the basic legal requirement to determine what effects its actions could have on nearby residents and the surrounding environment,” he said.
GEO secured a contract with ICE earlier this year to reopen a shuttered 1,250-bed prison in Hudson as an immigration detention center, dubbed Big Horn. The company currently operates the Aurora immigration facility, which has been the subject of numerous complaints about living conditions, medical neglect and public health concerns.
“We know how Coloradans, including me, are concerned about the opening of another immigration detention facility carrying out what I’ve said before is an often illegal and inhumane mass deportation policy,” Weiser said, noting that his office has received thousands of complaints about the Aurora facility.
NEPA, the federal environmental law, requires agencies to compile an environmental impact statement, complete an environmental assessment or seek a valid exemption from environmental review before major actions like construction. The Department of Homeland Security has done none of that, and the lawsuit contends that both development and operation of a new detention facility would stress the town’s water infrastructure, worsen air pollution and endanger nearby protected wildlife. A mule deer migration corridor is half a mile from the site, and a protected habitat in the Box Elder Creek is about one mile away.
Hudson’s recent Water Supply Master Plan, for example, recommends expanding the drinking water treatment plant and opening another well if the facility reopened and reached capacity. The lawsuit also notes that when it operated the site as a private prison, GEO violated wastewater pretreatment requirements, which have become more strict in the years since.
“There is no indication in the public record that Defendants considered the water resource impacts of their decision prior to entering into a contract to renovate and operate the facility,” the lawsuit reads.
Homeland Security has previously completed environmental reviews for new immigration detention centers pursuant to NEPA, including for sites run by private contractors. Because the department has not explained its change in position for the Big Horn project, state lawyers argue it violated the Administrative Procedures Act. Additionally, the lawsuit alleges that the agencies violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by not ensuring the facility is “appropriate” for immigration detention. Its previous use as a private prison does not automatically make it suitable for immigration detention.
“This has been a shuttered facility for quite some time,” he said. “It can’t just be picked up and put into use without going through the required reviews. They are there for a reason.”
Weiser said it will be up to a judge whether to merge the two similar lawsuits.
The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new lawsuit.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont is losing the people who keep us alive
description:
The state can regulate healthcare prices, but it can't stop people from leaving.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont is losing the people who keep us alive.
text:
This commentary is by Matt Swenson, the founder of Omnidex Solutions, an independent research and strategic analysis company. He lives in Vermont.
Vermont’s healthcare debate has spent years arguing about prices. I think the scarier question is simpler: Can you actually get care when you need it? For me, that’s not some abstract policy question. It’s personal. 
I moved to Vermont partly for its reputation for good medical care, after a rough career in environmental toxicology that left me with permanent injuries and health problems to manage. Vermont doctors have done right by me. The physicians themselves are good; what’s gone downhill is the system around them, especially primary care inside the big hospital networks. I eventually switched to direct primary care, and it’s been a relief. I can actually get seen, and it feels like medicine again instead of fighting an institution. 
That’s why the current contraction worries me. The University of Vermont Health network just announced changes affecting 199 positions, with 55 new or restructured positions being created. Dartmouth Health cut 124 positions and eliminated hundreds of vacant positions at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and its southern clinics. Even UVM Health’s own leadership acknowledges that the system is financially strained while patients struggle to afford and access care. 
This isn’t just one bad round of layoffs. Vermont’s physician census found only 529 primary care doctors practicing in 2024, down from 569 in 2022 and 634 in 2004. Health Commissioner Rick Hildebrant has acknowledged that the state hasn’t done enough to reverse that trend. The state’s own health assessments point to familiar problems: burnout, paperwork, compensation and even difficulty finding housing when doctors relocate here. Rural Vermont has it worse than Chittenden County.
That should change how we think about health policy. The Green Mountain Care Board has regulated hospital budgets since 2013, and now Vermont is moving toward reference-based pricing to rein in commercial hospital costs. Fine — affordability matters. But price can’t be the only thing we measure. 
Vermont needs an access-to-care dashboard alongside all that financial regulation. Show us specialty wait times, delayed surgeries, emergency room boarding, transfer delays, canceled procedures and how many practices are actually taking new patients. You can make healthcare cheaper on paper while making it harder to actually get. That’s not a win.

READ MORE

Hospital administration needs the same hard look. Every dollar spent on administration, consultants and communications staff ought to be examined openly, especially when Vermont is losing the people who actually treat patients. The question is not whether every administrative position is unnecessary. The question is whether the system is directing enough of its resources toward patient care and access. 
Compare that with education spending. Vermont recently put roughly $100 million in one-time funding to soften the education property tax increase, even while spending near the top of the country per pupil as enrollment continues to fall. Shuffling general fund money around can hide a tax increase for a year. It doesn’t fix what’s broken. 
Gov. Phil Scott is pushing school restructuring again, but we’ve covered much of this ground before. Act 46 and predecessor laws helped drive a consolidation process in which 206 districts in 185 towns ultimately formed 50 new union school districts. After a decade of restructuring, Vermont is still arguing about consolidation, declining enrollment and costs. 
Scott reminds me of Mr. Rogers sometimes — soft-spoken, always looking for the nice way to say things, never wanting to pick a fight if he can avoid one. That’s a fine way to run a neighborhood. It is not a strategy for a workforce crisis. You don’t fix a shrinking physician pipeline or a hollowed-out rural health system simply by being agreeable at the negotiating table. Being liked has kept Scott popular for years, but popularity isn’t the same thing as confronting difficult structural problems. At some point, the nice-guy approach has to give way to naming the problem and pushing back on the institutions making it worse. 
For the doctors we’re trying to recruit, taxes stack up alongside housing, pay, workload and whether there is real opportunity here. The same problem applies to single-payer generally. Changing who writes the check doesn’t make more doctors. A new financing system doesn’t build an operating room. An insurance card doesn’t mean much when nobody is taking new patients and the specialist can’t see you for six months. 
Here’s the other half nobody wants to say out loud: None of this gets paid for by wishing for the Vermont of 40 years ago. We’re not going to tax our way to a healthy system on top of an economy that isn’t growing. If Vermont wants the revenue to rebuild capacity, it needs a real future-tech economy — not hopes and vibes. 
That means competing for data centers and the tax base that can accompany them instead of watching investment land across the border. It also means bringing serious artificial intelligence into our hospitals — not as a gimmick or a substitute for physicians, but as technology that can assist diagnostics, triage and administrative work. Used intelligently, technology should take weight off clinicians and free the providers we already have to spend more time treating patients. 
Vermont can regulate its way toward lower prices. It cannot regulate its way to more doctors, more capacity or more economic growth. Those things have to be built. 
I sold my Vermont property years ago and have rented ever since, partly because I want a way out if the state keeps heading in this direction. I suspect plenty of other people are making the same calculation. And I understand why young Vermonters leave. 
If I were young today, looking at the housing, the taxes and healthcare getting harder to reach every year, I wouldn’t walk out of this state. 
I’d run.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. Supreme Court agrees to address whether those serving life for felony murder can seek parole
description: Felony murder is a charge brought when a victim dies during the commission of another felony, even if the perpetrator never intended or planned to kill.
text:
The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania chamber at the Capitol in Harrisburg. (Photo from the Unified Judicial System of Pennsylvania)The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has agreed to address the question of whether their March decision finding mandatory life sentences for second-degree murder unconstitutional should apply in the cases of those already sentenced.
On Tuesday, the court granted an appeal petition filed on behalf of Jerome Coffey by the Abolitionist Law Center in April. Coffey was convicted in 1994, and has spent more than 30 years incarcerated. The Abolitionist Law Center claims no physical evidence linked him to the crime, that a key prosecution witness recanted a statement, and that his trial counsel provided ineffective assistance.
Second degree murder, also known as felony murder, is a charge brought when a victim dies during the commission of another felony, even if the perpetrator never intended or planned to kill. Until recently, the charge came with a mandatory life without parole sentence, regardless of the circumstances of the crime or whether the person sentenced was directly responsible for the victim’s death.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That changed after a landmark ruling in a case called Commonwealth v. Derek Lee. In 2014, Lee took part in an armed home robbery in Pittsburgh. While he was in a different room, his accomplice shot and killed the victim, Leonard Butler.
Lee was charged with second-degree murder, and sentenced to life in prison without parole. The Abolitionist Law Center represented him in an appeal that wound its way to the state Supreme Court, which found requiring a life sentence in all cases of felony murder violated the state constitution’s ban on cruel punishments.
While the court ruling found mandatory life sentences for second-degree murder unconstitutional, it did not address the question of what’s known as “retroactivity,” meaning whether it should apply to those who were sentenced before their decision.
Instead, the justices  gave the state legislature 120 days to pass legislation addressing the question, but lawmakers were unable to come to a consensus by the July deadline.
Who’s serving felony murder sentences in Pennsylvania prisons?

More than 1,100 people are currently serving mandatory life without parole sentences for felony murder. More than half of them are older than 50 years old and a majority have spent over 25 years in prison.
“Mr. Coffey is one of more than 1,100 people who are waiting for the promise of the Supreme Court’s decision in Lee to be fulfilled,” Bret Grote, legal director at the Abolitionist Law Center, said in a statement. “We are determined to ensure that Mr. Coffey and all those who are serving this unconstitutional sentence have their rights vindicated and are provided the opportunity to return to their communities.”
While Coffey’s appeal petition requested the court review his sentence and the circumstances of his conviction, the court only agreed to take up the question of whether old second-degree murder sentences before the mandatory life sentence was struck down can stand.
In September, attorneys asked the high court to exercise its rarely used “King’s Bench power” which allows the justices to bypass lower courts and take up questions of immediate public importance.
According to Quinn Cozzens, an attorney with the Abolitionist Law Center, the decision to take up Coffey’s appeal appears to signal the court is taking another avenue to decide the same question, though it may end up taking slightly longer.
“Ordinarily, the briefing and argument would be done in the next six months or so,” Cozzens said, though he emphasized timelines in court cases can vary widely. “Then it’s however long the court wants to take after that” to issue a decision.
“We’re pretty happy that the court recognizes the urgency of this situation ,” he added.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC 12 detour opens after storm damage leaves hundreds waiting for Outer Banks ferry
description: Dare County officials declared a state of emergency for Hatteras Island on Saturday, barring visitors and non-resident property owners from entering.
text:
Most of the North Carolina's ferries have been in service for 25 years or more, and it's estimated that in the next 20 years most of the fleet will reach the end of its “useful life.” (Photo: NCDOT) An approximately three-mile line of vehicles stretched through Rodanthe on Monday as hundreds of vacationers sought to board the emergency ferry leaving Hatteras Island on the North Carolina coast. 
Last week’s nor’easter — a coastal storm with the strongest winds blowing from the northeast — severely damaged portions of North Carolina Highway 12, the only road connecting Hatteras Island and the northern Outer Banks. 
Dare County officials declared a state of emergency for Hatteras Island on Saturday, barring visitors and non-resident property owners from entering. 
The North Carolina Department of Transportation announced it would open a temporary one-way gravel detour for NC 12 at the Pea Island Visitor Center on Wednesday, allowing northbound traffic through a single-lane stretch. For visitors who expected to leave Saturday, that meant days of uncertainty over food, medications, and responsibilities back on the mainland. 
On Sunday, NCDOT began operating the emergency ferry route between Rodanthe and Stumpy Point. Three vessels with room for about 25 to 30 vehicles, depending on the cars and trucks that are onboard, are transporting passengers back to the mainland. 
The fleet can move about 250 vehicles in 24 hours, according to Dare County, and the crossing itself takes about two hours. 
“There’s definitely just an air of frustration, and it’s understandable,” Island Free Press editor-in-chief Joy Crist said. “That frustration grows the closer you get to the front of the line, because that’s where people have been waiting 24 hours.”
Based on Hatteras Island, Crist has been reporting on the storm and its aftermath. She covered a Virginia couple who invited hundreds of other stranded visitors and local residents to their wedding on Saturday. 
Crist has also shared updates on the recovery process and talked to visitors waiting for the ferry.
“The silver lining of that is that there’s been so many local volunteers and organizations that have just been going up there and grilling out and handing out hot dogs and snacks and water,” she said. 
‘We’re dumping money into the ocean’: Outer Banks seeks state help for long-term NC 12 fix

Crist says closures of NC 12 happen fairly frequently — rain closed the highway earlier this summer, and overwash also happens occasionally. But the nor’easter did enough structural damage to the road to prompt the state to bring in emergency ferry service between Stumpy Point and Rodanthe, the first time that’s happened since underwater erosion caused the Bonner Bridge to close in December 2013. 
The agency announced Tuesday morning that NC 12 would open at 3 in the afternoon, a day ahead of schedule. 
The temporary one-way gravel detour will initially only carry northbound traffic, allowing visitors to leave the island. After the northbound traffic congestion subsides, southbound traffic will open, with alternating directions of one-way traffic. 
Dare County officials will announce when southbound traffic opens. There is no timeline for when the road will open for southbound traffic or when visitor access will be restored. 
NCDOT did not respond to requests for comment.
U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy, whose district covers the Outer Banks, said his office has been in touch with county and state officials about NC 12.
“While traffic is backed up and preventing many from traveling, it is vitally important that everyone work together during this critical time,” Murphy said on social media. “Emergency services must be able to reach those in need of medical attention quickly.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Eric Schmitt’s Hawks-Hawkeyes blunder and the politician he’s become
description: On Monday, Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt showed he still knows how old-fashioned politics works. He helped pass a college sports bill he spent months negotiating with Democrats Maria Cantwell and Chris Coons. They disagreed over major provisions, compromised and produced legislation that passed the Senate 77-22. A day later, a different Eric Schmitt showed up.[...]
text:
Eric Schmitt answers questions during a press conference after filing to run in the Missouri Senate primaries on Feb. 22, 2022 in Jefferson City (Madeline Carter/Missouri Independent).On Monday, Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt showed he still knows how old-fashioned politics works.
He helped pass a college sports bill he spent months negotiating with Democrats Maria Cantwell and Chris Coons. They disagreed over major provisions, compromised and produced legislation that passed the Senate 77-22.
A day later, a different Eric Schmitt showed up.
At a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, Schmitt accused former special counsel Jack Smith of perjury. His case rested on what he portrayed as evidence that Smith had attended an Atlanta Hawks game and used the trip to meet with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis.
He came armed with a poster board of texts he said contradicted Smith’s testimony.
“I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” Schmitt told him.
Schmitt called Smith a “villain” and proclaimed he’d go down in history as “a total dirtbag.”
There was one problem. Actually, two.
The texts on Schmitt’s poster didn’t mention Atlanta.
And Smith didn’t attend an Atlanta Hawks game. He attended an Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar said Schmitt, working from clearly wrong information, owed Smith an apology.
Instead, he went on The Charlie Kirk Show.
“It was the only NBA game going on at that time in Atlanta,” Schmitt said. “He claimed later that he was at another game.”
Then came his defense:
“Here’s the thing — my job is to ask the questions.”
Just asking questions.
Missouri’s Eric Schmitt bungles accusation against former special counsel Jack Smith in heated hearing

Schmitt won a seat in the state legislature in 2008 with 55% of the vote in the middle-class suburbs along Interstate 44. Over eight years, he built a conservative record that regularly involved working with Democrats.
He stood with Democratic Gov. Jay Nixon to push insurance coverage for autism treatment. He helped legalize CBD oil for people with intractable epilepsy, drawing on his son Stephen’s experience. After Ferguson, he championed legislation limiting municipalities’ reliance on traffic fines and court fees.
The AFL-CIO endorsed him in 2012.
In a 2014 video tour of the Missouri Senate chamber in Jefferson City, Schmitt said lawmakers’ different backgrounds and opinions made respect important, and that the room reminded him of the need for “a more civil tone in politics, now more than ever.”
Schmitt said he had been inspired by Jack Kemp to “take that conservative message outside of the Republican echo chamber.”
The goal wasn’t merely to beat people who disagreed with you. It was to persuade them.
That changed as Schmitt headed toward the U.S. Senate.
In the year before Schmitt launched his Senate campaign, he used “radical left,” “tyranny” or “tyrant” on Twitter twice, according to an analysis by St. Louis Magazine. In the following year, he used them more than 100 times.
Last year, he said opponents of the president’s mass deportation program had nothing left but “the Marxist playbook, which is political violence,” and that federal money was flowing to a “radical ecosystem” of nonprofit groups and activists “working to undermine our civilization.”
At the National Conservatism Conference last year, he rejected the idea of America as a creed anyone can adopt. He waved off the notion that its meaning lies in a Statue of Liberty poem or in “all men are created equal.” America, he said, is a people and a homeland handed down by particular ancestors, and he described Americans as descendants of Europe’s Christian pilgrims.
Then he drew the line. Of the “radicals” he accused of tearing down statues and mocking American history, he said: “America doesn’t belong to them — it belongs to us.”
Schmitt has an explanation. He says he hasn’t fundamentally changed; the country and the left did.
Perhaps. But that doesn’t explain the transformation in his rhetoric or political style.
Republicans who knew him offered another explanation.
In 2022, former U.S. Sen. John Danforth, who was backing an independent candidate against Schmitt, told The Kansas City Star that prominent Republicans he wouldn’t name had called to reassure him about Schmitt’s candidacy.
“All of them said the same thing to me,” Danforth recalled. “Which was, in fact, some of them used the same word to describe Eric, and the word was malleable.”
“And one of them said during this campaign he’s been playacting,” Danforth said. “In other words, he doesn’t really believe it.”
The two Eric Schmitts on display this week sandwich a report by Axios that he has grown close to Vice President JD Vance, who has faced similar questions about his own ideological transformation. Schmitt is seen as a top prospect to be Vance’s running mate if Vance seeks the presidency in 2028.
Monday showed the Eric Schmitt that Missouri used to see much more often: ambitious and partisan, but willing to treat people on the other side as negotiating partners.
Tuesday showed the Eric Schmitt who has increasingly defined his national political career: certain of his enemies’ bad faith, eager to escalate and willing to reach the verdict before all the facts are in.
Whether that Schmitt represents a genuine conversion or, as one Republican told John Danforth, some measure of “playacting” is something only Schmitt can know.
Either way, that’s the Eric Schmitt now stepping onto a bigger national stage.
