title: Pingree, Russell to meet on debate stage once, days before November election
description: Incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree and Republican nominee Ron Russell will meet once on the debate stage this election, days before voters head to the polls on Nov. 3..  The debate will be jointly hosted by Maine Public, NewsCenter Maine and the Portland Press Herald on Oct. 29 in Portland.  The race is a […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine questions witnesses during a field hearing in Biddeford on Aug. 17, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree and Republican nominee Ron Russell will meet once on the debate stage this election, days before voters head to the polls on Nov. 3.. 
The debate will be jointly hosted by Maine Public, NewsCenter Maine and the Portland Press Herald on Oct. 29 in Portland. 
The race is a rematch for Maine’s 1st Congressional District, after Russell in 2024 lost by over 20% of votes to Pingree, who has held the seat since 2009. 
Russell said this week that he agreed to the debate, but felt the date is too close to Election Day.
“That, in my mind, is a tremendous disservice to the voters in Maine,” Russell said. “The fact that we cannot do a debate for a federal office until five days before the election ends, 24 days after voting has already begun, that is criminal, in my opinion.” 
In a statement, the congresswoman said her campaign told the news organizations that she was available any time after Oct. 5, and they returned with the final date.  
“I look forward to taking the debate stage, speaking directly to Maine voters about the issues that matter most and making clear what’s at stake in this election,” Pingree said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: Secretary of State
description: The Nov. 3 general election features a race between the elected clerk of New Mexico’s second-largest county and her opponent, a longtime rancher and nurse practitioner, who are vying to lead the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office.
text:
Republican Ramona Goolsby, left, is running against Doña Ana County Clerk Amanda López Askin, a Democrat, in the Nov. 3, 2026, race for New Mexico secretary of state. (Courtesy photos)
The Nov. 3 general election features a race between the elected clerk of New Mexico’s second-largest county and her opponent, a longtime rancher and nurse practitioner, who are vying to lead the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office. 
Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver, a Democrat, is nearing the end of her second and final four-term term leading the office, which oversees elections; collects and maintains business records; and enforces campaign finance and lobbyist requirements, among other duties. 
The candidates seeking to replace her are Democrat Amanda López Askin, who currently serves as Doña Ana county clerk, and Republican Ramona Goolsby, who came to New Mexico in 2019 after retiring as a nurse practitioner and rancher. 
The next secretary of state will take over an office that Toulouse Oliver has repeatedly said is inadequately funded for its wide remit of election-related and other responsibilities. 
The upcoming legislative session will also determine whether New Mexico will become an early primary state for the upcoming Democratic presidential primary, which raises the prospect of the Secretary of State’s Office being required to oversee two elections in a short period of time. That includes the November 2027 local election as well as the Democratic presidential primary just four months later in February 2028. 
Source NM spoke to both candidates about their visions for the office, which pays an annual salary of $144,714. Their answers below have been edited for clarity and concision. 
Ramona Goolsby
 
Ramona Goolsby, Republican secretary of state candidate (Courtesy photo)
Republican Ramona Goolsby said she has spent much of her retirement in New Mexico pushing for transparency and accountability in New Mexico institutions. That includes aiding conservative efforts to repeal via referendum a number of election-related laws the Legislature passed in 2023. 
That failed referendum effort related to House Bill 4, aka the New Mexico Voting Rights Act, which established a permanent mail-in voter lists and established pathways for ex-felons to cast ballots, and Senate Bill 180, which provided means to secure sensitive voter data and made other changes. 
“I think the more transparency you have, the more trust there is,” Goolsby told Source NM. 
She said her interest in becoming secretary of state intensified after the 2020 election, which occurred amid lockdowns due to the COVID-19 pandemic. She ran unopposed in the Republican primary this June. 
“We saw things that were made, policy, during COVID that just didn’t add up,” she said. “We started searching for answers, and that’s how that’s how it started.”
What makes you the most qualified to be the next Secretary of State?
Leadership ability. Owning a ranch and having to hire and fire and make business decisions that my livelihood depends on; I have leadership ability. I was an office manager. I have been a supervisor at a hospital, dealing with employees and scheduling, and I also was in the military, and mission focus is extremely important. The secretary of state’s job is an executive level leadership office. It’s not running for county clerk. It’s completely different. It is about executive level leadership, which I have had a lot of experience with.
If elected, what new initiatives would you implement?
There’s several new things I would like to see implemented.
I would really like to make sure that we support the county clerks in their efforts to do voter roll maintenance. I honestly believe, and I’ve talked with county clerks, that they all want to do a great job, but they don’t have all of the tools they need to get that done. 
The other thing I would like to do is establish a transparency portal similar to the Sunshine Portal, where we take all of the information that is frequently requested via IPRA (the Inspection of Public Records Act), and we put that in a searchable database in a portal.
One of the most important jobs, I think, of the Secretary of State’s office, and we don’t focus enough on it, is the business aspect. Whether businesses survive in New Mexico and whether people can have jobs is an everyday consideration for people, not elections. So I think we really need to address our business environment. I have had people ask me even basic things like, ‘When you get in office, will someone answer the phone?’
How would you evaluate the performance of incumbent Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver?
I think she’s tried to do a good job. We have to make sure that everybody on the ballot is eligible, and that we all follow rules. We have problems with election finance. The CFIS system has so many glitches, and people have problems filing. People aren’t held accountable to their filings. I would say I think she tries, but it’s not been as robust an effort as I would have hoped.
If elected, how will you react if President Donald Trump’s administration tries to gain access to the state’s voter rolls again?
We will follow all laws. That is my answer to that. The reason he’s wanting access is that they make sure everyone’s eligible. Well, that’s our job. That’s the state’s job. Statutorily, that is what the secretary of state’s job is, and if I do my job, there should be no reason for anyone to have to get the voter rolls for that reason, right?
We have the ability to have the most pristine voter rolls in the nation. We just have not used all that we have available to make that happen. Maybe one of these days we can sit down and I can show you the analysis that I have done, and it does show that we definitely need to work on the voter rolls.
What steps will you take to strengthen the security of the New Mexico mail-in ballot system? 
I believe, honestly, that we should look at making sure the verification system that’s already in place is utilized, and then review and see if anything stronger is needed. It’s just following the law. That’s all we need to do right now.
Do you think SOS requirements should be loosened to make it easier for candidates in minor parties like the New Mexico Forward Party to get on the ballot?
I think everyone should have very similar access requirements. I believe that it’s not just the Forward Party that we’re talking about here. It is the declined-to-states that have significantly increased, and that is a huge bloc. If someone who is independent wants to represent their community, I don’t think they should have a harder time than anybody else. It’s about fair access.
Do you believe the SOS adequately maintains its voter rolls to prevent unqualified people from casting ballots? 
I think there are some deficits in the voter roll maintenance. 
I could give numbers and names, but I don’t feel that it’s an appropriate time to do that. But I’ll just say that I have access to information that shows there are some people who have moved out of state permanently and are still voting in New Mexico.
What election-related legislation would you support in next year’s session?
Voter ID is something that’s very important to the public. We need to make sure that our vulnerable populations, people that don’t have access to certain documents, that they are able to register and to vote. I think if there’s anyone that needs help, if there are elderly that need help, then I think it is our job, because ID is not just about voting. ID is also about getting your medicine at the pharmacy or checking in for traveling. If you don’t have valid ID, it hinders your life.
Let that be a debate. I mean, let them talk about it on the floor, not hide it in committee or kill it before it even comes to committee. 
You’ve said the 2020 presidential election suffered widespread ‘issues’ but that you don’t believe President Joe Biden rigged or stole the election. Do you believe Biden was the lawfully elected president? 
He was voted and put in. He was certified by the Congress. I wasn’t out protesting or anything like that. He was certified and he served. If someone asked who the president was, I told them it was Joe Biden because that’s who was in the White House, right?
Amanda López Askin
Amanda López Askin, Democratic secretary of state candidate. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
The Doña Ana County Commission appointed Democrat Amanda López Askin to lead the county clerk’s office following a scandal in 2018. Five days later, early voting began for the 2018 general election, which featured the closely watched 2nd Congressional District race between Democrat Xochitl Torres Small and Republican Yvette Herrell. 
“I started with that election. The second election I ran was in 2019, which was the first ranked-choice voting and first consolidated election in my community,” López Askin told Source NM. “And then my third and my fourth was a pandemic primary and a pandemic general. So, my experience speaks for itself.”
The Democratic nominee hails from southern New Mexico, and defeated Santa Fe County Clerk Katharine E. Clark in the June primary election, which she highlights as a geographic achievement of sorts. 
“Southern New Mexico candidates do not have the media hub here. We don’t have the donor bases in Santa Fe, and we don’t have the population of Bernalillo County,” she said. “I was told it could not happen. I could not win. It was really, really hard, but worth it.”
What makes you the most qualified to be the next Secretary of State?
Certainly connected to my current opponent, I’m the more qualified candidate. I’ve run 13 elections in the second-most-populous county, in arguably the most contentious elections in our state. 
If elected, what new initiatives would you implement?
I’m fortunate to have been in front and center for many of the pro-voting bills that have passed, and that would be the only Native American Voting Rights Act, which I participated in support of, which was embedded in the Voting Rights Act of New Mexico. So we did a lot of huge sweeping improvements. Those really do have to be really followed through and implemented well. I think that will be one of the things that is really important. 
The first challenge that I will have —and is not something that’s flashy — I have to do everything I can to support a larger budget for the Secretary of State’s Office. They have been historically underfunded. The clerks across the state in every county continue to run elections well despite being underfunded. And so our Legislature, I’m hoping for a lot of support, especially if we add an early primary in 2028.
How would you evaluate the performance of incumbent Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver?
Maggie has been in elections for 20-plus years. She’s been working in public service for longer than that, and so the sweeping kind of really pro-voter bills she’s been front and center for, and I’ve followed her lead. She has made substantial change and progress, as well as helped get New Mexico to be ranked No. 1 at one point in election administration in our country. She’s held national leadership positions. She’s well respected in every space that I go, connected to elections. So I am very proud to have her support, and I’m very proud to follow her.
If elected, how will you react if President Donald Trump’s administration tries to gain access to the state’s voter rolls again?
I think the great news about the executive orders that continue to come through is that they’re unconstitutional. I have had some disappointments with the Supreme Court, as I think many have, but I also think that there is a momentum of intolerance of things that are unconstitutional, and that is really kind of coupled with a lot of general frustrations with the current state of our country. So far, we are holding the line, and I would say there’s strength in numbers between the county clerks, other secretaries of state across the country, the attorney generals. We will be all hands on deck to fight an overreach by the federal government.
What steps will you take to strengthen the security of the New Mexico mail-in ballot system? 
Mail-in voting is extremely secure. To strengthen it would be to make sure we are fully funded, and then we have staff in each of our county clerks’ offices as well as the Secretary of State’s Office to make sure those checks and balances are continually supported. One of the things that I hear often is, ‘Oh, we need to increase the security of elections.’ And I say, ‘Well, staffing is also security. People are security.’ 
Do you think SOS requirements should be loosened to make it easier for candidates in minor parties like the New Mexico Forward Party to get on the ballot?
I don’t know what that magical number is. But I definitely want to have those conversations. 
Do you believe the SOS adequately maintains its voter rolls to prevent unqualified people from casting ballots? 
My team and the teams across the state and every county clerk’s office work diligently to remove those who appear in obituaries, any vital statistics information we have from the state, and we also count on family members and those who are aware of a potential death and those who actually move to remove their names from our voter rolls. Additionally, consider this: At noon today our voter rolls could be 100% accurate. At 12:01, something could have made them inaccurate, which means there’s always going to be folks that have moved or, unfortunately, have passed. 
We just got to do everything we can to pull those names and remove them, and that is a process. I would venture to say that I am comfortable where our voter rolls are, and that we will continue to follow the law.
What election-related legislation would you support in next year’s session?
I do think that the majority of the session is going to be talking about the timeline for an early primary. We have a local election in November (2027) and then we have recounts, runoffs that could potentially happen at the beginning of December. 
And early voting would, in theory, start Jan. 15. And so, clerks always rise to the occasion, and our communities collectively should be very proud of the work that they do. But it is going to be a lot of work, and we will need a lot of support.
Are there any federal election-related initiatives you support? 
I cannot think of one that’s been offered, something that has made a splash, that I can think of that I do currently.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina high schoolers say schools feel safer, but experts want more school resource officers
description: Dr. Ellen Essick said there is a lot of good news about mental health in the 2025 North Carolina High School Youth Risk Behavior Survey. But there are areas that clearly need attention when it comes to the overall well-being of North Carolina’s young people. Essick, section chief for N.C. Healthy Schools in the state […]
text:
Members of the Governor's Advisory Council on Student Safety and Well-Being plan to advocate for more permanent funding for school resource officers in 2027. (Photo: Getty Images) Dr. Ellen Essick said there is a lot of good news about mental health in the 2025 North Carolina High School Youth Risk Behavior Survey. But there are areas that clearly need attention when it comes to the overall well-being of North Carolina’s young people.
Dr. Ellen Essick, Section Chief for NC Healthy Schools, Department of Public Instruction (Photo: NCDPI)
Essick, section chief for N.C. Healthy Schools in the state Department of Public Instruction, presented her findings Monday before the N.C. Governor’s Advisory Council for Student Safety and Well-Being. Governor Josh Stein created the council in April 2025 to promote safe, welcoming, and inclusive schools while improving student physical, social, and emotional well-being.
Essick told the group that between 2023 and 2025, the survey saw a decrease in physical fighting at schools. And the percentage of students who missed school because they felt unsafe decreased from 14.6% in 2023 to 9.9% last year.
But the survey found sexual violence is a persistent problem.
Nearly 14% of female students and 6.6% of male high schoolers who responded to the anonymous survey said they experienced sexual violence.
“The percentage of students who said they experienced sexual violence was 10.1%, and it was pretty much even [for grades 9-12] across the board,” said Essick.
North Carolina high school students say they feel safer, according to the 2025 N.C. High School Youth Risk Behavior Survey. (Graphic: NCDPI)
The survey also asked about physical dating violence. Nearly 9% of all students, male and female, reported having experienced some form of dating violence in high school. Hispanic/Latino students (11.4%) and 11th graders (10.9%) experienced the highest rates of physical dating violence.
A question the state had not asked since 2021 delivered equally sobering results. About 30% of North Carolina high schoolers said they could get a loaded gun without their parents’ permission in less than 30 minutes. White students (38.8%) and male students (34.6%) reported the highest likelihood of being able to get a gun without adult permission, about the same as in 2021.
Districts seek recurring funds for SROs
To improve student safety, the advisory council will recommend an increase in school resource officers in 2027. The National Association of School Resource Officers recommends every school employ at least one SRO. In North Carolina, there are approximately 1,500 SROs, but over 2,500 public schools.  Existing SROs are also asking for additional training in dealing with juveniles, mental health challenges, and active assailants.
Advisory council members want a permanent state earmark for the SROs, replacing the current grant funding system that can fluctuate in each state budget.
Mark McHugh, the director of safety for Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, said the grant system is not working.
“With 185 schools, I got one SRO in the grant process last year,” said McHugh. “That’s our biggest hurdle right now.”
McHugh said that a dedicated SRO can cost upwards of $140,000 a year in salary and benefits, depending on the municipality a school district is working with. Even with a $40,000 grant from the state, districts struggle to come up with funds to pay the balance.
Emma Hodson, an attorney for Pitt County Schools, agreed more state funding is needed. “I do think local governments are pretty heavily subsidizing these programs, probably far in excess of what the state is contributing,” said Hodson. “We appreciate the recommendation on funding and would like to see the state do a little more if that is a goal.”
The N.C. Center for Safer Schools awarded $32.9 million to 198 public school units in 2025-26 through its school resource officer grant program. But demand eclipsed the grant money that was available, according to Karen Fairley, the center’s executive director.
North Carolina high schoolers show improvements in mental health 

North Carolina’s public schools requested more than $86.8 million in school safety grant funding for 2024-2025. The advisory council is recommending legislators increase school safety grants to $50 million annually and make the funding recurring.
The council is slated to meet again in November before releasing its final report to the General Assembly just ahead of the 2027 legislative session. Members are hopeful their recommendations will gain a little more attention next year as the state will have hundreds of millions of dollars in new funding from a settlement with the tech giant Meta.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Judge: Fired teacher offered students extra credit in return for cash donations
description: An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account. State records indicate that beginning in 2022, Stephanie Mullaley worked as a paraeducator and then as a full-time, long-term substitute high school teacher for the Clinton Community School District.  She was fired […]
text:
Clinton High School. (Photo via Google Earth) An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account.
State records indicate that beginning in 2022, Stephanie Mullaley worked as a paraeducator and then as a full-time, long-term substitute high school teacher for the Clinton Community School District.  She was fired on May 29, 2026, for allegedly violating the district’s ethics policy.
According to the findings of Administrative Law Judge Duane Golden, who presided over a recent hearing on Mullaley’s request for unemployment benefits, Mullaley shared her “personal educational goals” with her students during the 2025-26 school year.
In the spring of 2026, Mullaley allegedly told her students that she had set up a GoFundMe account to help pay for her education, adding that if they made cash donations to her account they could earn extra credit toward their grade in her class.
Some of the students in the class did contribute funds to the GoFundMe account, according to Golden’s findings. As Golden described it, the district then discovered Mullaley was “using her position as a teacher to pressure students to donate funds” and fired her.
Golden denied Mullaley’s request for unemployment benefits, ruling that her conduct amounted to job-related misconduct and demonstrated a “willful or wanton disregard” of her employer’s interests, rendering her ineligible for benefits.
Mullaley, Golden concluded, had “promised high school students in her class that they would receive extra credit toward their grade in her class if they donated to her GoFundMe account.  Students felt pressured to donate money to her personal GoFundMe page.”
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Mullaley for comment.
Online records show that a Stephanie Mullaley of Clinton launched a GoFundMe account earlier this year to pay for what she described as “a unique opportunity to travel to Ecuador” with her husband in July 2026. Mullaley indicated on the GoFundMe page she would be “interpreting for a medical mission team (and) helping bridge language barriers so that care and compassion can reach those who need it most,” and that her husband would be “assisting the team in any way he can.”
Donations, she wrote, would be used to pay for “transportation, including flights, buses, and boats, food and hotel accommodations.”
The account had a fundraising goal of $1,800 and netted $140 through six donations ranging from $5 to $50 before activity on the account was paused.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Battery energy storage to the rescue
description: Challenges for Maryland's electricity markets are many -- rising prices, surging demand, stalled projects -- but the answer is readily available in the form of grid-connected battery storage, writes Bruce Daggy, who said it works in other states and can work here.
text:
An electricity meter. (Photo by the Image Bank/Getty Stock)Maryland residents have multiple reasons to be concerned about the power grid. Energy costs are rising. Increasing demand is raising concerns about reliability. Marylanders are being told to accept new transmission lines and new gas pipelines. The state is even being told to keep operating polluting and costly coal-fired power plants to keep the grid stable. 
But what if there was an easier, cheaper option to solve some of these problems? It turns out there is. 
Grid-connected battery storage is addressing such problems currently in states like California, Texas, Arizona, and Nevada. In contrast, our regional grid, PJM Interconnection, has almost none — although it does have plans to start building battery storage. 
Looking at generation, battery storage can address a scheduled or unexpected supply disruption. No power plant runs all the time; batteries can plug a gap, at least for a few hours. Batteries also help address an often-cited challenge with renewable energy — that the sun sets and wind doesn’t always blow. In the same way batteries solve the intermittency problem, they help address peak demand. Their power can be discharged to the grid almost instantaneously when needed.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Batteries can also avoid or postpone the need for new transmission infrastructure. When demand is low, electricity can move down a transmission line to charge the batteries, getting it past the pinch point. This can help prevent a blackout or brownout later when demand rises.
When batteries are placed close to end users, they can again increase the reliability and quality of supply, provide backup power, and enable microgrids, such as the ones Montgomery County has built for its electric bus system.
In California, batteries enable the state to store excess solar power during the day and release it during the evening demand peak. In the last three years, this has cut in half the need to spin up expensive gas peaker plants, reducing both operating costs and emissions. The California grid has become more reliable as a result, with no alerts calling for voluntary conservation in the past three years. 
The picture is similar in Texas, where wind, solar, and batteries have stabilized the once dodgy grid. Texas may surpass California this year in energy storage. Battery storage is not some blue-state fixation; in fact, two-thirds of new battery storage in 2025 was in states won by President Trump. Battery storage is expanding rapidly across the country because it makes financial sense.
With all these benefits, you might wonder why Maryland doesn’t already have more battery storage connected to our grid. PJM had such a backlog in its interconnection queue that until recently, it wasn’t accepting new projects. 
Now there are three substantial battery storage projects under review by Maryland’s Public Service Commission for approval to be connected to our grid. A decision is expected from the Commission by Oct. 1. 
With the impacts of climate change intensifying and demand for electric power growing, it’s a critical moment for the state to take advantage of battery storage to stabilize our grid, help control costs and reduce harmful emissions. 
We shouldn’t wait any longer, but if there’s a silver lining to Maryland’s trailing other states, it’s that battery technology improved at the same time as costs have come down. Battery energy storage is now very affordable at grid scale and well positioned to make our lives better.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘If you can’t do it, I’ll do it’: Judge seeks to settle disputes in case of fatal shooting of border agent
description:
The hearing Monday was the first court proceeding in more than a year as Teresa Youngblut faces the possibility of the death penalty, if convicted.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘If you can’t do it, I’ll do it’: Judge seeks to settle disputes in case of fatal shooting of border agent.
text:
U.S. District Court Judge Christina Reiss speaks in Essex in Oct. 2021. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

BURLINGTON — A federal judge said she plans to advance the slow-moving case against a former Washington state resident accused of killing a U.S. Border Patrol agent in northern Vermont in January 2025.
Teresa Youngblut faces the possibility of the death penalty if convicted in the fatal shooting of David Maland that took place after a traffic stop on Interstate 91 in Coventry on Jan. 20, 2025. Maland, 44, of Newport, was the border patrol agent who pulled over the vehicle that Youngblut was driving.
The hearing Monday in federal court was the first proceeding in the case in a little more than a year. 
Judge Christina Reiss told the attorneys in the case she was worried that the discovery process, or the sharing of evidence collected by the government with the defense team, was not moving along as efficiently as she would like. 
“I am not willing to leave the discovery process unsupervised at this point,” Reiss said. 
The judge said she would set regular status hearings in the case moving forward to ensure that the process is advancing and any issues that may arise could be addressed in a quick fashion.
Reiss set the next hearing in the case for Nov. 23.

Theresa Youngblut appears at a hearing in U.S. District Court in Burlington on Tuesday, June 24, 2025. Sketch by Don Drake

The judge Monday also called on the parties to establish a schedule for the filing of pretrial motions.
“If you can’t do it, I’ll do it,” Reiss told the attorneys.
The hearing Monday that lasted roughly an hour also focused on the matter of electronic devices.
Reiss called on the government to come up with an inventory listing all of the electronic devices used by law enforcement that may have relevant information on them — including all work and personal devices. 
The defense team for Youngblut had raised concerns earlier this year that some of the devices may not have been preserved by the prosecution, and that data from those devices could be lost as time moves on, particularly personal devices used for work-related duties. 
Steve Barth, an attorney for Youngblut, told the judge Monday that he wasn’t asking at this point for the data on those devices. Instead, Barth said, he wanted to first see an inventory of how many devices with relevant information exist and whether any of them or the data stored on them may have already been lost.
Reiss told the prosecutors to develop that list and share it with the defense team. The list should include each device, who it belonged to, and what role that person played in the case, the judge said.
At one point during the hearing, Reiss asked Barth, “Have you gotten all the video evidence?”
“I don’t know,” Barth replied, adding, “I would say no.”
Dennis Robinson, one of four federal prosecutors in court Monday for the hearing, told the judge, “We have provided voluminous video evidence.” Robinson did not say how much video was turned over to the defense. He did add that he didn’t know of any other video evidence.
Robinson also said that the government would be producing another “tranche” of discovery evidence next month. 

READ MORE

Youngblut, 22, of Seattle, who was wounded in the deadly incident, was taken into custody days later on charges related to the shooting after being released from the hospital.
Felix Bauckholt, a German national known as Ophelia, was a passenger in the vehicle Youngbut was driving and was killed in the shootout. 
Prosecutors have stated in court filings that if they get a conviction, they will seek the death penalty for Youngblut. Vermont does not have the death penalty under state law, but this case is brought under federal law where the death penalty is permitted.
A defense filing earlier this year argued that evidence the defense has collected so far disputes a version of events from federal authorities about what led up to the deadly shootout.
That issue was not specifically raised during the hearing Monday. 
Youngblut and Bauckholt had been connected by law enforcement to a loosely linked group known as the Zizians.
The Zizians have ties to Bay Area communities in California known as rationalists, a movement of philosophically-minded people focused on logical reasoning and interested in raising alarms about the potential harm of artificial intelligence. Members of that group have been tied to six homicides across the country in recent years.
Youngblut, wearing bright orange prison clothing, did not speak during the hearing Monday and sat quietly between the three-member defense team.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Double digit increases in Rhode Island commercial health insurance premiums coming in 2027
description: Monthly health insurance costs are set to rise by double-digit percentages for the second consecutive year, though the sticker shock won’t be quite as sharp as last year. Commercial insurance rates for 2027, unveiled by Rhode Island Health Insurance Commissioner Cory King on Tuesday, are also lower than what insurers wanted, with King’s office cutting […]
text:
A fifth floor exam room in Rhode Island Hospital's Ambulatory Patient Center. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Monthly health insurance costs are set to rise by double-digit percentages for the second consecutive year, though the sticker shock won’t be quite as sharp as last year.
Commercial insurance rates for 2027, unveiled by Rhode Island Health Insurance Commissioner Cory King on Tuesday, are also lower than what insurers wanted, with King’s office cutting more than $86 million from what companies requested as part of the annual rate review process.
Little comfort to the combined total of 169,000 Rhode Islanders — roughly one-third of the state’s population — whose premiums will increase by 2.9% to 15.8%, depending on insurance plan and provider. 
“Rising health care costs continue to present a financial burden and barrier to care for too many Rhode Islanders,” King said in a statement. “The Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner is committed to working in collaboration with all stakeholders to make health care more affordable.” 
The smallest increase, 2.9%, is for the 36,685 small business employees whose employer buys plans from Blue Cross Blue Shield of Rhode Island. The largest, 15.8%, is for the 34,555 state health exchange participants who purchase plans from Neighborhood Health Plan of Rhode Island.
The push and pull between insurance companies grappling with their own rising expenses and Rhode Islanders already struggling to make ends meet has grown increasingly difficult for King’s office to navigate. Pricey prescription drugs and pressure to increase provider reimbursement rates to soothe staffing shortages have driven up insurers’ expenses. The precipitous drop in participation in the state health exchange in January, after enhanced federal discounts expired, also created riskier — and costlier — participant pools for insurers to cover.
Neighborhood and Blue Cross — the two commercial insurers that provide coverage to people who buy insurance through the state marketplace —  sought premium increases of 24.9% and 9.8%, respectively, for their combined 50,000 state health exchange participants.
King’s decision calls for more tempered increases: 15.8% for Neighborhood’s marketplace plan participants, and 4.9% for those with Blue Cross.
Spokespeople for Neighborhood and Blue Cross acknowledged requests for comment Tuesday but did not immediately provide responses. 
Attorney General Peter Neronha, whose office urged King to reject the marketplace plan hikes altogether, blasted the insurers for “inaction” leading to unaffordable consumer costs.
“Rhode Islanders deserve better than a system that consistently requires consumers to shoulder the financial burden of policy shortcomings while insurers enjoy their ever-increasing profits,” Neronha said in a statement Tuesday. “Rhode Islanders deserve innovative strategies to provide accessible, affordable, and high-quality care for all, and the only way to achieve this is through bold, collaborative reform of our health care system.” 
The state health insurance commissioner is required by law to guard the solvency of insurance companies, which in turn affects payments to hospitals and health care providers. But the commissioner also cannot legally approve a requested rate hike that is not in the public’s interest.  
With these competing mandates in mind, King’s office capped the administrative portion of insurers’ proposed rate increases at the rate of inflation. Last year, King vetoed any increases tied to administrative costs.
Also helping bring down insurers’ costs — and in turn, premiums for their plan participants — the termination of a state health assessment fee originally tucked into the fiscal 2026 budget. 
Lawmakers agreed to nix the $4 per-person monthly premium charge, which began in January, amid concerns that it violated federal rules under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
King’s review also cut away from cost increases for employees of large and small businesses who pay for insurance through their workplaces.
The 40,744 small business plan participants will see monthly costs rise by 3.8% on average, versus the 8.7% average increase sought by Blue Cross, Neighborhood and United Healthcare.
For the 68,548 large business plan participants, rates will rise by 9.5% on average rather than the requested 15.5%. Insurers who cover large business plans include BlueCross, UnitedHealth, Harvard Pilgrim, Aetna and Cigna.  
The Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner only reviews rates for fully insured plans, or those in which the insurer assumes financial risk for medical costs. That means the office does not inspect rates for the approximately 65% of Rhode Islanders with self-funded insurance — employer-sponsored plans in which the business, not the insurer, pays workers’ health care claims directly. 
Regulators in neighboring states have approved similar rate hikes for individual and small group market plans. In Massachusetts, the merged market increase was 10.8%, while Connecticut authorized an average 11.3% hike for individual plans and 14% for the small group market, according to King’s office. Comparisons for large business plans were not available since many states do not review plans sold to large employers.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Former SC Supreme Court Justice returns to private law practice
description: Former state Supreme Court Justice John Few has re-entered private practice after 26 years on the bench, opening his own law firm.
text:
Then-Justice John Few, right, talks with people in the lobby of the Statehouse in Columbia, S.C. on Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026. He dropped his bid for re-election to the state Supreme Court a month later. (Photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Former state Supreme Court Justice John Few has officially re-entered private practice after 26 years on the bench, opening his own law firm in Columbia.
“There will be no soft landing for me, as I plan to return to the active practice of law with the same energy and enthusiasm that has defined my career as a judge and justice,” Few said in a statement.
The 63-year-old stepped down from the state’s high court at the end of July, when his 10-year term ended.
Few faced a rare challenge to hold onto his seat — a contest even more unusual because his three opponents included former House Speaker Jay Lucas. Few dropped his bid for re-election in March, a day before the Legislature was scheduled to vote, after it became clear he would not win.
His withdrawal forced the race to be canceled and the application process to start over.
Five judges are seeking the open seat. Public hearings before a legislative screening panel are scheduled to begin Nov. 16. An election in the General Assembly is tentatively set for March 3.
Few could have remained on the bench until he was replaced. But he opted not to stay beyond his official term.
Five judges so far file to run for SC Supreme Court seat

Few said he will focus on litigating complex cases, taking his clients back into the same South Carolina courtrooms in which he presided as a judge.
Born in Anderson and brought up in Greenwood, Few practiced law in Greenville before becoming a circuit court trial judge in 2000. He was chief judge of the Court of Appeals before winning a seat on the state Supreme Court in 2016.
He earned a bachelor’s degree from Duke University and law degree from the University of South Carolina.
He has been a part-time law professor since 2005.

The fuel, often called red or dyed diesel, is a tax-exempt version of diesel used by tractors, bulldozers, portable generators and other off-road equipment. State Rep. Jim Pressel, R-Rolling Prairie, sent a […]
text:
Dozens of Indiana lawmakers have asked Gov. Mike Braun to help farmers with high diesel taxes during the national spike on prices. (Getty Images)Lawmakers want Hoosier farmers to be allowed to use off-road diesel fuel in their semi-trucks this harvest season to offset record diesel prices.
The fuel, often called red or dyed diesel, is a tax-exempt version of diesel used by tractors, bulldozers, portable generators and other off-road equipment.
State Rep. Jim Pressel, R-Rolling Prairie, sent a letter to Gov. Mike Braun Tuesday asking that farmers be permitted to use the untaxed fuel in their semi-trucks instead of highway diesel through January 1, as diesel hit a record average of $6.92 in September.
Fifty-one other lawmakers signed onto the letter, including House Speaker Todd Houston.
“Our offices have heard ongoing concerns from farmers across Indiana about diesel fuel costs and the impact those expenses are having on agricultural operations,” Pressel wrote.
Braun suspended Indiana’s gasoline use tax in April using an obscure law allowing the governor to declare an energy emergency. He lifted the state’s gasoline excise tax the following month using the same emergency powers, with the unofficial blessing of state lawmakers.
Both taxes remain suspended through at least Oct. 6. Braun is expected to reveal as early as this week whether he will renew the suspension for another month.
But he has not suspended the tax on diesel, which is 64 cents a gallon plus additional sales taxes. He has said most diesel users are companies and not regular Hoosiers motorists.
The average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline still hit $3.85 in Indiana Tuesday, despite the roughly 60-cents-per-gallon savings, according to AAA. The average cost of diesel: $6.86.
Pressel said farmers have been “forced to bear the full price of diesel while also dealing with the pressures that prompted the state’s emergency action” while taxes were suspended for other motorists.
“If Indiana can provide temporary relief to motorists during a period of high fuel prices,” he wrote, “we should ensure farmers who play a vital role to our state are not left behind.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Charitable entities one step closer to accepting electronic payments for raffle tickets
description: Nonprofit leaders say that state law needs to be modernized to allow charitable gaming operations to accept electronic payments for small games of chance, such as raffles.
text:
Paul Kennedy, with Good Intent Hose Company No. 1, speaks at a Sept. 28 press conference on charitable gaming while Jennifer Jarvis, with Lancaster Snow Angels, looks on. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)When the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the bingo nights, cookouts and block parties used to fundraise for volunteer firefighter gear and equipment, the Good Intent Hose Company No. 1 turned to online raffles to close the gap. 
“What our supporters helped us accomplish over these past six years is absolutely incredible. Because of their support, we were able to purchase three pieces of fire apparatus … we were able to purchase 20 sets of structural turnout gear without the use of grants,” said Paul Kennedy, the organization’s president emeritus and public information officer. “We contributed to countless other community needs.” 
A summer without church picnics? How COVID-19 is taking its toll on a NEPA tradition

That changed in August, when Good Intent suspended online raffles after learning it violated state law. 
“We found ourselves caught between modern fundraising technology and rules written for a very different time … but, very quickly, we realized this wasn’t just about Good Intent,” he continued. 
Just a month earlier, Lancaster Snow Angels returned $20,000 collected through electronic sales for the same reason. 
“That was support people had already offered. The funds we could have raised would have helped us build emergency reserves for older adults and veterans, and better prepare our team for disaster response,” group founder Jennifer Jarvis told a Harrisburg crowd on Monday. “When we obtained our licensing, the rules about accepting these payments were not made clear to us. We would never have knowingly broken the law.” 
The organization, led by Jarvis, offers free snow removal for seniors, veterans and people with disabilities alongside other disaster response services. 
Sen. Devlin Robinson (R-Allegheny) said such payments were temporarily allowed during lockdowns, but the underlying law never changed. 
Sen. Devlin Robinson (R-Allegheny) says charitable gaming needs to be modernized to allow for electronic payments at a press conference on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Pennsylvania’s antiquated law is still built around the way people paid for these things decades ago. Today, people use their phones and cards to pay for just about everything,” Robinson added. “Most of us don’t walk around with pockets full of cash anymore, and we probably don’t write checks either. So why should we expect the organizations that serve our communities to rely on cash and checks when they are trying to raise money?”
His bill, Senate Bill 416, would allow fire companies, churches, veterans groups and other nonprofits to accept online payments for small games of chance, such as raffles or pull-tab games. It passed the Senate unanimously last summer, but didn’t have a House committee vote until Tuesday.
It again advanced unanimously, though Gaming Oversight Committee Chair Patrick Harkins (D-Erie) said he hoped future budgets would consider direct financial support to the state’s thousands of fire departments.
The bill now moves to the House floor for further consideration.

title: Judge rejects Anchorage state House candidate’s challenge to August state primary result
description: Anchorage Superior Court Judge David Nesbett has rejected speedy consideration of a lawsuit seeking to put a disqualified Anchorage state House candidate on November’s election ballot. That means Republican Sarah Short will not be a listed candidate for House District 13 and Democratic candidate Lisa Keller will run unopposed. Short’s case remains open but i[...]
text:
Sarah Short, Republican candidate for House District 13, is seen in a photo from 2025. (Sarah Short photo)Anchorage Superior Court Judge David Nesbett has rejected speedy consideration of a lawsuit seeking to put a disqualified Anchorage state House candidate on November’s election ballot.
That means Republican Sarah Short will not be a listed candidate for House District 13 and Democratic candidate Lisa Keller will run unopposed.
Short’s case remains open but is largely moot. Nesbett’s decision, issued Sept. 18, was followed a week later by rejections of various temporary restraining orders and emergency hearings requested by Short. 
The first absentee ballots were sent to voters on Sept. 18, and Short had requested actions that could have disrupted mailings. 
“I should’ve been given a chance for arbitration or something like that,” she said.
The Division rejected Short after she failed to submit a Public Official Financial Disclosure form ahead of the June 1 candidate filing deadline. 
That form, required by state law, is supposed to list all of a candidate’s income and financial links in the previous year. The disclosure is intended to prevent corruption.
Short said she completed the form but technical problems prevented her from submitting the signature page. 
“Yes, I did file late, but that’s because I waited on the stupid Republican Party,” she said. “I won’t do that again.”
The Division of Elections does not immediately disqualify candidates who file blank or incomplete forms, but it does disqualify those who file no form at all. 
Short has said that she attempted to file the form on time but was stymied by technical errors. 
The Alaska Public Offices Commission, which collects the forms, informed Short on June 2 that it had not received her form. 
She said she submitted the relevant documents on June 3 but was still rejected. State law allows 30 days for revisions, and Short said she should have been covered under that law.
Short didn’t file a legal challenge until September, and Nesbett concluded that her delay in filing was an important factor in determining whether or not to take up her legal challenge before the first general election ballots were sent to voters.
“Plaintiff’s asserted urgency … stems from her own delay, not from any new circumstance that would justify shortening the court’s normal briefing schedule,” he wrote.
Short had previously said that she would register as a write-in candidate if her lawsuit failed; as of Monday, the Division of Elections did not list her as a write-in option. 
In Alaska, only registered write-ins are allowed to participate in general elections.
By phone, Short said she has the paperwork but has not yet turned it in. 
“I don’t believe I’m going to win, but I believe the problems that I’m having with APOC and the political parties, that’s the story,” she said. “We’re worried about ‘get out the vote,’ but I can’t even get on the ballot.”

text:
The deadline for voter registration before the November election is Monday, Oct. 5, 2026.(Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony) This coming Monday — Oct. 5 — is the last day for Kentuckians to register to vote ahead of the November general election. 
Registering can be completed online, via mail or by returning voter registration cards to your local County Clerk’s office. As of August, the state has about 3.3 million registered voters. 
In order to vote next month, online registration must be completed on Monday by 4 p.m. local time. Mailed registrations must be postmarked by Oct. 5. 
The general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3. The ballot will include local and statehouse races, as well as federal elections for the U.S. House and Senate. One constitutional amendment regarding governors’ pardon powers will be on the ballot. 
According to the Secretary of State’s Office, the qualifications for voters to register in in Kentucky are:

Be a U.S. citizen and a Kentucky resident for at least 28 days before the election. Non-U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals do not qualify.
Be at least 18 years old by the next general election. 
Cannot be a convicted felon. For some with an expungement, executive pardon or executive order, the right to vote may be restored. 
Cannot have been judged mentally incompetent in a court of law or have voting rights removed.
Cannot claim the right to vote outside Kentucky.

To request an absentee ballot or learn more information about voting in Kentucky, visit the online voter information portal.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma judge publicly reprimanded
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – The Oklahoma Supreme Court publicly reprimanded a Tulsa county judge, saying her conduct was “indefensible” and reflected a lack of impulse control and judgment. The state’s high court though did not order  Tulsa County District Judge Sharon Holmes to face removal proceedings as had been recommended by a state agency that investigated […]
text:
Pictured is the entrance to Oklahoma Supreme Court chamber in the Oklahoma Capitol. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – The Oklahoma Supreme Court publicly reprimanded a Tulsa county judge, saying her conduct was “indefensible” and reflected a lack of impulse control and judgment.
The state’s high court though did not order 
Tulsa County District Judge Sharon Holmes to face removal proceedings as had been recommended by a state agency that investigated the complaints, according to an order released Monday.
Holmes, 67, on Tuesday declined to comment.
Tulsa County District Judge Sharon Holmes (Photo provided by the Oklahoma Supreme Court Network)
Holmes was accused of having improper ex parte communications with jurors and a criminal defendant appearing before her without others present, which “created the appearance of impropriety, undermining the public’s confidence in the independence, integrity and impartiality of the judiciary,” the Supreme Court said.
On three occasions, she ignored sentencing guidelines and allowed defendants to enter programs for which they were not eligible, according to the Council on Judicial Complaints report.
In another instance, she yelled at a public defender and was observed as “very hostile and very nasty,” according to the Court.
A report by the Council on Judicial Complaints, a state agency that investigates complaints against judges, also included an incident where “Holmes left the bench and approached an agitated defendant with her fists raised as if she was going to fight him.”
“Judge Holmes’ behavior in these instances was undignified, and her conduct displayed a lack of temperament required of a judge,” the Oklahoma Supreme Court  said.
The Council report said Holmes failed to be candid and honest with investigators, and her testimony contradicted the evidence.
But while the allegations were serious, they do not establish that Holmes’ conduct was an excessive use of judicial authority, the court wrote.
The Council on Judicial Complaints had issued a non-binding recommendation that Holmes be brought before the Council on the Judiciary for removal proceedings.
Holmes, a former assistant district attorney, was first sworn into judicial office in 2015 and won reelections.
She was most recently elected unopposed for another term.

title: National group backing Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins puts $650,000 into Alaska campaign
description: A national organization has put $650,000 into an Alaska political group, saying it aims to boost the campaign of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. Alaska political experts say Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, stands a strong chance of winning the general election after finishing first in the primary election[...]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democratic former state House member, won the state's gubernatorial primary last month. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)A national organization has put $650,000 into an Alaska political group, saying it aims to boost the campaign of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.
Alaska political experts say Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, stands a strong chance of winning the general election after finishing first in the primary election in August. He faces a divided field of three Republicans who are likely to split the GOP vote in the general.
The Democratic Governors Association disclosed Saturday that it had contributed $650,000 to a newly formed Alaska independent spending group called “Forward Frontier.”
“Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is running a strong campaign focused on driving down costs, supporting Alaska schools, and bringing people together to get things done,” DGA spokesperson Johanna Warshaw said in an emailed statement Sunday to the Anchorage Press. “The DGA is proud to help ensure JKT is elected governor this November so he can deliver the change Alaskans are looking for.”
Kreiss-Tomkins, in an interview Sunday, said that campaign finance law bars him from coordinating with the DGA-aligned group and that he only learned about about the contribution Sunday. “We’ll see what they do,” he said.
The $650,000 represents a significant sum in Alaska’s gubernatorial race, given that most candidates leading up to the primary struggled to raise more than $1 million. In addition to Kreiss-Tomkins, the field includes former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, conservative activist Bernadette Wilson and former Attorney General Treg Taylor.
GOP groups have not disclosed similar national fundraising or spending in the gubernatorial race, though Republican-aligned political consultants from outside Alaska formed their own new independent spending group last week.
“Kodiak PAC” was registered by Casey Phillips, a Virginia-based consultant who describes himself as the “Carrot Top of political ads.” Kodiak PAC’s aim is to “support the election of a Republican governor in Alaska,” the group said in its state registration.
Phillips didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Monday. The Republican Governors Association, which has financially supported GOP candidates in past Alaska gubernatorial races, also didn’t respond to a request for comment.

name: Washington State Standard
title: PacifiCorp’s sale of Washington assets may not be in Utah’s public interest, experts say
description: Utah state watchdogs and advocates are skeptical of a move by a major regional utility to sell its assets in Washington.
text:
Transmission lines lead away from the coal-fired Intermountain Power Plant near Delta, Utah on Monday, Feb. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)As PacifiCorp readies to sell its Washington service area to Gem, an affiliate of Portland General Electric Company, Utah state watchdogs and advocates are skeptical, saying the deal in its current form may not be in the public interest.
The company has proposed to sell its Washington service area for approximately $1.9 billion. But before that, it needs the approval of the public service commissions in the states where it operates: Utah, California, Idaho, Oregon, Washington and Wyoming.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Operating PacifiCorp in six states with different policies has had its “share of difficulties,” Dick Garlish, president of Rocky Mountain Power said in a testimony to the Utah Public Service Commission in April. For example, other PacifiCorp states, excluding California, refuse to pay for costs associated with the Washington Climate Commitment Act, including making its natural gas Chehalis power plant compliant with the law.
“As a result, PacifiCorp has been forced to absorb approximately $45 million annually of the actual costs of providing power from the Chehalis plant,” he said. “This is unsustainable, and exacerbates the financial challenges PacifiCorp now faces.”
The company has been under extraordinary financial pressure in recent years, he said in his testimony. The company’s credit ratings and financial outlooks have been going down, according to different firms, stemming predominantly from wildfire liability issues and “adverse regulatory outcomes,” Garlish said.
That’s especially true in Utah, where Republican leaders have pushed the company to draft studies contemplating splitting the company into two systems, one serving blue states and another for red states with fossil-fuel focused energy strategies.
 Application is lacking

When news about the Washington assets sale broke in February, Utah House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, was enthusiastic.
“We want a divorce from the three states that don’t look like Utah,” he said then. “This is the first step forward, as I’ve had the conversations to talk with Rocky Mountain Power, they’re excited. This will be a great benefit to the citizens of the state, helping keep lower prices here in the state of Utah.”
However, different watchdogs and advocates, including the Utah Office of Consumer Services say that Rocky Mountain Power’s application is so far flawed and that the company failed to meet its burden of proof to show the sale would be in the public interest.
Garlish said the service area transfer would not harm Utah ratepayers. It would even be positive, he said, because PacifiCorp is expected to provide a $68.9 million rate credit to customers in Utah over three years, in addition to other benefits.
The sale, he said, also “improves PacifiCorp’s system load and resource balance, improves PacifiCorp’s financial position and helps manage its risk, and relieves PacifiCorp from the obligation to meet Washington’s climate laws.”
But, Leah Wellborn, a consultant speaking on behalf of Utah’ Office of Consumer Services, said in testimony before the public service commission in August that the company is only offering a short-term view of the sale’s long-term impact, and flaws in the company’s analysis led to an “overestimation of the benefits to Utah.”
Wildfire risks are driving up costs for Northwest utilities

A different economic analysis conducted by the office shows “net harm in the post-transition period to Utah,” Wellborn said. The Washington buyer is also getting the resources at a cost below market value.
“Any allocation of the gain on the sale to Washington or PacifiCorp should not be at the detriment of the remaining jurisdictions, given the negotiations on price were determined by (Portland General Electric) and PacifiCorp, and not the states facing increased costs due to the resource reallocation assumed and negotiated by the Company,” she said.
About $504.7 million of the $1.9 billion is the gain on the sale. PacifiCorp is proposing to retain 32% of that and share the remaining 68% with its customers. That would mean $68.9 million for Utah. However, for advocates that amount should go way up.
Because of the economic harms and risks of the sale, the office is recommending imposing several conditions to approve it, including additional rate credits of $106 million, which, with the $68 million proposed by PacifiCorp would make up a total of $175 million. They also want a commitment from the utility to reduce expenses and continued monitoring during the transition period, ensuring “risk of excess costs borne by shareholders, rather than customers.”
PacifiCorp hasn’t filed official replies to those comments. Simon Gutierrez, a spokesperson for the company said in an email on Friday “we welcome the opportunity to demonstrate the clear public benefit of this transaction through the Commission’s review process.”
 The risk of coal and natural gas

The Utah Division of Public Utilities hasn’t reached a definitive conclusion, but said in testimony the company’s paperwork lacks updated depreciation schedules, decommissioning costs, estimates of the remaining life of the power generation that PacifiCorp seeks to reallocate, as well as meaningful net present value or risk studies.
The sale would provide numerous benefits to Utah ratepayers and could help further Utah’s energy goals, Matt Pernichele, a Utility Technical Consultant for the Utah Division of Public Utilities, said in the August testimony. The full company’s net power costs would decrease if the sale is approved, and could allocate additional generation to Utah, which would lead to economic growth.
However, that would also represent risks to Utah, Pernichele said, as PacifiCorp operates many aging coal and natural gas power plants, as well as some wind farms. The company hasn’t released a depreciation study of its coal plants, which went into service between 1955 and 1983. But the last depreciation study, published in 2018, called for all of them to close and be replaced by 2042.
Despite that, the company “seems to have few plans to replace these plants,” Pernichele said.
“Due to increased demand, current lead times for combined cycle gas power plants are five to seven years. This leads to the strong possibility of having to replace at least 5.5 GW of dispatchable generation in the span of a decade or so,” he said. This would be expensive and likely require PacifiCorp to greatly increase its already large debt load.”
If those plants were to retire without replacements in place, market prices in the Utah, Idaho and Wyoming service area would probably increase, Pernichele said. Operating and maintaining thermal plants also becomes more expensive as they age. So, there should be a new depreciation and decommissioning study before making a final reallocation of the company’s assets.
Thermal generation also emits greenhouse gases and other pollutants, which represent substantial risks if there are any regulatory changes during their remaining operating life.
“Such regulations could impose costs from additional pollution control measures, impose restrictions on operating times or overall emissions that would make them less economical to run, or even cause them to shut down prematurely,” he said. “Under the Company’s proposal, Utah ratepayers would take an additional 8.1 percent of these risks along with an increased allocation.”
Wind farms, as a group, are also producing less energy than expected. Their cost has, however, stayed the same, making the power from these facilities more expensive than anticipated, so the agency is also recommending a thorough economic analysis of the plants.

description: Iowa Gov. text:
The Iowa State Capitol as seen Jan. 9, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds has called for special legislative session to take place Friday, Oct. 2, to amend the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction (MEGA) program and provide incentives for a steel mill project in Lee County.
Tuesday’s announcement comes one day after Reynolds and other Iowa Republican leaders joined President Donald Trump in the Oval Office as he announced plans for the company Mesabi Metallics to build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa.
The facility will be the largest steel plant in the United States, according to Trump, and will create 1,750 permanent jobs paying $49 per hour as well as 6,000 temporary construction jobs.
The facility is set to be operational by 2030, according to the White House, producing 7.5 million tons of steel per year in its first phase by processing iron ore from a Minnesota mine also owned by Mesabi Metallics.
While U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick said Monday that “I think this deal is done,” the governor’s office said in a statement, “the state of Iowa and Mesabi Metallics have executed a memorandum of understanding outlining the terms of the partnership” which will necessitate some action by the Iowa Legislature.
According to a news release from the governor’s office, the special session will make changes to the state’s Major Economic Growth Attraction program, the state’s incentive program focused on attracting large-scale development projects representing more than $1 billion in capital investment to the state. With the Mesabi Metallics project set to be a $15 billion investment, the news release said, “adjustments are needed to the MEGA program.”
“On Friday, the legislature will return to the Iowa State Capitol to advance the most consequential economic development opportunity ever for our state,” Reynolds said in a statement. “With reasonable and limited updates to an already-existing economic development program, we will accelerate major capital investment into our state, strengthen our economic trajectory, and shape the future of our state and region for generations.”
Lawmakers will convene to discuss legislation amending the MEGA program on Friday, Oct. 2, at 8:30 a.m., according to the news release. Details have not been shared about specific changes being made to the program.
Republicans hold a trifecta of control at the Iowa statehouse. Democratic legislative leaders say they want more information about the proposal — and about the steel mill project — but support bringing new employment opportunities and business to the state.
“Almost 10,000 Iowans have been laid off since the beginning of 2025, so today’s announcement of a special session to bring a new steel plant to Iowa is a welcomed step toward creating good-paying jobs and strengthening our economy,” House Minority Leader Brian Meyer said in a statement. “Iowa House Democrats are committed to making sure this is a good deal for Iowa taxpayers and working Iowans.”
Senate Minority Leader Janice Weiner said Senate Democrats “are ready to go to work for Iowans.”
“Ultimately, our goal Friday will be to ensure that any final deal is in taxpayers’ best interests,” Weiner said. “We still have a number of outstanding questions regarding this project, and I am hopeful that a deliberative process will deliver the answers Iowans need.”

title: Calculator allows individuals to see the fiscal effects in their areas if Amendment 3 passes
description: The constitutional amendment that would reduce non-school homestead property taxes is the biggest policy proposal on the 2026 statewide ballot. Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would lower the annual assessment growth cap from 10% to 5% for non-homestead properties such as […]
text:
Several public websites provide calculators for homestead property owners in Florida to plug into to determine what the reduction in property taxes would amount to if Amendment 3 passes. (Google Earth)The constitutional amendment that would reduce non-school homestead property taxes is the biggest policy proposal on the 2026 statewide ballot.
Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would lower the annual assessment growth cap from 10% to 5% for non-homestead properties such as commercial buildings and rental units, and would require people moving to Florida after Dec. 31 to wait 5 years of continuous residency before qualifying for the full increased exemption.
It would also reduce revenues collected by local governments for essential services, which has caused many locally elected officials up and down the state to oppose the measure.
Several public websites provide calculators for homestead property owners in Florida to plug into to determine what the reduction in property taxes would amount to.
Now a calculator prepared by the Florida Policy Institute allows Floridians to type in their area codes or select a county from a drop-down list to view the projected revenue losses for county and municipal operations, along with special districts. The website also allows individuals to search by a specific service or view statewide effects.
“We really hope this will be a one-stop shop and something easy to use where people can see how the amendment would impact the community,” said Sonia Lindell, director of communications and marketing for the Florida Policy Institute.
“There is still a lot of information that Floridians would need,” added Sadaf Knight, CEO of the institute.
“There is a lack of understanding to a certain degree about what our property taxes fund and how those impact all of us in our day-to-day life. And so, what we’re hoping with our calculator is to show that these are not just services that you might typically think of running the local government … but it’s also things like mosquito control …. What we wanted to illustrate is what property taxes fund and what’s at stake so it can become more real for people and understand what the other side of the ledger really is when it comes to Amendment 3’s impact.”
Although the site shows actual reductions in revenues to local governments if the measure is passed, other sites provide information regarding what homeowners’ personal reduction in property taxes would be if the proposal is approved by 60% of the voters in November.
When Gov. Ron DeSantis announced his property tax proposal in late May, the state simultaneously unveiled a public calculator that encouraged homeowners to estimate how much they would save on their tax bills if his proposal became law. However, that was before the Legislature approved the ballot language in a bill the following week.
That calculator initially applied the exemption to the entire millage rate, which became inaccurate after the Legislature removed school taxes from the proposed amendment.
That prompted Jacksonville-based Casey Vockell and his father Steve, a state-certified appraiser, to create their own calculator, called MyExemptionCheck.com.
“I took the average tax rates [of a county] and then extrapolated out the non-school portion,” he said Monday in a brief phone interview. “So when you look up Hillsborough, if you’re in the lower end it’s going to overestimate it, whereas if you’re in the higher end it’s going to estimate it, but it’s a lot closer because it’s not just using the full millage rate. I think the millage rate in Tampa [Hillsborough County] is 20, and 11 of it might be what’s exempt. It’s a big difference.”
Other sites say they give an accurate portrayal of savings on property taxes, such as from Florida TaxWatch. There are similar calculators on the websites of various county property appraisers around the state.

title: News orgs banned from White House accuse Trump of First Amendment violation
text: WASHINGTON — The three news organizations that President Donald Trump barred from entering the White House grounds earlier this month have asked a federal judge to ensure their reporters continue to have access after a temporary restraining order expires in early October. Attorneys for CNN, MS Now and Politico filed paperwork late Monday requesting a preliminary injunction from the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, arguing that without it the administration is likely to again revoke press passes for journalists at those news organizations and possibly others. “The President has stated that there will be ‘Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,’ … leaving other news organizations covering the White House to face the prospect that their access may likewise depend on the President’s view of their coverage,” the brief states. “And each day the ban remains in effect, the public loses access to essential reporting on the President and his administration.”Trump announced on Sept. 18 that he planned to prevent reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico from reporting on White House grounds. Those news organizations filed a lawsuit a few days later, after several of their reporters were denied entry at a security checkpoint and had their press passes confiscated by Secret Service officers. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly, who was nominated during Trump’s first term, issued a temporary restraining order on Sept. 23, requiring the White House to return the press passes and allow the journalists it had barred back in. That order expires Oct. 8, but could be replaced by a preliminary injunction if the judge agrees with the request filed by the three news organizations this week. That 49-page brief argues the president’s ban retaliated against the news organizations “for engaging in speech, publication, and newsgathering activities that the First Amendment protects but the administration disfavors.”The attorneys representing the journalists wrote that Trump administration officials claiming the ban was related to national security concerns were “not credible.” They later wrote that “the President’s own words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House and denying them the access they had as of September 18 is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech—adverse action intended to cow them into conforming the content of their reporting to the President’s preferences and to threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation.” The administration's response brief is due Friday.

title: Governor, Cabinet approve designation of CAIR as a domestic terrorist group
description: Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Florida Cabinet on Tuesday designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and two other organizations as domestic terrorist groups.
