name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey cruising in reelection bid with Trump high on voters’ mind, survey shows
description: A new MassINC Polling Group survey finds that Bay Staters are still concerned about Gov. Maura Healey’s response to affordability concerns, even as she appears poised to win reelection with relative ease.
text:
GOV. MAURA HEALEY remains a strong favorite to win a second term in November as her Republican challenger, Mike Minogue, struggles to break through to a sizable chunk of voters and as President Trump’s unpopularity colors public sentiment in permanent ink.
If the election were held today, 54 percent of likely voters would pick Healey or lean in that direction, and 32 percent would pick Minogue, according to a new CommonWealth Beacon/MassINC Polling Group survey (Toplines | Crosstabs).
For all of the money Minogue has splashed on the contest — he’s contributed more than $15 million to his campaign so far — the former Abiomed executive does not seem to be reaching all voters less than two months away from Election Day. Twenty-seven percent of respondents still haven’t made up their mind about Minogue, and 16 percent said they have never heard of him. Even among Republican voters, only about half view their party’s nominee for the corner office favorably.
Perhaps most crucially, Minogue has yet to win over many independent voters not registered under a party label — the largest chunk of the electorate, and one that any Republican challenger needs to tap to find success in a state dominated by Democrats.
Minogue is underwater with a net favorability rating of minus 12 points among unenrolled or third-party voters, according to the poll. Nearly 45 percent of those voters either don’t know who Minogue is or have not decided how they feel about him.
Healey, by comparison, fares much better with independents, with her favorability netting out five points in the black among that subset. Overall, 52 percent of respondents rated Healey favorably and 33 percent rated her unfavorably.
The latest poll, which involved 800 likely voters contacted between September 14 and September 22 and has a credibility interval of 4 percentage points, is a more encouraging assessment for Healey than another MassINC Polling Group survey published in May. That poll put the governor’s net favorability rating at minus 6 points. That poll involved all registered voters, not just likely voters, which is a group typically a bit less favorable to Democratic candidates. There has also been a significant amount of campaigning since then, which may have influenced voter leanings.
With partisan polarization now a nearly inescapable fact of life, Trump remains an influential figure in the gubernatorial race — a dynamic Healey and the state Democratic Party have energetically sought to exploit, often pitching Minogue as an enabler of the president and Healey as a bulwark against his reach. The party has dubbed him “MAGA Mike,” and invoked the moniker continually.
It’s not hard to see why Democrats are eager to tie Minogue to Trump. Only 25 percent of Bay State likely voters view the president favorably, while 67 percent see him unfavorably, according to the new poll. More than a third of voters said they support Healey as a means to oppose Trump; in fact, independent voters were more likely than Democrats to view their vote for Healey as an anti-Trump maneuver.
One respondent, an independent woman who lives in Lynn, described her top priorities in the election as “finding voices that aren’t afraid to go against Trump’s wishes — voices in his party as well as Democrats.”
Another woman, a Democrat who lives in Woods Hole, similarly said her main focus in the election is both “the cost of living” and voting “for anyone who speaks out against Trump/MAGA.”
Healey for most of her first term has styled herself as a moderate Democrat, often echoing her popular Republican predecessor, Charlie Baker. Her approach at times has irked progressive activists, who wanted the chief executive of such a blue state to be more unabashedly left wing.
Yet the new poll finds that Democratic voters are mostly satisfied. Healey’s favorability rating among Democrats (+73 points) is nearly the same as that of progressive darling Ed Markey (+70 points), who just fended off a US Senate primary challenge from the more moderate US Rep. Seth Moulton. (Like Healey, Markey is cruising in his reelection bid. Fifty-four percent of voters say they’d pick him or lean that way if the election were today, compared to 28 percent who back Republican nominee John Deaton.)
Pollsters asked Healey supporters to explain why they intend to vote for her. The most common answer, offered 54 percent of the time, was “I think she has done a good job,” followed by 40 percent who “agree with her policy positions.” That wasn’t the case for Minogue backers, who were most likely to name their chief reason for picking the Republican candidate as “to oppose Maura Healey.”
Still, support for the governor has not widely translated into a clear consensus about what she has done well in her first four years. In June, a poll by Suffolk University and The Boston Globe found that more than half of voters could not identify a signature accomplishment for Healey.
Voters were pretty split about Healey’s top accomplishments in the new CommonWealth Beacon survey, too. The most common answer, health care, drew only 30 percent of respondents. Twenty-one percent, when offered a list of issues, answered “none of the above.”
There’s much more consensus about Healey’s shortcomings. About six in 10 voters said she has been least successful in addressing the state’s overall cost of living, and nearly half said she is struggling to tackle housing costs.
However, that might be less a reflection on Healey as an individual officeholder than a snapshot of the broader climate. Ask any politician what they’re hearing most from constituents: affordability concerns are as inescapable as Cape traffic on a summer weekend.
Indeed, inflation and the cost of living were the most common answers when voters were asked to use their own words to describe their top priorities in November’s election. For MassINC Polling Group president Steve Koczela, that’s nothing new.
“We see it on every single poll we do,” he said. “No matter of whom and about what, it goes costs and housing as [issues number] one and two.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Poll shows voters on track to retain legal cannabis and 2024 gun law
description: The CommonWealth Beacon survey asked voters to name their top issues at the ballot box in their own words. When the polling group reviewed those answers, guns and marijuana were the only ballot questions people cited as reasons to get out and vote.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS VOTERS LOOK like they’ve largely made up their minds on two of the highest-profile questions on the November ballot. They seem on track to retain legalized recreational marijuana and a sweeping new gun law passed in 2024, according to a new poll. 
In a MassINC Polling Group survey (Toplines | Crosstabs) for CommonWealth Beacon, attitudes toward the other seven ballot questions were more mixed, with percentages of likely voters saying they expect to vote yes hovering in the high 40s and low 50s. 
But the two final questions on the ballot are bucking that trend. Sixty-one percent of likely voters said they would vote no on Question 8, which if approved would end legal sales of recreational marijuana and create civil penalties for possessing more than a small amount of recreational cannabis. Twenty-seven percent of respondents said they would vote yes.  
Question 9, a referendum on whether to keep the state’s sweeping 2024 firearms law, looks set for a resounding affirmation of the law, with 70 percent of respondents saying they would vote to keep it and 18 percent saying they would repeal it. 
These two are also the questions voters seem most sure about, with just 11 percent of voters undecided on each. That is the lowest undecided share of any of the nine questions on the ballot. 
“People don’t want to go backwards on these two things,” said Steve Koczela, president of the MassINC Polling Group.  
“They might not love the Legislature,” Koczela said of voters, pointing to their strong support two years ago for a ballot question to audit lawmakers. “But they approve of what the Legislature did on firearms, at least.” 
The survey of 800 likely voters was conducted online September 14 through 22. It has a credibility interval of plus or minus 4 percentage points.  
Question 1, which would apply the public records law to the Legislature and governor’s office, has the support of 63 percent of respondents with 14 percent opposed. That’s lower than the support seen in a UMass Amherst/WCVB poll in August, which found 84 percent support for the measure with just 7 percent opposed. 
The public records question is considered a natural heir to state Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s successful ballot push last cycle to allow her office to audit the Legislature. That audit attempt, which the Legislature has vocally resisted, is stuck in a political and legal morass at the moment.  
The CommonWealth Beacon survey asked voters to name their top issues at the ballot box in their own words. When the polling group reviewed those answers, guns and marijuana were the only ballot questions people cited as reasons to get out and vote. 
“Those are your two marquee ones that were actually drawing people out,” said MPG vice president Rich Parr. 
In 2016, nearly 54 percent of Massachusetts voters approved legalizing recreational marijuana. A decade later, they are being asked to become the first state to dismantle the market. The repeal campaign is led by the Coalition for a Healthy Massachusetts and is backed by the national anti-legalization group Smart Approaches to Marijuana, which is funding a similar effort in Maine.  
The ballot question would still allow adults 21 and older to possess up to one ounce of pot without criminal penalty, and it would leave the state’s medical marijuana law in place.  
Question 9 is a veto referendum, a mechanism that lets voters decide whether to keep a law the Legislature has already passed. The 2024 law cracked down on ghost guns and 3-D printed guns, strengthened the state’s red flag law, and expanded the definition of assault weapons, among other changes. Gun rights groups gathered enough signatures to force a referendum but missed the window for the 2024 ballot.  
Most of the other seven questions still lean toward a win, but by less, and with 20 to 25 percent of voters still undecided. That puts them in “kind of a gray area where it really could move,” said Parr. 
Question 6, which would create a conservation fund that would still depend on legislative appropriation, has 56 percent support to 24 percent opposition.  
Four questions failed to crack 50 percent support in the poll, or just made it over that line, which public opinion experts and ballot question veterans agree leaves the campaigns on shaky ground. 
“It’s different than a candidate poll where the margin is the best predictor,” Koczela said. In ballot questions, “the yes percent tends to be the best predictor. And if you have a yes percent that’s right around 50, then you’re watching nervously.” What’s more, pollsters generally expect undecided voters on ballot questions to break toward the status quo. 
Most of the ballot campaign money tends to be spent between Labor Day and Election Day, Koczela noted, and “you do kind of see support move the most just in the last eight to 10 weeks.” 
On Question 4, allowing Election Day voter registration, yes holds the lead, 53 percent to 33 percent. Question 7, which lowers the lot size requirements to build single-family homes, has support at 51 percent and opposition at 24 percent.  
Question 2, letting Committee for Public Counsel Services employees unionize, fell below half support, with yes in the lead, 48 percent to 25 percent. Question 5, rewriting the state’s revenue cap, is also narrowly below majority support, with 47 percent in favor and  26 percent opposed. 
Apart from the two repeal efforts, Question 3 to create all-party primaries looks most endangered, even as the margin stays close. It had the support of 43 percent of likely voters, with 36 percent opposed and 20 percent undecided. 
Despite the record-tying number of questions, and the irritation from Beacon Hill with advocates doing an end-run around the usual legislative process, voters aren’t eager to hand over their direct democracy leverage.  
More than three-quarters of respondents said “it is a good thing for the voters to decide these issues” and just 15 percent said lawmakers should be deciding more of them. 
With nine questions on the ballot, the pollsters said the usual rules may not apply. Campaigns will compete with one another for attention, which could blunt opposition spending. 
“The numbers may be more sticky than they usually are,” Koczela said. “Or some of these undecideds might just not have heard about the ballot question and might be very persuadable.” 
Many of those undecided voters face unfamiliar subjects, he noted.  
“Some of these are esoteric issues,” Koczela said. ”They’re not all things like marijuana legalization.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire has a chance to build something better for kids
authors: Sonjia Tainter, Tricia Brannen, Stacy Neville, Leigh Ann Reynolds, Alisha Langill
description: New Hampshire has an important decision to make. Resources resulting from the state’s litigation with Meta create a rare opportunity to invest directly in the young people who were at the center of the concerns that led to this case. The question now is what we choose to build with that opportunity. For years, conversations […]
text:
"According to the 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 82.6% of New Hampshire high school students reported using social media several times a day, while 75.1% reported spending three or more hours a day on recreational screen time outside of schoolwork." (Getty Images)New Hampshire has an important decision to make. Resources resulting from the state’s litigation with Meta create a rare opportunity to invest directly in the young people who were at the center of the concerns that led to this case. The question now is what we choose to build with that opportunity.
For years, conversations about young people and social media have focused largely on what we want kids to do less of: less scrolling, less screen time, fewer harmful online experiences. Those conversations matter, but they leave out another question that is just as important: What are we giving young people to connect to when they put the phone down?
New Hampshire’s own data makes that question worth asking. According to the 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 82.6% of New Hampshire high school students reported using social media several times a day, while 75.1% reported spending three or more hours a day on recreational screen time outside of schoolwork. At the same time, 34.2% reported persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness, and 15.9% said they had seriously considered suicide during the previous year.
Those numbers don’t mean that social media alone caused the mental health challenges facing young people. We know it isn’t that simple, and telling kids to get off their phones isn’t a mental health treatment plan. What we do know is that young people need meaningful relationships, places where they feel like they belong and opportunities to connect with other people in real life.
We recently asked young people involved with Project Promise’s Youth in Government three simple questions: Where do you feel most connected? What do you wish existed in your community? And what does “real-life” connection mean to you?
Their answers weren’t about complicated programs or systems. They talked about sports, hiking, theater, clubs, being outdoors, spending time with friends and having places to hang out. One young person wanted more public spaces with activities. Another wanted a community center and more clubs. Another wanted a youth leadership group that could bring young people from different schools together.
Riley shared that they feel most connected doing extracurricular activities, such as sports and Youth in Government, because they are surrounded by people “who are passionate and want to be there like me.” Vander described real-life connection as “making friends, being a part of something, and/or having fun.”
That idea of being part of something matters. Tricia Brannen, executive director of YouthWell New Hampshire, described belonging as one of the most important protective factors for young people. “Knowing they matter, that they are supported, and that they are seen creates a powerful sense of connection that strengthens their mental health and helps them navigate challenges and thrive,” she shared.
We already see evidence of the importance of supportive adults in New Hampshire’s youth data. Nearly 74% of high school students reported having at least one teacher or other adult at school they can talk to if they have a problem, and more than 85% said they would feel comfortable seeking help from an adult other than a parent about an important question affecting their life.
Those relationships don’t only happen in schools. They happen with coaches, mentors, youth workers, librarians, camp counselors, recreation staff and other adults who show up in the places young people spend their time. They happen in afterschool and summer programs, sports, arts, outdoor education, libraries, community centers, mentoring programs and youth leadership opportunities.
The challenge is that having a great opportunity somewhere in New Hampshire doesn’t necessarily mean a young person can participate in it.
Leigh Ann Reynolds, of New Hampshire Environmental Educators, said that what keeps young people from participating is transportation, cost, time, awareness and geography. “You can have a great program or opportunity, but if a young person doesn’t have a way to get there, it isn’t really accessible,” she said.
That is especially true in rural communities, where an opportunity might be miles away from where a young person lives. But Reynolds also raised another barrier that is easier to overlook: whether young people actually feel like these spaces are meant for them. Sometimes adults create opportunities we think young people should want instead of asking young people what they are interested in and giving them a real role in shaping what is available.
Capacity matters, too. Stacy Neville, vice president of operations at The Granite YMCA, shared that workforce shortages can prevent programs from expanding even when physical space is available. Families may be looking for programs and organizations may want to serve them, but without enough qualified staff, there is a limit to how many young people can walk through the door.
That is why an investment in real-world opportunities has to consider both the opportunities themselves and what makes them accessible. Transportation matters. Scholarships and affordability matter. So do trained staff, safe and accessible spaces, strong community organizations and enough capacity to actually serve young people when they show up.
No single program or sector can do all of this. A young person might find belonging on a basketball court, discover something they love through environmental education, build confidence on a stage, spend afternoons with a trusted adult at an afterschool program, learn how to recognize when a friend needs help through a prevention program and, at another point in their life, need professional mental health support. Young people don’t experience their lives in the funding silos adults create, and our response shouldn’t either.
This is why organizations across New Hampshire are coming together through Fund IRL NH. We believe resources resulting from social media litigation should be used to strengthen the programs, places, relationships and supports that help young people thrive in real life. That includes afterschool and summer programs, sports and recreation, outdoor experiences, arts, mentoring, libraries, youth leadership and other positive youth development opportunities, alongside prevention and mental and behavioral health supports.
New Hampshire also has an opportunity to think beyond a collection of short-term projects. These resources can help address the barriers that keep young people from participating in opportunities that already exist and strengthen the capacity needed to reach more youth. They can help communities build something that lasts beyond the life of a single grant.
As decisions are made, young people and families should have a meaningful role in the process. We should pay attention to rural communities and places where young people have fewer options. We should be transparent about where the resources go, who they reach and what difference they make. Most importantly, resources intended to address harm to young people should result in meaningful investment in young people.
When we asked young people what real-life connection meant to them, they talked about friends, sports, hiking, theater, leadership, the outdoors and places to hang out. More than anything, they talked about having somewhere to go and being part of something.
If we’re going to ask young people to put the phone down, let’s make sure there is something meaningful waiting for them when they do. New Hampshire has an opportunity to turn accountability for harm experienced by young people into stronger communities, deeper connections and more opportunities for them to thrive.
Let’s fund something worth logging off for.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Thoughts from Kansas farmers as the US careens toward moral and fiscal bankruptcy
description: In recent weeks, I have had a number of conversations with other farmers. They cover the spectrum from Millennials to Gen Zers to folks of my generation, with many of that last group remembering the heartache of the 1980s. During that time, lots of folks lost their farms, and the effects were felt throughout rural […]
text:
A view of rain across fields July 17, 2026, from Coronado Heights. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)In recent weeks, I have had a number of conversations with other farmers.
They cover the spectrum from Millennials to Gen Zers to folks of my generation, with many of that last group remembering the heartache of the 1980s. During that time, lots of folks lost their farms, and the effects were felt throughout rural America as bankruptcies were frequent occurrences.
The essence of a bankruptcy for an individual or an entity is either to reorganize one’s financial affairs or completely liquidate assets, in effect, to start over. Bankruptcies are not reflections on a person’s character, but sometimes an indication of unexpected circumstances that could not be reasonably foreseen.
I soon realized that some of the farmers on the other side of our conversations were not referring to the possibility of the nation experiencing financial bankruptcy, although the current budget deficit of nearly two trillion dollars was clearly on their minds, as was the reckless spending on monuments and misadventures around the world.
They were referring to a social and moral bankruptcy. Keep in mind that many of these folks had voted for Donald Trump in 2024, with some also voting for him all the way back to 2016. Many admitted the error of their ways in their prior votes and acknowledged that they had been conned.
Mind you, these folks are typically salt of the earth types who place high values on trust, integrity and keeping one’s word. They see a nation that is adrift, one that is “led” by a president aided and abetted by people who have no moral code. They see a nation that has lost the respect and the trust of the world, and they realize that regaining that trust and respect may take decades.
Their concerns go well beyond the damage to the world markets that have bought American farm products for decades.
My generation has seen a lot in our lifetimes — wars, utter disregard for human life, discrimination based on race and religion, the rise of fascism, the poison of big money pouring into our politics, the recklessness of social media. The list is lengthy. But until the Trump era, we have been able to rely — for the most part — on leaders who functioned with a moral code and a sense of duty.
Bipartisanship also meant something. Our late Sen. Bob Dole is a great reminder of those days.
Even in the most difficult of times, a moral code prevailed. Now, it has become a free-for-all.
History will look back on this era and not be kind in its telling. This nation is bankrupt — in the most fundamental of ways. This goes to the core of our humanity. Perhaps it is difficult to admit that one was wrong with a certain decision. But way more is at stake here than, say, some decision about one’s business or personal life.
This is about the core values that have defined our nation for generations. For many Americans, the conversation starts with that person in the mirror.
Ben Palen is a Kansas native and a fifth-generation farmer and agriculture consultant in Colorado and Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Political notes: Refunds for utilities, input for Fitzwater, new jobs for Coale, Peterson
authors: Bryan P. Sears, William J. Ford
description: Some money may be coming your way from your electric company -- one day -- Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater wants to hear from you and Tom Coale and Scott Peterson land new gigs, in political notes.
text:
BGE, Delmarva Power and Pepco said they will ask state regulators to OK the return of $160 million to ratepayers, after a court win led to the return of tens of millions in improperly collected tax payments to the utilities. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)A win in Maryland’s top court will result in credits for customers of the state’s utility companies — eventually.
How much and when remain open questions.
BGE, Delmarva Power and Pepco announced Monday they will ask the Public Service Commission to greenlight the return of $160 million to ratepayers. The money comes from their share of an expected refund from the Maryland comptroller after the Maryland Supreme Court ruled power companies in some cases had been incorrectly taxed.
Roughly $110 million would go to BGE customers, $20 million for Delmarva Power customers and $30 million for Pepco customers.
The Board of Revenue Estimates last week estimated the total cost of the refund in the Potomac Edison case could run roughly a quarter-billion dollars.
“We know many Maryland families and businesses are feeling pressure from higher energy costs, and we are committed to doing everything we can to help,” Valencia McClure, Exelon senior vice president of governmental, regulatory and external affairs, said in a statement. “Providing these tax savings to customers is another example of The Exelon Promise in action, taking practical steps today to provide relief, protect customers and work with policymakers and regulators on long-term solutions that keep energy safe, reliable and affordable.”
Even with sweeping utility reform legislation in place, regulators fight rising rate requests

A spokesperson for BGE could not provide details on how much the average customer might receive — or when. But when the legislature approved a plan two years ago to provide $200 million in credits to customers, based on usage, the two payments worked out to an average of about $40 each.
Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) said last week that she disagreed with the July decision from the Supreme Court of Maryland, but called on utilities to return the money to ratepayers.
“The utilities should provide a full public accounting of all refunded taxes, including interest, to ensure that Maryland ratepayers receive the full amount owed to them,” Lierman said through a spokesperson Monday.
New chief of staff for LG
Changes are coming to the staff of Lt. Gov Aruna Miller.
Scott Peterson, media relations and communications manager for outgoing Montgomery County Executive Marc Elrich (D), is headed to the State House, where he will take over as the lieutenant governor’s new chief of staff, replacing Geri Royale Byrd.
Elrich, in a recent meeting with reporters, praised Peterson for bringing “his experience with other Maryland jurisdictions to help us better communicate with our residents and the media. Since then, he’s helped bring focus and clarity to this media briefing and many other facets of county communications. And I’ve appreciated his insight, his help to highlight our victories and provide direction for how we share our stories, and to manage the difficult moments.”
Peterson is scheduled to join Miller’s office on Wednesday, replacing Byrd who left last month to become deputy secretary at the Department of Commerce.
Prior to joining Elrich’s staff, Peterson managed communications for leaders in Baltimore City and Prince George’s County, as well as spending nearly a decade at C-SPAN.
There ought to be a law, Frederick version
Frederick County officials are asking voters to help them shape the county’s legislative agenda for the 2027 General Assembly.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater (D) asked residents for their input on a survey that will help shape her office’s legislative package. The survey asks residents to choose between eight areas as their main prority for the session: agriculture; education; public safety; energy; safe and accessible transportation; data centers; housing; and social justice.
After choosing a top priority, residents can summarize what they “would like to see surrounding your topic of choice.” Residents can also jot down any priorities not listed in the eight choices.
The survey will remain open through Thursday and a summary of responses shared at a town hall Oct. 7.
Coale hangs a shingle
Annapolis lobbyist Tom Coale, a partner at Perry Jacobson for the past three years, is leaving the firm to start his own government relations and public affairs firm, he announced this month. The Coale Firm launches Wednesday.
“My practice has grown well beyond any one issue area — housing, energy, biotech, procurement, economic development — and launching my own firm felt like the natural next step to give all of that room to grow,” Coale said in a press releae announcing the change.
Perry Jacobson co-founders Tim Perry and Jonas Jacobson praised Coale’s time at the firm and said they looked forward to collaborating with Coale’s new practice.
Coale said his firm will work in his “core practice areas,” with particular focus on housing finance and land use policy, economic development, procurement, and energy and infrastructure development. He will also maintain his zoning practice, representing clients before local boards and agencies on land use and entitlement matters.
Coale holds a law degree from Georgetown University Law Center, and is vice chair on the board of the Baltimore Regional Housing Partnership.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Historian Heather Cox Richardson sees Jackson’s bid for Senate as path to reclaim democracy
description: Historian Heather Cox Richardson described a Troy Jackson win as a step toward reclaiming American democracy Monday night in Portland.  “This is our moment,” the widely known scholar and Maine resident told a packed auditorium at the University of Southern Maine of the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee sitting beside her.  Known for her daily substack […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson (left) speaks with historian Heather Cox Richardson on Sept. 28 in Portland. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Historian Heather Cox Richardson described a Troy Jackson win as a step toward reclaiming American democracy Monday night in Portland. 
“This is our moment,” the widely known scholar and Maine resident told a packed auditorium at the University of Southern Maine of the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee sitting beside her. 
Known for her daily substack “Letters from an American,” which boasts over 3 million subscribers and connects daily headlines to long-term patterns in American history, Richardson has a public following rare to academics (so much so that her name was floated as a potential candidate for the U.S. Senate seat back when former Democratic nominee Graham Platner dropped out). 
Taking the stage with the now-nominee, Richardson urged attendees to talk to their family and neighbors and ensure they are registered so they can vote in Maine’s Senate race and others that could be consequential for the balance of power in Congress. 
The pair spoke about Jackson’s record as former president of the Maine Senate and his policy stances, notably his support for Medicare for All, universal childcare and an end to the Iran War.
Healthcare in particular was top of mind for Jackson, a former logger from Allagash, because his son’s partner recently gave birth to his first granddaughter.
“She was two weeks early, and if they had been up in Aroostook County where I live, I mean which could have happened, it’s about an hour and a half to get to the nearest birthing center,” he said, noting the closure of many across the state. 
Richardson noted that several of Jackson’s pitches — for Congress to reclaim its authority and the U.S. Supreme Court to be reformed ethically — are about going back to a period when laws were enforced. 
“I think you’re right,” she said. “We need to go back in order to go forward, and that’s the wonderful position we’re in. We’re reclaiming something old in order to create something new.” 
Beside the academic, Jackson’s plainspoken nature and northern Maine dialect were on display, and he joked with the interpreters about whether they could understand him. 
“He might not be the best speaker. He might not be the most polished person,” Mary Kay Weisenberger of Auburn said. But, she added, “He’s real — that’s what comes across when you come to these events.”
Weisenberger and her wife Claire Hebert had attended Jackson’s first town hall in Lewiston last month. Then, Hebert had been worried she would just be voting by default for Jackson, who replaced Platner in late July. On Monday night, she said, “Now I’m not.”
“Greed has become the end all and be all and I believe Troy is above that,” Hebert said. “I hope he proves me right.” 
Maine’s U.S. Senate race has become one of the most expensive midterm races in the country, drawing over $110 million in advertising, according to a recent Washington Post analysis.
The night began with a surprise appearance by Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, who is back in Maine on what she called the “Hegseth holiday,” after Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced a resolution last week to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran War.
Pingree said, “nobody can out-authentic Troy.” While in Maine’s 1st Congressional District on Monday, Pingree also plugged the tight second district race, advocating for Democratic nominee Matt Dunlap over Paul LePage. 
“We’re not going to fix the problems that we have unless we take back the House and the Senate,” Pingree said. She later added, “Do not make me get on a plane with Paul LePage.”

title: Head of JobsOhio board to be deposed in federal civil lawsuit against FirstEnergy
description: The chairman of the JobsOhio board, Josh Rubin, will be deposed Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 in advance of a federal civil trial in which Akron-based FirstEnergy is the defendant, according to court records.  In the suit, state pension systems and other investors accuse FirstEnergy of failing to tell them of “an illicit campaign to […]
text:
FirstEnergy's headquarters in Akron. (Photo from Google Maps.)The chairman of the JobsOhio board, Josh Rubin, will be deposed Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 in advance of a federal civil trial in which Akron-based FirstEnergy is the defendant, according to court records. 
In the suit, state pension systems and other investors accuse FirstEnergy of failing to tell them of “an illicit campaign to corrupt high-profile state legislators in order to secure legislation favoring the company.”
Larry Householder, the former speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence for his role in the scheme, which prosecutors called one of the biggest bribery scandals in state history. 
After a hung jury, FirstEnergy’s former top executives face a second state criminal trial over their involvement.
Rubin served as an advisor to the executives and then formally signed on as a lobbyist. He and JobsOhio didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Financially struggling FirstEnergy in 2018 and 2019 paid more than $60 million through 501(c)(4) dark money groups to pass and protect a $1.3 billion ratepayer bailout. 
Gov. Mike DeWine signed the law and briefly defended it as good policy even after the FBI started making arrests in 2020. 
His administration had numerous connections to FirstEnergy and the legislation, including a legislative affairs director who, as a FirstEnergy lobbyist, started one of the dark-money groups through which the utility funneled $25 million.
DeWine’s then-lieutenant governor, Jon Husted, was a staunch supporter of the bailout. 
In 2017, FirstEnergy made a $1 million dark money contribution to an independent political group supporting Husted, although a spokeswoman said it wasn’t affiliated with Husted.
DeWine’s nominee to chair the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, Sam Randazzo, received a $4.3 million bribe from FirstEnergy just before his appointment. While working as head of the state utility regulator, Randazzo helped write the bailout legislation.
After Randazzo was charged criminally, he became one of two participants in the scandal to die by suicide.
Rubin, who is scheduled to be deposed in the civil litigation, is a longtime advisor to DeWine. In September 2023, DeWine made Rubin chairman of JobsOhio, the state’s controversial economic development agency. 
JobsOhio is legally exempt from most open meetings and records laws even though it was created by the legislature, the governor appoints its board, and it leases the state’s lucrative liquor franchise for much less than it’s worth.
JobsOhio has used more than $2 billion in proceeds from the arrangement to make grants and loans to private businesses — including FirstEnergy — in the name of economic development.
Rubin’s appointment to chair the JobsOhio board is also controversial among good government watchdogs because he is a lobbyist with dozens of clients, including many that are seeking money from JobsOhio. 
One of his clients, Intel, has received more than $150 million in commitments from JobsOhio and more than $2 billion from DeWine’s executive branch, which Intel is paying Rubin to lobby.
Before he joined the JobsOhio board, Rubin advised FirstEnergy’s top executives.
On Dec. 18, 2018, just after they were elected, DeWine and Husted attended a dinner meeting with FirstEnergy CEO Chuck Jones and Vice President Michael Dowling at the Columbus Athletic Club.
Rubin, who would within weeks become a FirstEnergy lobbyist, was there. The men discussed Randazzo’s suitability to be the state’s top regulator of the monopoly industry FirstEnergy was a part of, court proceedings showed.
Rubin advised the executives not to tell DeWine that they were going straight from the dinner to meet with Randazzo, the Associated Press reported in February. 
It was at that meeting at Randazzo’s German Village condo that the $4.3 million bribe was negotiated, prosecutors said.
An audit performed by the utility commission after the conspiracy had been exposed found that FirstEnergy paid Rubin’s lobbying firm, the CJR Group,  $300,000 between 2018 and 2019.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lansing protesters block Flock cameras over license plate reader contract
description: As Lansing residents press the city to end its automated license plate reader contract with Flock Safety, members of DeFlock Lansing and the Michigan Capitol Visibility Brigade gathered at the intersection of Michigan Avenue and Pennsylvania Avenue, where four Flock cameras are installed.  At its Aug. 24 meeting, the Lansing City Council voted 7-1 in […]
text:
A sign reading "Flock Out!" blocks a Flock license plate reader camera in Lansing, Mich. on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)As Lansing residents press the city to end its automated license plate reader contract with Flock Safety, members of DeFlock Lansing and the Michigan Capitol Visibility Brigade gathered at the intersection of Michigan Avenue and Pennsylvania Avenue, where four Flock cameras are installed. 
At its Aug. 24 meeting, the Lansing City Council voted 7-1 in favor of a resolution requesting the city administration and Lansing Police Department terminate all contracts with Flock, pointing to privacy concerns and the growing number of local governments reconsidering the use of automated license plate reader technology. 
“The mayor has not acted on this resolution, so we’re out here doing more than the mayor to keep Lansing safe from AI-powered mass surveillance by blocking the view of these four cameras for the next hour,” said John Warmb, an organizer with DeFlock Lansing.
In a statement shared with Michigan Advance, Lansing Mayor Andy Schor said he was speaking with a variety of parties about the contract. 
“We have a contract that goes for another year and a half that we cannot unilaterally get out of,” Schor said. “As such, I’m talking to those interested and impacted. We have heard from the Deflock Lansing folks, as well as City Council after taking this up four days after the resolution was introduced. I am also listening to those that didn’t have an opportunity to be part of that conversation at City Council including Constituents, victims of crime, different constituency, groups, and others before making any final determinations.”
Protestors from DeFlock Lansing hold signs to block automated license plate reader cameras at the intersection of Pennsylvania Ave. and Michigan Ave. in Lansing on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Protesters from Michigan Capitol Visibility Brigade carry signs in opposition to Flock cameras in Lansing, gathering at a major intersection where four cameras are located on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson)Protestors from DeFlock Lansing hold signs to block automated license plate reader cameras at the intersection of Pennsylvania Ave. and Michigan Ave. in Lansing on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Warmb said they would like to see the city adopt an ordinance banning the use of automated license plate reader cameras, but acknowledged that these processes can take time.
“I would love to see some action from the mayor to just cover these cameras up in the meantime,” Warmb said. “It is clear that the citizens and city council do not want these in our community.”
Multiple communities across the state have begun to cancel their contracts with Flock. While local law enforcement officials have described the cameras as a tool for deterring crime, tracking stolen vehicles and responding to AMBER Alerts, opponents have pointed to the lack of legal guardrails around the technology, and their potential for abuse by law enforcement officials. 
At least 22 law enforcement officials have been arrested, fired or placed on leave following a USA Today investigation into alleged misuse of Flock cameras, including a Florida police officer who was charged with four felony counts of accessing a computer network without authorization after Flock audit logs showed he had searched a woman’s license plate at least 189 times over an eight-month period.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
William Lawrence, a Lansing-area political organizer and Democratic candidate for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District who has made opposition to big tech a cornerstone of his campaign, joined protesters in opposition to the cameras. 
“This is a violation of our right to privacy, which is enshrined in the Fourth Amendment,” Lawrence told Michigan Advance. “For over 200 years, people in this country have held a healthy suspicion of concentrated power at the top of big business and government and this is a violation of that. It’s been developing for a couple of decades now, but now is the time where people are drawing the line and saying it’s time. No further.”
Lawrence will face U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) in the general election on Nov. 3. 
Barrett is a co-sponsor of Rep. Tim Burchett’s (R-Tenn.) Protection Against Mass Surveillance Act, which bars federal agencies from purchasing and deploying automated surveillance systems like Flock cameras. The bill would also bar state, local and tribal governments from using federal funds to purchase and operate automated surveillance technology.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Assembly GOP candidates in competitive seats try to distance themselves from their party
description: Republicans’ control of the Wisconsin Assembly is up in the air this November, and GOP candidates in competitive districts are taking steps to convince voters to allow them to extend their 16-year streak of leadership, including by distancing themselves from Republican leaders in Washington, D.C. and in Wisconsin. Barry Burden, director of the University of[...]
text:
The entrance to the Wisconsin Assembly chambers. (Baylor Spears | Wisconsin Examiner)Republicans’ control of the Wisconsin Assembly is up in the air this November, and GOP candidates in competitive districts are taking steps to convince voters to allow them to extend their 16-year streak of leadership, including by distancing themselves from Republican leaders in Washington, D.C. and in Wisconsin.
Barry Burden, director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison Elections Research Center, told the Wisconsin Examiner in an email that the 2026 election environment is “more advantageous to Democrats than the 2024 environment was.”
Part of that environment can be seen in the approval ratings of President Donald Trump. A Marquette Law School poll released in September found that Trump’s approval has declined to 37% — down from 40% approval in July; 63% of respondents said they disapproved of the job Trump is doing. 
A recent Marquette poll found that 46% of Wisconsin voters said they would vote for Democrats in legislative races, while 42% said they’d vote for Republicans. The survey did not deliver detailed information on specific districts. 
“The party is all but certain to make additional gains,” Burden said of Wisconsin Democrats. “The question is whether the wave will be sufficient to put them over the top.”
Republicans hold a 54-seat majority in the 99-seat state Assembly. Democratic lawmakers need to hold all of their current seats in the Assembly and pick up five additional seats to flip the body, a steeper task than in the Senate where Democrats are looking to pick up at least two seats to take control.
Assembly Speaker Robin Vos (R-Rochester) and Rep. August Tyler (R-Walworth), who is heading up the Republican Assembly Campaign Committee, did not respond to requests for an interview from the Examiner. In an interview with the New York Times, Vos described Trump as a “drag” on the party and said Republicans have worked to recruit center-right candidates to run in competitive districts.
“There’s nobody in Wisconsin that I think is yearning for a hard turn left or right,” Vos told the New York Times.
Assembly GOP candidates are sending out mailers that claim that politicians in Washington — where Republicans currently control every branch of government — are “driving up costs and increasing inflation.”
Instead of embracing their party’s leadership in Wisconsin, Republican candidates are also highlighting the moments where they have disagreed with their leadership to position themselves as independent voices.
A law that expanded Medicaid coverage for postpartum mothers and another measure that expanded breast cancer screenings are major reference points for Republican Assembly candidates. The bills had been held up by Vos until at the end of the legislative session. In a late-night press conference a group of Republican Assembly lawmakers — each from the most purple districts in the state and most of whom are now running for reelection — said they had convinced Vos and other caucus members to let the bills through. They also blamed Democrats for the bills almost failing.
A mailer for Rep. Patrick Snyder (R-Weston) includes a photo of him standing at the podium in the state Capitol talking to reporters during the press conference. Snyder faces a challenge from John Kroll, a Democratic Marathon County Board supervisor. 
The image is accompanied by text that says Snyder’s work “wasn’t about the spotlight” and he will “always challenge the political leadership of either party if it’s the right thing to do for Marathon County’s families.” The same mailer pitches Snyder as an “old-school public servant” who has had “no problems bucking his own party to extend postpartum care for new mothers.”
In a Facebook post Friday, Rep. Bob Donovan (R-Greenfield) said he would “stand up to anyone to get stuff done for my local community” including Republican leadership, adding that  he “did it when I fought for postpartum Medicaid expansion & Gail’s law, and I’ll do it again.” Donovan faces a challenge from Democrat Ben Brist, an army veteran. Donovan won his 2024 election in with 51.6% of the vote compared with 48.4% for his challenger

During a recent WisPolitics event, Joe Handrick, a former Republican Assembly member, said that Democrats can only flip the Legislature if Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley has a “really, really big” win against Republican Tom Tiffany. His prediction was that it would have to be a win of more than 4 or 5 points.
“If Tom Tiffany ties in the state of Wisconsin or loses by a couple of votes, the Republicans will maintain the Assembly,” Handrick said. “These Assembly Republicans outperform the top of the ticket.”
Handrick said swing voters’ interaction with Republican incumbents can help swing them their way.
“They can vote for one person for governor or president and then they’ve been voting for Assembly Republicans. The incumbents — every day when you’re an incumbent you’re helping somebody. You’re helping them with a problem with the DNR or with the driveway or helping them get their Medicaid issue resolved,” Handrick said. “Those Assembly Republicans have always done better than the top of the ticket and there’s no reason to think they won’t this year.” 
Assembly Minority Leader Greta Neubauer (D-Racine) told the Examiner in an interview that Republican candidates’ strategy to try to distance themselves from the rest of their party won’t work. She said that Democrats’ path to the majority is helped by Trump’s unpopularity. 
“Trump is deeply unpopular across our battleground districts, and that’s more than the five that we need to flip in order to gain a majority,” Neubauer said. “We have a real opportunity here to put forward a new vision. We know that it is not easy to beat long-term incumbents, but we feel that we have the winning formula this year.”
Neubauer said Wisconsinites are “smart enough to see through these half-hearted attempts by Republicans to distance themselves from their own party.” She noted that Snyder, who has been in office for nearly a decade, has often voted in line with his party.
“He, of course, has not actually fought back against the Trump administration and Republicans in Washington who are doing nothing to address the cost increases that voters are experiencing,” she said. “Pat Snyder is an establishment Republican, and I think his voters understand that, and this strategy will not work.”
“Republicans understand that people are unhappy with their party, and they are not excited about showing up to vote Republican this fall,” Neubauer said. “Pat Snyder can try to tell his voters that he’s not a Republican, but at the end of the day, there’s going to be an R next to his name, and he went right along with his party in giving a tax break to data centers, in refusing to adequately fund our schools and thereby increase their property taxes,” Neubauer said. “Pat Snyder and his colleagues across the Republican battlegrounds have been with Robin Vos every step of the way, and I do think that their strategy is not going to work.”  
 
The Republican Assembly Campaign Committee has raised $10.6 million this year to fuel the party’s efforts to keep control. The majority of the funds were donated by Diane Hendricks and Elizabeth Uihlein, billionaires who have contributed millions to help get Republicans elected up and down the ballot in Wisconsin. Hendricks and the Uihleins have also donated millions to the Republican Party of Wisconsin, which has, in turn, channeled millions to Republican gubernatorial candidate Tiffany. 
The Assembly Democratic Campaign Committee has reported raising more than $3.3 million this year.
Neubauer said Assembly Democrats’ formula for winning is a combination of candidates who understand the challenges of their local communities having direct conversations with voters and a “robust” paid media program.
Neubauer said that Democrats just have a “different” fundraising model. She said she expects there to be spending similar to the last election cycle when $1 million or more was spent in the most competitive seats and that money for Democrats tends to come later in the cycle. 
“Assembly Republicans have raised a lot of money from three billionaires whose financial interests are directly tied to whether Republicans control the state Assembly,” Neubauer said, adding that the ADCC has more than 2,500 donors from across every county in the state. “Our candidates and our members are on the phone every single day, calling donors to bring in the dollars that we need to get our message out. And often those dollars come in in more like $50 or $100 checks than several-million-dollar checks, so we are going to continue to work hard to make sure that we have the resources that we need to compete… I am confident that we will be able to bring in the resources that we need to communicate this year.”
Burden noted that individual Democratic candidates have in some cases outraised their opponents. He named Assembly District 88 where Brandy Tollefson, the Democratic candidate and a De Pere school board member, reported raising more than $80,000 over the year compared with her opponent,  incumbent Rep. Benjamin Franklin (R-De Pere), who reported raising more than $27,000.
“Although the Republican Party has been outraising the Democrats, individual Democratic candidates have been doing well raising funds,” Burden said. “This pattern has also been happening nationally in that federal Republican Party committees have been raising more but Democratic candidates have mostly been outraising their Republican opponents within districts and states. Big donations from a few wealthy individuals are keeping Republicans more competitive this year in Wisconsin, but the money alone will not guarantee them victory.”
Here are the most competitive Assembly races to watch in the Nov. 3 election:

Assembly District 21: The district is open following the retirement of Rep. Jessie Rodriguez, a longtime Republican incumbent. She won her 2024 term with 51.4% of the vote to 48.6% for her challenger. Democrat Daniel Bukiewicz, the mayor of Oak Creek, is facing Dylan Pfaffenbach, a Republican student at Carroll University, in November. 
Assembly District 26: Rep. Joe Sheehan (D-Sheboygan) faces a challenge from John Belanger, a Republican and former Sheboygan alderman. Sheehan won his 2024 election with 51.5% of the vote compared to 48.5% for his opponent, who was the Republican incumbent at the time.
Assembly District 30: Incumbent Rep. Shannon Zimmerman (R-River Falls), who was first elected in 2016, faces a challenge from Kevin Knoke, a Democratic veteran and educator from Hudson. Zimmerman won his 2024 election with 54.3% of the vote compared to 45.7% for his Democratic rival.
Assembly District 51: Rep. Todd Novak (R-Dodgeville) faces a challenge from Democrat Ben Gruber, a conservation warden in Wisconsin who is member of AFSCME Local 1215. Novak won his 2024 reelection bid with 51.7% of the vote compared to 48.3% for his Democratic challenger. 
Assembly District 53:  Republican David Daniels and Democrat Becky Nichols, a former Menasha city council member, are running for an open seat. It’s open due to the retirement of incumbent Rep. Dean Kaufert (R-Neenah).
Assembly District 61: Rep. Bob Donovan (R-Greenfield), who was first elected in 2022, faces a challenge from Democrat Ben Brist, an army veteran. Donovan won his 2024 election in with 51.6% of the vote compared with 48.4% for his challenger.
Assembly District 85: Rep. Patrick Snyder (R-Weston) faces a challenge from Democrat John Kroll, a Marathon county board supervisor. Snyder won his 2024 reelection bid against his Democratic challenger with 53.2% of the vote compared with  46.7% for his challenger.
Assembly District 88: Rep. Benjamin Franklin (R-De Pere) faces a challenge from Democrat Brandy Tollefson, a De Pere school board member. Franklin won his first term with 50.3% of the vote compared with 49.7% for the Democratic candidate.
Assembly District 89: Rep. Ryan Spaude (D-Ashwaubenon) faces a challenge from Bobby Lindsey, a retired law enforcement professional and a Marine Corps veteran. Spaude won his first term in 2024 with 51.4% of the vote compared with 48.6% for his opponent. 
Assembly District 92: Rep. Clint Moses (R-Menomonie) faces a challenge from Democrat Jeremiah Fredrickson, a fish farmer from Elk Mound. 
Assembly District 91: Democratic Rep. Jodi Emerson, who was first elected in 2018, faces a challenge from Republican Bruce Stabenow, an Osseo resident and small business owner. Emerson won her 2024 election with 51.6% of the vote compared with  48.4% for her Republican challenger. 
Assembly District 94: Democratic Rep. Steve Doyle faces a challenge from Keith Purnell, a Republican Army veteran. Doyle was first elected to the Assembly during a May 2011 special election and has been reelected since. He won reelection in 2024 by just 223 votes against the Republican candidate. The seat will be one of Democrats’ top seats to protect and the party has  already invested over $1 million in.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Debate over data center growth in Georgia heats up race for governor
description: As Georgia becomes a national leader in new data center construction, debate over how to regulate the booming industry has become a hot issue in the race for governor. The two candidates have proposed contrasting visions for how to deal with the massive, power-hungry facilities that help power and advance artificial intelligence, but voters don’t […]
text:
DeKalb County residents gathered before a county commission meeting on Nov. 20, 2025, to protest a data center proposal in Ellenwood. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderAs Georgia becomes a national leader in new data center construction, debate over how to regulate the booming industry has become a hot issue in the race for governor.
The two candidates have proposed contrasting visions for how to deal with the massive, power-hungry facilities that help power and advance artificial intelligence, but voters don’t seem entirely sold on either’s plan. Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, is pitching a statewide temporary “pause” on new data center construction to study the strain these facilities place on local communities, the environment and electricity bills, as well as potential benefits they may provide to some communities.
“Let us take a pause, assess fully, assess comprehensively, assess the impact that these data centers are having on our environment, on our utility bills, what it means to have them in communities,” Bottoms said in a recent press conference in Cobb County, where local opposition to data centers has grown.
Her Republican opponent, healthcare executive Rick Jackson, a billionaire who has invested in a data center in Texas that has faced local opposition, has argued that local elected officials should have the authority to welcome or reject these projects. Jackson pitched his plan as an opportunity for local governments to bolster the tax base and decrease – or even eliminate – residential property taxes.
“Every community should decide,” Jackson said at a September press conference in Cobb County. “And every community should get a financial benefit to lower their property taxes or anything else, with the right guardrails on these data centers and making sure that they do everything right, this could be one of the biggest economic benefits to a community if they want one.” 
But some advocates and residents living near proposed data centers across the state worry that  local communities lack the leverage to negotiate with data center developers, wonder whether the promise of lower property taxes will ever come true and question whether a temporary pause might lead to policy that effectively regulates these mammoth facilities.
Bottoms’ push for a pause
Former mayor of Atlanta Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for governor, speaks at a press conference in downtown Marietta on Sept. 14, 2026 where she discussed her proposal to pause data center construction in Georgia. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
In Cobb County, where county commissioners extended its local data center moratorium until early 2027, Bottoms said temporarily pausing construction on data centers would be one of the first things she would pursue as governor, though she was unsure whether it could be accomplished  through an executive order or if it had to be done legislatively.
“We’re going to use every tool in the toolbox to make sure that that pause takes place statewide,” she said.
Peter Hubbard, a Democrat who was elected to the Georgia Public Service Commission in 2025, joined Bottoms in Cobb County where he outlined four policy proposals aimed at regulating data centers. Hubbard said that data centers should be powered with clean energy sources and pay for that infrastructure, operate with full transparency without the use of nondisclosure agreements, enact safeguards that protect the local community and natural resources and mandate the use of union labor “wherever possible.”
Peter Hubbard, Democratic member of the Public Service Commission, joined Atlanta’s former mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for Governor, at a press conference in downtown Marietta on Sept. 14, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“I think if we take these actions, if we raise the barrier for data centers to do business in the state, and we make them pay their fair share, then we will be better for it,” Hubbard said.
Bottoms kept her speech focused on a data center pause, but when asked if she supports Hubbard’s proposal, she said that she was “in complete alignment with what Commissioner Hubbard has proposed.”
“You will hear me talk more about it as I look to his leadership to help guide how we need to move forward as a state,” she said.
Other states, including ones led by governors from both major parties, have temporarily halted data center development. New York’s governor, a Democrat, became the first to order a statewide moratorium on large-scale data centers in July. Texas’ governor, a Republican, ordered his own ban in August and broadened that order this month. 
Jackson punts to local control and touts lower taxes
Jackson disagrees with Bottoms’ approach and has said on the campaign trail that he believes communities should be able to decide whether data centers are built. Currently, local governments make decisions on data center projects and propose regulations, and Jackson said it should stay that way.
Healthcare businessman Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate for governor, speaks at a press conference in Marietta on Sept. 16, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“The county commissioners are voted by the people, so they need to decide,” Jackson said at the Cobb County press conference.
But Jackson also said that local governments can make those decisions with “guardrails” in place. In an Atlanta Journal-Constitution op-ed Jackson balanced his support of data centers with five conditions for their development. He said he would sign an executive order establishing stricter environmental standards for approving data center proposals and requiring the state to be transparent about tax incentives, utility costs and projected benefits.
At the recent press conference, Jackson added that he wanted “to educate people on the benefit if they want (a data center),” saying that some counties are expecting they “will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in.” Some counties, like Effingham County where OpenAI plans to build a $20 billion data center, pledged to lower property taxes with revenue they bring in.
Jackson’s stance aligns with Georgia’s business community, with Chris Clark, president and CEO of the Georgia Chamber of Commerce, agreeing with the local control approach. Clark said Jackson’s proposal allows communities to continue negotiating with developers while giving them the opportunity to diversify their tax base. The Georgia Chamber of Commerce has endorsed Jackson.
“I think what Rick Jackson has said has been clear. It’s the community’s decision,” Clark said. “If this fits with what you want in your community, then you need to be able to do that project, move forward, just like if it’s a manufacturing, a distribution, or a Buc-ee’s.”
Industry backs local control, but residents push back
In suburban and rural Georgia communities, residents and advocates interviewed for this story say Jackson’s stance maintains the status quo. 
Bill Wright, who spent four years organizing against data center projects in Northern Virginia before relocating to Chatham County near Savannah, dismissed Jackson’s proposal and said that developers and tech companies hold much of the leverage during negotiations.
“They’re completely outgunned by these developers. They don’t have the wherewithal to push back. They’re susceptible to financial incentives, and they’re wooed by campaign donations,” Wright said. “So, when you say ‘leave it up to the local community,’ of course you have to do that to some extent, but you have to give the community help.”
Wright, who’s been advocating against the OpenAI development in Effingham County, which neighbors Chatham, said leaving regulatory decisions to individual counties ignores the footprint  data centers have beyond the county’s border and argued that statewide regulations are “absolutely essential.”
“Let’s say Effingham County approves Project Camellia. Well, that has an effect on the surrounding counties as well that have absolutely nothing to say about what’s going on there,” Wright said.
Data centers in Georgia are largely unregulated statewide. Developers usually submit a “development of regional impact” review in the initial stages that outlines basic information, such as project size, revenue and estimated water usage. That review, however, is designed to be a communication mechanism for local officials – and not a state regulatory tool. The Public Service Commission also passed a rule that was intended to ensure data centers, which consume large amounts of electricity, pay for some of the energy infrastructure Georgia Power builds to accommodate them, but critics don’t believe that rule fully protects residential ratepayers.
Outrage over surge of data centers in Georgia inspires wave of bipartisan bills

Lawmakers from both parties during the 2026 legislative session introduced about 20 bills aimed at regulating the massive facilities, but those bills never made it to the governor’s desk for a signature.
South of Atlanta in Fayette County, retired resident Diana Dietz has watched the QTS data center campus expand beyond its original plan. She was also skeptical that local governments had the ability to shield residents from data centers when there is local pushback.
“The elected officials do what they want, which is they approve these things for the most part,” Dietz said. “They approve them. You might get one or two who vote no, but they’re not the majority.”
But Clark with the Georgia Chamber of Commerce pushed back on the notion that communities aren’t well equipped to negotiate with developers or that companies want to force projects onto communities that do not want them.
“They want to go in and be a good partner, and if a community doesn’t want them, there’s plenty of communities that do, and so I think I kind of push back a little bit on that assumption that they’re rolling over local elected officials. I think that’s an easy narrative, but kind of hard to roll over when they control zoning, water and are either recruiting them or not recruiting them to town,” Clark said.
Pro-data center group launches in Georgia to try to win over critics

The Georgia Chamber of Commerce launched the Georgia Digital Infrastructure Alliance over the summer aimed at swaying critics. Clark said that part of that initiative was creating a “data center-ready community designation” checklist that helps communities advance data center proposals “responsibly and transparently,” but Dietz had little confidence in the idea of relying on voluntary standards proposed by the industry.
“[They’re] going to serve the same Kool-Aid as the industry does,” Dietz said.
Moratorium against concrete policy
While community members and advocates largely welcomed Bottoms’ call to pause new data center developments, they were also concerned that a moratorium won’t be enough if it’s used as just a period to study the issue that won’t lead to state regulations.
Maurice Carter, president and co-founder of the local nonprofit Sustainable Newton in Newton County, has been active in community discussions regarding data centers that have plans or have started development in the county, including one from Amazon and another from Google. The county eventually passed a moratorium in January, adopted new regulations in August and lifted the pause in September.
“I’m not a believer in a moratorium just for the sake of a moratorium. In other words, you better use that year or those six months we did here in Covington, right?” Carter said, referring to a city in Newton County. “You better use that time to get the right things in place.” 
Wright was more blunt about having a pause to study the issue and pointed to his home state of Virginia where state studies did not produce effective regulations.
“This business of studying something, it’s usually a delaying tactic,” Wright said. “Anytime you can’t make a decision, you sanction some blue-ribbon panel to come up and kick the can down the road a little farther.”
“I would like to hear (Bottoms) say no tax incentives for data centers. These are the wealthiest corporations in the world … You can get these guys without giving away the store. They want your land. They need it to operate, and so there’s no need to make so many concessions to these folks,” Wright added.
But TaNisha Cameron, a spokesperson for the Bottoms campaign, said that the pause would be used to “work with the General Assembly to develop clear statewide standards and rules for communities, utilities, developers, and residents.”
Bottoms’ call for a temporary moratorium was met with less enthusiasm from the business community. Clark with the Georgia Chamber of Commerce, warned that a statewide pause, as proposed by Bottoms, would disrupt economic development and hurt communities that are in discussions with potential data centers developers.
“We’ve become a digital economy. Every single business in Georgia – everything you do, I do, this conversation we’re having right now – all flows through one to two to three, maybe even five data centers every day,” Chark said in an interview. “If we’re going to build them, the communities that want them should get that economic benefit. So that’s where we are as a business community.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Race for Ohio Treasurer decides who invests the state’s billions and how
description: The nation is keeping an eye on Ohio’s November general election, particularly the governor’s race and those at the top of the ballot. But no matter who is elected to be the next governor, as secretary of state, or to a seat in the legislature, they all have to partner with the leader of the […]
text:
(Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)The nation is keeping an eye on Ohio’s November general election, particularly the governor’s race and those at the top of the ballot. But no matter who is elected to be the next governor, as secretary of state, or to a seat in the legislature, they all have to partner with the leader of the office that oversees the $280 billion in Ohio’s financial accounts.
“We need to make sure people do know that this is one of the most important offices that their votes do matter on this year,” said Seth Walsh, a former Cincinnati community organizer and current Cincinnati City Council member who is the Democratic nominee running for Ohio Treasurer of State.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state treasurer’s office has the authority to invest state money, and oversee the debts for the state, while also watching over programs for things like small business loans, investment opportunities for Ohioans, and homebuyer savings resources.
The office also works with county recorders in the state, and keeps records on topics like state government salaries, state revenue, and state spending, among other numbers, through the Ohio Checkbook.
Walsh is running against Republican former state lawmaker Jay Edwards in the race.
Walsh was uncontested in the Democratic primary in May, while Edwards won in a tight race against fellow legislator Sen. Kristina Roegner, R-Hudson.
That primary race was treated as a test of endorsements, with Edwards touting support from Vice President JD Vance and Ohio GOP U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno, while Roegner was endorsed by Ohio GOP candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy.
In previous comments to reporters about running again for elected office, Edwards said he wants to help maintain the “Trump Republican Party.”
State Rep. Jay Edwards, R-Nelsonville. (Official photo.)
The Nelsonville resident served as a state representative for the 94th District from 2017 to 2024, chairing the Ohio House Finance Committee during his last two years in office.
If elected again, he said he plans to focus on “keeping taxpayer money in Ohio” as treasurer.
“I don’t see any reason why the state treasurer spends so much money with Wall Street banks, and the Wall Street investors in the state,” Edwards said. “We want to support community banks, credit unions, right here in the state of Ohio.”
On the topic of the unclaimed funds account held under the Ohio Department of Commerce, which other lawmakers pledged to use to pay for sports stadiums and other venues, Edwards said Ohioans he talks to know “it’s very negative, what was done in the budget, and I can tell you, if I was finance chair, it wouldn’t have happened.”
“The one good thing that has came from that is a lot of people are now claiming their unclaimed funds, it kind of shined a light on that,” Edwards told the Capital Journal.
An effort to use the funds as lawmakers planned has been blocked by a state court, but the lawsuit remains ongoing.
Walsh is staunchly against using the fund for projects like sports stadiums. In a pre-primary interview with the Capital Journal, he said the treasurer’s office “has a fiduciary responsibility to be on that lawsuit saying absolutely not.”
The Democratic nominee has made his way across the state talking to those who work in community development, conversations that have bolstered a plan he’s had to use local resources to reinvest in the state.
Seth Walsh. (Photo provided by Seth Walsh for Ohio Treasurer)
“I’ve always believed we can use the state treasurer’s office to rebuild Ohio, but now I see the tools and I see the experts who know how you can use these tools really well, that can help educate us on how we can build out from there,” Walsh told the Capital Journal.
Walsh said he has talked to Ohioans of all backgrounds and political leanings in the last year, and a common theme has arisen.
“In general, what I hear around Ohio … people just feel very left behind by everybody,” Walsh said. “They feel like the work has been set up in a way in which they don’t win and there’s no path to victory, and they’re tired of just feeling like no matter what they try to do, it doesn’t get better.”
Edwards has heard the same in his discussions at county fairs and other campaign events.
“I don’t think there’s any doubt that people are struggling, and electricity prices, and property taxes, and gas prices and things are a struggle for people, and so we’re trying to talk about solutions to try to fix some of those issues,” he said.
One plan at the top of the list for Edwards is to revitalize the Ohio Checkbook. Because he’s heard voters talk about wanting to know exactly where their tax dollars are being spent, he thinks the record-keeping arm of the treasurer’s office could be a simple way to bring that information to the forefront.
“We’d really like to try to figure out how we can invest in the Ohio Checkbook, to make it simple, so whether you’re a farmer in Northwest Ohio or a mechanic in Southeast Ohio, you can log in there, you can see how the state’s spending your money,” Edwards said.
Through all the discussions, even with those who were forthright about their plans not to vote for him, Walsh said the idea was to understand where voters are, and how the treasurer’s office can help.
“I see my job (as treasurer, if elected), and I think the job of any elected official is you have to be fearless in just having conversations with people,” he said. “You don’t have to agree, and you don’t have to vote for me to make me want to make your life better.”
