title: Pillen, Walz lean into conservative support in dueling endorsements for Nebraska governor
description: OMAHA — Republican Gov. Jim Pillen and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont each leaned into conservative support from former lawmakers Monday in dueling events for Nebraska governor that also featured the National Rifle Association. Pillen held a smaller gathering at 88 Tactical, a shooting range and gun training facility just outside Omaha, w[...]
text:
The Republican and Democratic 2026 candidates for Nebraska governor: Republican Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, left, and former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Republican Gov. Jim Pillen and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont each leaned into conservative support from former lawmakers Monday in dueling events for Nebraska governor that also featured the National Rifle Association.
Pillen held a smaller gathering at 88 Tactical, a shooting range and gun training facility just outside Omaha, where he hailed endorsements from the NRA and former state Sen. Tom Brewer, who represented north central Nebraska.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, poses at a campaign event where the National Rifle Association pledged its support behind Pillen’s reelection bid on Sept. 28, 2026, at 88 Tactical outside Omaha. To Pillen’s immediate right is John Commerford, chair of the NRA Political Victory Fund, and former state Sen. Tom Brewer at far left. To Pillen’s immediate left is Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In 2023, Brewer achieved his long-sought goal to pass NRA-backed legislation for “constitutional carry,” to allow concealed carry without the need for a permit or training. In Brewer’s eighth and final year in 2024, he passed a law to allow teachers and staff at small schools or colleges to carry a weapon on school property, if approved ahead of time.
“It’s black and white,” Pillen said Monday. “If we can’t stand up and defend ourselves, if somebody’s against that, it’s just absolutely hard to comprehend.”
Walz held a virtual roundtable with former state Sens. Tim Gragert of Creighton, Mark Kolterman of Seward and John Stinner of Gering. All three represented reliably conservative districts but had more moderate records in the Legislature than Brewer. Kolterman and Stinner had already endorsed Walz before Monday.
The trio spoke against Pillen’s handling of the state’s budget, property tax relief and open, accountable government. They said Walz was the best choice for governor.
“These senators know the stakes,” Walz said. “They’re putting Nebraska over party, and I’m proud to have them with me.”
‘A lifetime of work’
Brewer, a 36-year military veteran, said he, too, is good friends with Walz, who he said is a really nice person. But when Nebraskans elect their governor, he said, “You need to look at a lifetime of work.”
“You need to look at what they’ve actually done and how that’s going to impact the state of Nebraska, and that’s where I think I would like you to think through specifically the Second Amendment,” Brewer said.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signs State Sen. Tom Brewer’s proposal to allow concealed carry of handguns without a permit or training on Tuesday, April 25, 2023. Brewer, at left, and nearly half of Nebraska’s state senators joined the signing. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
On Brewer’s long-sought bill in 2023, for instance, Walz voted against. For multiple years, she avoided taking a position.
“That bill is up in my house, framed as one of those pieces of legislation that I’ll be the proudest of,” Brewer said Monday. He said he “jumped” at the chance to speak about the Second Amendment and Pillen, who Brewer said never showed a sign of hesitation for his bill.
Brewer chaired the Legislature’s Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee for four years. He served in the Legislature between 2017 and 2025, all eight years with Walz.
‘What is right for Nebraskans’
Gragert, a military veteran of 40 years, was a close ally of Brewer’s and supported his “constitutional carry” legislation repeatedly, as did Stinner and Kolterman. Gragert said everyone can “agree to disagree,” but at the end, “we must be willing to do what is right for Nebraskans.”
“After serving with Lynne for four years, I believe she is a person who will listen to everyone before making a final decision,” Gragert said.
Then-state Sens. Tim Gragert of Creighton, Mark Kolterman of Seward and John Stinner of Gering in their legislative offices in November 2022. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska News Service)
As a veteran, Gragert said, he lives by three basic values that are “essential” for a good leader: integrity, trust and selfless service. He said Walz has all three, in addition to communication skills that are “second to none.”
“You can’t ask for anybody better,” Stinner said of Walz’s character.
Kolterman said that in the officially nonpartisan, one-house Legislature, where lawmakers do not caucus by party, it came down to who could do the best job. He said he feels the same for the governorship and believes Walz could finally achieve long-sought efforts for lasting property tax relief by amending a formula distributing state aid to local school districts.
Pillen, too, has made school funding reform a top priority. Kolterman’s successor, state Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, worked with Walz on school funding in the Legislature, and Pillen has praised Hughes’ ongoing efforts.
Kolterman and Gragert served six years with Walz during their eight years of service between 2015 and 2023. Gragert served one term, from 2019 to 2023, and did not run for reelection. Kolterman chaired the Nebraska Retirement Systems Committee between 2016 and 2022; Stinner chaired the Appropriations Committee between 2017 and 2022.
Pillen backs ‘stand your ground’ law
Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, a longtime prosecutor, including as U.S. attorney for Nebraska between 2018 and 2021, said Brewer’s legislation in 2023 was a “historic win” for the self-defense of Nebraskans. He said it put some “real meaning” behind the Second Amendment.
“This is one of those issues where you just can’t sit in the middle,” Kelly said.
John Commerford, chair of the National Rifle Association Political Victory Fund, left, speaks at a campaign event for Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen on Sept. 28, 2026, at 88 Tactical outside Omaha. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
John Commerford, chair of the NRA Political Victory Fund, said Washington, D.C., and President Donald Trump have been a “core part of the golden age of the Second Amendment.” But Commerford said the “restoration of the Second Amendment, the core expansion of those true freedoms, happens at the state level.”
“It’s happened right here in Nebraska,” Commerford said, describing Brewer’s 2023 legislation as “getting rid of a government permission slip to exercise a core Second Amendment right.”
But Commerford said there’s more work to do.
Pillen initially told reporters that another four years would be focused on helping educate the next generation and getting more people involved, so Nebraskans never take their rights for granted. 
Asked by an attendee whether he would specifically support making Nebraska a “stand your ground” state, allowing the use of deadly force outside a home if someone fears death or serious physical harm, Pillen said “100%.”
“I think that anything we can do to strengthen the Second Amendment in Nebraska is a no-brainer,” Pillen said.
Republican frustration
Stinner has repeatedly criticized Pillen’s policy choices of pursuing tax cuts that then require cutting state spending. Pillen has long said he wants to “run the government like a business.”
“If I ran my business the way they’re running the state right now, I’d be bankrupt, and they’ve just got to get off this ‘my way or the highway,’ which I know that you will,” Stinner told Walz. “You’ll bring the people together. You’ll bring the right management and put this thing back on its tracks.”
Former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, bottom left, hosts a virtual campaign roundtable for Nebraska governor with former state Sens. Tim Gragert of Creighton, John Stinner of Gering and Mark Kolterman of Stinner. (Screenshot by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Asked about Walz’s Republican endorsements, Pillen said he understands many people are “ticked off” with higher than $6 diesel fuel, but he doesn’t “play politics” with some groups.
“When you say ‘no’ to everything like we have, and you invest and don’t spend, yeah, ticks people off everywhere,” Pillen said. “It’s OK. It’s a free country, and I respect that, but it’s OK that we don’t agree about everybody. God forbid if every Republican agreed on everything.”
Pillen’s campaign manager, Taylor Sliva, hit back harder and said Walz’s event was “just another example of liberals pretending to be moderates to trick Nebraska Republicans.”
“Don’t listen to what they say — just look at their voting record,” Sliva said in a statement. “They have been voting with Democrats their whole political careers.”
Walz, meanwhile, called the NRA endorsement “another distraction” meant to take away from her work. She said she’s focused on Nebraskans and what’s next.
Walz has pledged to appoint Democrats, Republicans and independents throughout her administration if elected. Asked whether Walz is considering appointing her latest endorsers, or whether she had already offered appointments, spokesperson Sophie Mestas did not say.
“As governor, Lynne will bring together people and voices from all sides of the aisle,” Mestas said in a statement. “Right now, her focus is on reaching Nebraskans across the state and earning their votes.”
Third-party candidates
In addition to Pillen and Walz, two third-party candidates from Omaha will appear on the ballot for governor: former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom, for the America First Party, and Rick Beard, for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, top left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, top right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, bottom left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First Party, bottom right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Lindstrom’s time in office was the same as Stinner and Kolterman, and Kolterman said Lindstrom would have been a “formidable candidate” but got in too late. Lindstrom, until early this year, had been a lifelong Republican. He later launched a nonpartisan campaign this summer, which went up in smoke over allegations of petition fraud. 
Kolterman said Walz had “worked her tail off,” and he, Stinner and Gragert said they’re confident Walz can win, contrary to Lindstrom’s concerns that she can’t.
Lindstrom has repeatedly said he believes he can win and isn’t intending to play “spoiler” or take away votes and help Pillen or Walz. Lindstrom unveiled his own new support Monday, from Nebraskans Against Government Overreach, a group which Lindstrom said had “worked tirelessly at the Legislature for years, standing up for conservative values, individual liberty and common sense.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and the tools you need to cast your vote in Nebraska’s Nov. 3 general election.]
The new America First Party has made no secret of its intention to appeal to Republican voters. The separate Nebraska Working People Party has been accused of the opposite for Democrats.
“So I have a serious question for members of the Nebraska GOP,” Lindstrom said in a Monday Facebook post. “Help me understand why you support Jim Pillen. What has he done that has earned this kind of loyalty? I’m genuinely asking, because I haven’t seen a reason the Republican Party should be working this hard to protect one politician.
“The Republican Party should stand for principles, not personalities.”
Pillen, meanwhile, said he and his team are just at “halftime” in office and that wherever he goes, he hears “nothing” but assurances and thanks for his conservative record. He has heavily encouraged voter turnout this November, describing voting Monday as one of the “highest callings of democracy.”
“My opponents in this governor’s race — however many are on the ballot and whatever kind of parties that they’re named at — if I’m black, they’re white. If I’m red, they’re blue,” Pillen said. “There’s no comparison, and all you have to do is look at the facts and study it.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Trevor Lee resigns from Utah House as AG charges him with fraud
description: Trevor Lee, a Republican representative from Layton and one of the most controversial figures in the Utah Legislature, has resigned after being charged with fraud on Monday.  Lee is facing four felony charges in 3rd District Court after being accused of forging employment documents to obtain a home loan, according to court documents filed by […]
text:
Rep. Trevor Lee, R-Layton, is pictured on the House floor at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the final night of the legislative session, Friday, March 6, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Trevor Lee, a Republican representative from Layton and one of the most controversial figures in the Utah Legislature, has resigned after being charged with fraud on Monday. 
Lee is facing four felony charges in 3rd District Court after being accused of forging employment documents to obtain a home loan, according to court documents filed by the Utah Attorney General’s Office.
Lee said in a prepared statement sent through the House of Representatives on Monday that he was resigning because of personal reasons and did not mention the investigation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Due to personal circumstances that require my attention, I no longer feel I can give my constituents the time, attention, and service they deserve,” Lee said. “I will always be grateful for the people I have met, the relationships I have built, and the opportunity I have had to serve the people of Utah.”
His resignation is effective immediately and the Davis County Republican Party will hold a special election to fill the vacancy for the rest of the year, the remainder of his term. Lee, who represented House District 16 since 2023, lost his reelection bid during the June primaries, so he wasn’t returning to the Legislature next year.
“I appreciate Rep. Lee’s service and accept his resignation,” House Speaker Mike Schultz said in the statement released by the House. 
Lee didn’t respond to a request for comment about the charges on Monday, though a delivery indicator message showed he received it. He is known as one of the state’s most conservative Republican lawmakers, sponsoring unsuccessful measures this year seeking to bar immigrants from public assistance and focusing on removing legal protections for Utah’s transgender community. 
According to the investigation conducted by the Utah Attorney General’s Office, Lee had requested $93,000 in cash advances from Trent Spafford, CEO of the water treatment company Enevive, to show increased income in order to get a home mortgage. 
Utah lawmaker denies claims he tried to help a company win a grant in exchange for $93K

“Lee said he would make Spafford ‘whole’ by securing Spafford’s company a government contract with Hill Air Force Base,” the charging documents say.
Lee indicated he was the sales director of Blue Logic, another water treatment company, with a monthly salary of $15,833 in his mortgage paperwork. He also said he worked for Enevive from July 2024 to October 2025 for a monthly salary of $13,761, attaching offer letters for both companies.
A representative from Blue Logic said the company “had made Lee an offer that Lee never accepted, that Lee asked for the letter to help obtain a home loan, that Lee was a contract employee rather than a full-time employee, and that the letter was prepared to help Lee as a friend and was not accurate,” according to the charges. 
Spafford, the CEO of Enevive, told investigators the documents attached to Lee’s mortgage application from his company were fraudulent and that his signature was forged.
After initially denying signing Spafford’s name, court documents say Lee later confirmed to prosecutors that “the Enevive employment contract was not signed by Spafford and that he had signed it.” He also acknowledged that he knew Blue Logic could not afford to pay him the salary he had indicated in the loan application.
The Enevive income Lee reported was also contradicted by his W-2, the filing says. The total wages he reported in 2024 from the company were $55,634.
Prosecutors reviewed Lee’s loan documents, which charging documents said secured him a $1 million conventional loan structured as a refinance, returning $317,190.99 in cash to Lee.
The investigation backs up claims against Lee that were publicized by Spafford and another of Lee’s former bosses, Jason Walton, president of Moxie Pest Control, just before the Davis County Republican Party Nominating Convention and calling on voters not to reelect him. Walton said at the time that when Lee worked for him in 2013, he doctored checks to boost his pay.
Lee told Utah News Dispatch of the checks in April, “This was something I did as a stupid college kid and paid my debt. I’ve gotten married and I’m now the proud father of 5 wonderful children.” He denied any improper business dealings with Spafford.
Lee is charged with one count of communications fraud and one count of mortgage fraud, both second-degree felonies carrying a possible penalty of one to 15 years in prison. He also faces one count each of forgery and possession of a forgery device, third-degree felonies with a potential penalty of up to five years in prison.
An initial court appearance had not been scheduled for Lee as of Monday evening.

title: Judge considers whether to overrule Alaska’s lieutenant governor on candidate’s eligibility
description: An Anchorage Superior Court judge may rule by mid-October on whether or not Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom acted correctly when she restored Republican state House candidate Jose Tagle to November’s general election ballot. In an order signed Tuesday, Judge Josie Garton declined to promptly overturn Dahlstrom’s decision but left the door open for subsequent action[...]
text:
(Getty Images)An Anchorage Superior Court judge may rule by mid-October on whether or not Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom acted correctly when she restored Republican state House candidate Jose Tagle to November’s general election ballot.
In an order signed Tuesday, Judge Josie Garton declined to promptly overturn Dahlstrom’s decision but left the door open for subsequent action on a legal challenge filed by the Alaska Democratic Party against Dahlstrom and the Division of Elections.
The delay means absentee voters in House District 22 — where Tagle is running against Democratic incumbent Rep. Ted Eischeid — are receiving ballots with Tagle’s name. 
If Tagle is ruled ineligible, any votes for him will be thrown out. 
Dahlstrom disqualified Tagle on Aug. 31 for failing to submit an accurate Public Officer Financial Disclosure form on time. She also disqualified Republican gubernatorial candidate Treg Taylor at the same time, for the same reason.
Four days later, Dahlstrom reversed herself, restoring Tagle and Taylor to the ballot after a Department of Law review found forms filed by dozens of other candidates also had problems. 
A subsequent review by the Alaska Beacon found many of those problems were illusory or minor.
The Alaska Democratic Party has not challenged the decision that restored Taylor to the ballot, but it has continued to fight Tagle’s eligibility.
The party filed its initial lawsuit in July, arguing that the division should have disqualified Tagle when he submitted a blank form. The division regularly disqualifies candidates who file no form. 
The Division of Elections opposed the party’s position, saying the Alaska Public Offices Commission is in charge of certifying whether a form is complete or not, and the time to disqualify Tagle would be after the primary. 
Garton agreed, ruling on Aug. 14 that Tagle had 30 days to amend his form and thus the Division of Elections acted correctly by keeping Tagle on the primary ballot.
But Tagle didn’t fix his form until after the 30-day deadline, and Garton’s August ruling didn’t address what would happen if the Division of Elections approved his general-election candidacy.
The Alaska Democratic Party asked in September for Garton to issue an order enforcing Tagle’s removal from the general election ballot, but in last week’s order, Garton deferred.
She said the party’s post-primary filing raises different issues than the lawsuit it filed before the primary, and therefore, both the party and the Division of Elections need to exchange new written arguments and possibly hold new oral arguments as well.
The Democratic Party and the Division of Elections have asked Garton to rule no later than Oct. 16; she has not yet approved that request. 
Garton’s ruling may not be the final word — in an early-September news conference, Gov. Mike Dunleavy said that any decision on candidacy may have to be decided by the Alaska Supreme Court.
Early, in-person voting begins Oct. 19. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: UConn is giving CT students a science project to help address air quality issues
description: Student-built air purifiers can partially address poor school air quality, but teachers said CT must focus on a larger, long-term fix.
text:
Legislators and advocates gathered Monday afternoon to cheer a new partnership with the University of Connecticut: distributing air purifiers students can build to science classrooms throughout the state.
The subtext of the project was not altogether positive, however. Yes, advocates agreed, it’s an exciting hands-on lesson for kids — but once in use, the air purifiers will address real air quality problems in school buildings. Many schools still rely on aging, ineffective HVAC systems that no longer filter out germs or pollutants effectively, putting both students and teachers at risk of health complications.
The state took a swing at improving school air quality in 2022, when the airborne COVID-19 virus was still fresh in everyone’s mind. The General Assembly crafted new options for schools to fund HVAC renovations and introduced mandatory air quality reporting requirements; however, advocates said the momentum has since dropped off. 
Many districts still aren’t upgrading or maintaining their HVAC systems or complying with the reporting mandate.
“Honestly, we’ve seen a trail-off of interest, right? Like this sort of, ‘Oh, well, we’re not gonna die,’” said Kate Dias, president of the Connecticut Education Association, the state’s largest teachers’ union. “But I think somewhere along the line, we’d like a better threshold than … ‘It’s not gonna kill us today.’”
Dias said 60% of school districts have not submitted their mandatory air quality reports and what has been submitted often contains gaps and errors.
“That does signify that we’re not really taking this as seriously as we need to on the ground level,” Dias said.
Sen. Julie Kushner, D-Danbury, who co-chairs the General Assembly’s working group on indoor air quality, was somewhat more forgiving.
“We went from a three-year inspection to a one-year inspection, and we added in a five-year inspection … so I think the districts are also having some trouble coming into, really understanding what it means to come into compliance,” Kushner said.
Leslie Blatteau, president New Haven Federation of Teachers, speaks during a press conference regarding school indoor air quality at the Connecticut State Capitol in Hartford on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
New Haven Federation of Teachers President Leslie Blatteau said the problem is particularly acute for districts that are already struggling with funding.
“The reality of two Connecticuts shows up here again. That the schools that serve more low-income students and families are at a disadvantage when it comes to how we fund our capital budgets,” Blatteau said.
Rep. Jennifer Leeper, D-Fairfield, who also co-chairs the indoor air quality working group, said schools that want to renovate their HVAC systems can now apply to the state for reimbursement as they would for other capital projects. The reimbursements are tiered based on district wealth, though Leeper acknowledged it doesn’t cover the full cost for anyone.
“Surely, even 20% of these really large expenses are often more than a local district can shoulder, so we’re continuing to try to find better solutions,” Leeper said.
But Kushner said the time to act is now.
“I don’t think we need another working group or a commission. We need schools and school districts and municipalities to understand that the program is there, that it is available to them,” Kushner said.
That participation can be through a construction project or the UConn project, she added.
Marina Creed, director and cofounder of the UConn Indoor Air Quality Initiative, said testing found the air purifiers removed 99.4% removal of airborne viruses in minutes. They also capture potentially harmful mold and dust particles.
“Well-designed and properly maintained HVAC systems remain the gold standard for healthy school buildings,” Creed said. “In-room filtration provides an important additional layer of protection.”
Enrolled schools will also receive air quality monitors to show students (and teachers) whether the purifiers are effective. The program is already operating in 18 districts and is accepting applications statewide. Creed said there is funding to fully outfit 967 schools with one air purifier per room.
Information from the UConn Indoor Air Quality Initiative during a press conference regarding school indoor air quality at the Connecticut State Capitol in Hartford on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Public Health Committee co-Chair Sen. Saud Anwar — a medical doctor specialized in treating lung diseases — said there’s a direct link between a school’s internal air quality and students’ ability to learn. 
“The indoor air is going to determine how they will breathe or how they will not be able to breathe,” Anwar, D-South Windsor, said. “If a child has allergies or asthma, their ability to comprehend, understand, participate in the school and activities is restricted.”
He also noted that children who go to school with poor air quality are at greater risk of developing asthma, while those who already have the condition will experience worse symptoms. Up to 1 in 5 children in some urban school districts have asthma, which Anwar tied directly to the quality of indoor air.
Julianna LaRue, an environmental activist with the Sierra Club, said air quality issues will only become more acute over the years. The reason, she said, is climate change; extreme weather events such as wildfires add harmful particulates to the air, while longer periods of high temperatures heighten the need for effective air conditioning.
Dias reiterated that air purifiers alone won’t be enough.
“While I love the science of this and I love the opportunity and I love the fact that it works, the long-term solution is not asking the children to solve the problem. The long-term solution is to set this as a top priority,” Dias said.
School administrators and board of education members were not present at Monday’s press conference. The Connecticut Mirror reached out to the Connecticut Association of Public School Superintendents and the Connecticut Association of Boards of Education for comment but did not receive a response from either in time for publication.

name: WyoFile
title: Malnutrition killed Wyoming pronghorn in peak summer as vegetation withered during record heat, severe drought
description:
Stunted lowland vegetation in the Green River Basin doesn’t bode well for one of the state’s premier herd's survival the coming winter.
The post Malnutrition killed Wyoming pronghorn in peak summer as vegetation withered during record heat, severe drought appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
On a Tuesday in early August, Brandon Scurlock received the second notification in as many days that one of the 50 GPS-collared pronghorn he’s been monitoring died.
An old female, PH143, had keeled over in the willows along the receded shoreline of Big Sandy Reservoir. 
“It was a whole carcass,” recalled Scurlock, the wildlife management coordinator for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Pinedale Region. He phoned the state’s Wildlife Health Lab for some guidance. 

Brandon Scurlock, wildlife coordinator for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Pinedale Region, at a March 2026 meeting in Pinedale. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

There was no sign of epizootic hemorrhagic disease, a midge-spread and sometimes devastating ungulate killer that tends to flare up during periods of drought. And there was no sign of internal bleeding or injury. 
“I wasn’t too concerned,” Scurlock said. “Pronghorn die.” 
Cracking open the mature doe’s femur, he gained some insight about why. In a healthy animal, the marrow within would be off-white and firm. Instead, it was red, gelatinous and “pretty nasty.” It was an indication that PH143 was in rough shape. 
Two days later, the collar from another marked pronghorn transmitted a mortality signal, this one clear across the Green River Basin in the embattled Dry Piney Creek drainage. 
“We started to think something might be going on,” Scurlock said. 
By Sept. 13, a seventh collared pronghorn had died. Overall, 14% of the tracked animals in the ballyhooed Sublette Pronghorn Herd perished in the span of six weeks. One doe even took her last breaths in an irrigated alfalfa field. 


A dead doe pronghorn found by Wyoming Game and Fish Department staff in a Calpet-area alfalfa field on Sept. 10, 2026. (Devin Gearheart/Wyoming Game and Fish Department)


PH143, a member of the Sublette Pronghorn Herd, in her final resting place on Aug. 4, 2026. (Brandon Scurlock/Wyoming Game and Fish Department)


Even though the animals died at a time of year when ungulates are typically in good shape and readying for winter, malnutrition is the suspected primary cause for the rash of deaths. 
“Interestingly, all seven of those individuals were non-migratory,” Scurlock said. “I think that’s a poor strategy this year: To basically live [all year] on the winter range.” 
Notably, 88% of pronghorn in the Sublette Herd are either migratory or nomadic, according to the U.S. Geological Survey’s migration database. Only 12% of the population resides in the same spot year-round. Yet this summer they accounted for 100% of the unusual deaths. 
One explanation is that the vegetation in those low-elevation areas is especially parched. Coming off the warmest, least-snowy winter in the state’s history, with record late-summer heat all across the region, plant growth was bleak. 
Surveying the antelope bitterbrush plant in the Prospect Mountains — not far from where Scurlock found PH143 dead near Big Sandy — Game and Fish terrestrial habitat biologist Troy Fieseler found “large-scale mortality” of the important winter browse species, with up to 90% of the shrubs dead in places. 
“He measured basically zero growth on bitterbrush leaders,” Scurlock relayed. 
The Prospect Mountains, pictured here in November 2025, experienced mass die-offs of shrubs important to wintering elk, mule deer and pronghorn in summer 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
On live plants in the hardest-hit areas, fresh leaders that sprouted this summer averaged just over a quarter inch — just 10% of the average growth. 
“And it started defoliating a couple weeks ago,” Scurlock said of the bitterbrush. “Pretty rough shape.” 
It’s no secret that record heat and widespread drought has wreaked havoc on Wyoming ecosystems and their inhabitants. Although the extraordinarily mild winter had some positive effects for wildlife like elk, there’s been significant fallout. The heat and aridity has hindered fire scar recovery, led to “unprecedented” black bear conflicts and triggered emergency orders for livestock. 
There are some silver linings and bright spots. 
Although wildfires burned more than 63,200 acres of Wyoming through late September, that’s just a fraction of the acreage that ignited during 2024 (810,000 acres, second most ever) and 2025 (250,000 acres). 
And there have not been any major outbreaks of wildlife diseases that often correlate with drought. 
“Going into the summer, as dry as it was, I anticipated to see more [epizootic hemorrhagic disease] outbreaks, but so far we’ve only had one, southeast of Lander,” Deputy Chief of Wildlife Martin Hicks told the Game and Fish Commission last week in Evanston. 
Hicks also presented some promising data on the productivity of Wyoming’s pronghorn. Biologists and wardens surveying the state’s herds tallied more than 60 fawns per 100 does, a ratio that exceeds the five-year average. 

Statewide, Wyoming pronghorn herds were surprisingly successful at producing fawns in summer 2026. Whether the youngsters survive the winter and are recruited into the population remains to be seen. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department) 

“If you would make me wager a bet, I would have lost that bet,” Hicks said, “because I thought for sure our fawn production would significantly decrease.”  
Even within the Green River Basin, there has been a mixed bag of impacts. Scurlock spent last weekend helping staff a hunter check station, and the migratory mule deer coming out of the Wyoming Range were looking plump and healthy, with good antler growth.
“Tons of body fat on them, but I think they’re going to need it this winter,” Scurlock said. “There’s not going to be much to eat.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Board presses for a recommendation on Canton charter school’s fate
description: The Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board wants to vote in October on whether SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy in Canton can keep its charter.
text:
The Mississippi Charter Authorizer Board wants a recommendation by Wednesday on whether to revoke the charter of SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy so it can vote on the matter on Oct. 26. 
The board voted unanimously on Monday to ask that Kim Turner, the attorney general’s director of the state agencies division, produce a status update by Wednesday. The board also asked to get Turner’s recommendation on whether to revoke the school’s charter by Oct. 9. That deadline will give attorneys for the school and the authorizer board two weeks to send additional responses. Then, at its October meeting, the board will vote on whether to accept Turner’s recommendation.
A sign for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy is shown Thursday, Dec. 19, 2025, in Canton. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Without Turner’s recommendation, the board can’t act.
Turner served as the hearing officer in May when attorneys for the board and the school argued their respective cases for whether SR1 should keep its charter. If Turner recommends revoking the charter — and if the authorizer board accepts her recommendation — SR1 would become the first charter school the state forces to close.
Without a decision about its charter, some of SR1’s funding is at risk.
Mississippi First, a nonprofit that distributes grants to the state’s charter schools, has until Wednesday to approve SR1’s reimbursements for the 2025-26 fiscal year.
Angela Bass Credit: Courtesy photo
Mississippi First has held off on reimbursing SR1’s grant-related expenses since December, when the charter board began the process of revoking the school’s charter. The organization also has not yet communicated with school officials about renewing the grant for the 2026-27 fiscal year, according to Angela Bass, executive director of Mississippi First. 
Bass said she is waiting on an official finding on the school’s fate before she can renew or close out the Charter School Program grant agreement, which provides federal funding from the U.S. Department of Education to open and expand high-quality charter schools. 
Bass asked board members Monday for a decision before the Wednesday grant deadline. 
“As the period of uncertainty continues, the window for SR1 to appropriately use these resources continues to narrow,” Bass wrote in a Sept. 9 email to authorizer board Executive Director Lisa Karmacharya. “This creates a practical concern for all involved.”
Bass said she was in communication with federal programs staff about extending the grant deadline, in case the school keeps its charter.
SR1 is at risk of losing its charter because of alleged severe financial mismanagement by its Chief Executive Officer Tamu Green. The school had one day’s cash on hand during fall 2025 monitoring, its cafeteria failed to meet federal safety guidelines, and leadership didn’t disclose all vendor contracts upon request, according to board attorney Dillon Pitts. 
Tamu Green, CEO of SR1, listens as Letitia Johnson, finance director for the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board, answers questions during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Meanwhile, Green can seek up to $300,000 per year in reimbursements for school supplies and equipment through the grant administered by Mississippi First. Last year, he was reimbursed for over $50,000 in Chromebook and charging cart purchases, as well as other technology and supplies. Green and his staff said in a Sept. 3 letter to Bass that the purchases will meet “specific instructional and operational needs of the students” this school year. 
When requesting reimbursement for the technology, Green touted the school’s third grader’s 88% pass rate on the state standardized reading test, and a satisfactory monitoring report by Mississippi First staff of school leaders’ prior spending of the grant.
Bass also expressed concern about the impact the delay will have on students at the Canton charter school, whose students may be deprived of the bulk of the federal funding to support their education.
“We’re thinking about the kids who are being served,” Bass told Mississippi Today on Friday. “They have allowed them to open their doors for this year, and it’s really not setting them up for success that they cannot access their funds.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Kemp temporarily suspends the state fuel tax as prices at the pump continue to soar
description: Georgia drivers may soon see a little temporary relief at the pump after Gov. Brian Kemp suspended the state’s motor fuel tax as gas prices continued to surge. Kemp issued an executive order Monday declaring a state of emergency for gas supply disruptions. The suspension will take effect Tuesday and run through Oct. 29. “Global […]
text:
Stickers on a gas pump in Acworth blame President Donald Trump for high gas prices. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderGeorgia drivers may soon see a little temporary relief at the pump after Gov. Brian Kemp suspended the state’s motor fuel tax as gas prices continued to surge.
Kemp issued an executive order Monday declaring a state of emergency for gas supply disruptions. The suspension will take effect Tuesday and run through Oct. 29.
“Global markets remain unstable and are subjecting Georgians to unpredictable price shocks on basic goods and services, including but not limited to gasoline and diesel fuel prices,” Kemp wrote in the order. “The factors driving these market shifts are inherently unpredictable, and therefore, difficult, if not impossible, for the citizens of our state to budget for, worsening the impact on hardworking Georgians.”
Kemp has suspended the tax several times during his time in office, including in 2022 when the launch of the war in Ukraine caused oil prices to rise sharply, in the fall of 2023 as inflation spiked, in 2024 following Hurricane Helene and earlier this year after the outbreak of the Iran war.
The motor fuel tax is 33.3 cents per gallon for gasoline and 37.3 cents per gallon for diesel. It brought in just under $193 million to the state in August, according to the state Department of Revenue. Money collected through the tax is used to maintain roads and bridges, and the state has previously dipped into reserves to make up for funds lost through other suspensions.
As of Monday, the average gallon of unleaded gas will set you back $4.19 in Georgia according to AAA, better than the national average of $4.47, but a darn sight worse than last year’s statewide average of $2.87.
If the suspension were in effect Monday, the cost to fill a 15-gallon tank would drop from $62.85 to $57.90, but drivers should not expect to see prices drop immediately.
That’s because the tax is collected at the distributor level and passed on to consumers, which means the fuel sitting in the tank at your local filling station has already been taxed at the normal rate. Drivers can expect to see prices decline once that gas is cycled through.
Gas prices have skyrocketed in recent months as uncertainty in the Strait of Hormuz continues, and in an election year centered around affordability, high gas prices have become the most visible symbol of the challenges facing consumers.
Both of Georgia’s gubernatorial candidates have weighed in on the situation, with Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms calling on Kemp to pause the rate last week and Republican Rick Jackson’s economic platform calling for the automatic suspension of the fuel tax when prices increase past a certain rate. The election is Nov. 3.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa.’s latest online age verification bill would restrict access to adult content
description: Experts warn that, while such measures may be intended to protect children, they can ultimately wind up burdening adults, posing data privacy concerns, and restricting access to First Amendment-protected material.
text:
The Pennsylvania Capitol in Harrisburg. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)A bill advanced through the Senate Judiciary committee Monday with bipartisan support that would require Pennsylvanians to provide proof of their age, such as state identification documents, when accessing websites with at least one-third of their material consisting of adult content. The goal, according to the bill’s sponsor, Sen. Cris Dush (R-Jefferson), is to protect minors.
“When it comes to the protection of children from exposure to pornography, the only verification measure, if any, is clicking a button indicating you’re 18 years old,” Dush said in committee. “Why should we not protect our kids from pornography websites the same way we protect them from online gambling?”
But experts warn that, while such measures may be intended to protect children, they can ultimately wind up burdening adults, posing data privacy concerns, and restricting access to First Amendment-protected material.
“We believe [these laws] burden adults’ rights to access lawful speech, that they can destroy people’s ability to be anonymous online, and that they are privacy and data security disasters waiting to happen,” said Aaron Mackey, the deputy legal director at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit focused on digital civil liberties. “In the name of protecting children, you are making it such that people have a pretty difficult, if not impossible, time avoiding providing information that directly or indirectly identifies them.
The bill is one of several to advance in recent years that would age gate parts of the internet in Pennsylvania, and require all users, including adults, to provide additional, sensitive data to affected websites. 
In 2024, a Democrat-backed bill that would have required what’s called age assurance for social media sites passed the House, but stalled in the Senate. “Age assurance” is less restrictive than “age verification,” allowing companies to employ a broader set of tactics to ensure the age of its users, but it still would have required social media companies to collect sensitive data.
Sen. Cris Dush (R-Jefferson) answers questions about his bill, S.B. 603, in a Senate Judiciary Committee meeting on Sept. 28, 2026 (photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star)
That bill was opposed by the American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania and others.
According to Megan Iorio, senior counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), any transmission of sensitive data over the internet carries inherent risk, though lawmakers can require safer practices. As it stands, Dush’s bill would require adult sites not to retain age verification data, but does not get into specifics.
“If a company collects that information and stores it in an insecure way, then it’s subject to, potentially, data theft,” she said. “And if they use that information in other ways, like to profile users or to sell that information, those are other privacy concerns.”
Sen. Maria Collett (D-Montgomery) was one of two lawmakers on the Senate Judiciary Committee to vote against the bill Monday. Both supported the measure’s aims, but specifically cited the bill’s lack of specifics on data privacy in its current form.
“I think with the proliferation of Flock cameras, Ring cameras, and people sort of being online all the time no matter what, our data is increasingly not becoming our own,” she told the Capital-Star.
Collett had another concern as well about what it might mean to give sensitive information to a website providing adult content.
“Who among us hasn’t gotten a scam email from someone that says, ‘I’ve seen what you look at online. I’ll tell everyone you know unless you send me $1,000 in cryptocurrency,” she said. “These scams are just ubiquitous, they are everywhere, and they will target every population. If you’re someone who is lawfully visiting a site that you’re looking at adult material, and you’re using it in an appropriate manner, we have to be mindful that that data collection can’t then be used as a tool to exploit you further.”
Sen. Steven Santarsiero (D-Bucks) shared Collett’s data privacy concerns, but said he would vote to advance the bill anyway, though he would like to see it amended down the line.
“It’s important for us to send a message to these content sites that we are serious about this issue,” he said, though he noted he would like to see the bill changed before final passage. “I suspect this will not be the last word on this and we’ll be back.”
Courts have ruled against most online age verification requirements. A Supreme Court ruling changed the landscape.
Sen. Maria Collett (D-Montgomery) discusses S.B. 603 in a Senate Judiciary Committee meeting on Sept. 28, 2026 (photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star)
Pennsylvania is not alone. Around the country, laws requiring age verification to access parts of the internet, whether social media or adult content, have become more common in recent years.
But according to Mackey, lawmakers have been attempting to require age verification to prevent minors from accessing certain websites for decades. Though court precedent has largely prevented that.
“Legislators’ and lawmakers’ desire to age gate the internet essentially did not come long after widespread adoption of the internet,” he said. “It has long been a claim that, in the name of protecting children, rather than having parents have responsible conversations about what content their kids can access online, or having the states promote allowing parents to have access to tools like content filtering and monitoring … the state should set a default — a restrictive one.”
While states passed laws, many were, and some still remain, held up in litigation. But a 2025 U.S. Supreme Court decision in a case called Free Speech Coalition, Inc. v. Paxton allowed a Texas law requiring age verification for pornography to stand. While the decision noted such laws would be subject to heightened scrutiny, it opened a door for other states to require ID checks for adult content.
Numerous bills modeled after Texas’ law were introduced around the country. According to Trace Mitchell, an attorney at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), Dush’s bill is one of them, but it has a unique quality.
“Unlike [Texas’] law, which was enforced by a state attorney general, this law is enforced by a private right of action, which means that every website that is even arguably covered faces the threat of a lawsuit,” he said. “The cheapest way to avoid that is to put up an ID check.”
Mitchell added that another component of the bill is almost bound to lead to such lawsuits. That’s the clause noting that a website must employ age verification if more than one-third of its content is considered pornographic.
“There’d be no way for a website to prove they fell outside the scope of this bill without first going through discovery,” he said. “Discovery is almost always the most expensive part of a lawsuit, so even if you win, you’ve already paid for most of the lawsuit.”
“The predictable result is far more age gating, even by websites that may not fall within the scope of the bill, and significantly greater burdens on adults’ constitutionally protected speech and expression,” he added. “Anonymity is incredibly important. It’s often what makes speech possible and allows people to engage in free expression without worrying it will be used against them … The Supreme Court itself has long recognized that.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: ‘It could be the edger’: USC’s Dawn Staley launches leadership program for students
description: USC women’s basketball head coach Dawn Staley is lending her time and name to a new leadership program at the college.
text:
University of South Carolina women’s basketball head coach Dawn Staley is lending her time and name to a new leadership program at the Columbia college. This fall, the Dawn Staley Leadership Academy welcomed its first group of 110 students studying for careers in sports, entertainment, tourism, retail and fashion merchandising, the school announced Monday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — University of South Carolina women’s basketball head coach Dawn Staley is lending her time and name to a new leadership program at the state’s flagship university.
This fall, the Dawn Staley Leadership Academy welcomed its first group of 110 students studying for careers in sports, entertainment, tourism, retail and fashion merchandising.
“When I connect myself to things, it takes over my heart,” said Staley, head coach at USC since 2008.
“I want to share the things that I’ve learned throughout my life with young people. If it resonates with them, I think it’s a great thing,” said the three-time NCAA national championship head coach and former Olympian.
USC’s Dawn Staley to attend 2024 Olympics as part of US presidential delegation

Students participate in an eight-week introductory course with regular appearances by Staley herself. The course provides students one credit hour. Classes cover topics including leadership, personal values, recovering from difficulties and managing emotions.
“For me, leadership starts now,” Staley said, adding they need to learn the skills before being thrown into a leadership position.
“I just want young people to get everything and be equipped to handle whatever challenges that are faced in and out of their profession, in and out of relationships, in and out of anything that they deem a challenge,” Staley said. “I want them to lean into challenges.”
Students who complete the introductory course can compete to be among the 35 selected each year to continue on through the rest of the academy. Those who successfully complete the remaining three courses, providing six total credit hours, and a community project will graduate with a special leadership certificate.
“This credential will tell employers not simply what these students have studied, but how to lead in uncommon and transformational ways,” said Michael Sagas, dean of USC’s College of Hospitality, Retail and Sport Management.
In addition to class time, participating students can attend outside events, such as immersion trips to championship organizations, workshops and career coaching. Sagas said the school plans to bring in industry leaders for candid conversations about the leadership process.
Carolina Panthers owner donates $5M to USC for scholarships, professorships

“I hope they learn what the value of communication is, what the value of resiliency is, what the value is making real connections. They’ll have to go out into the community and make an impact,” Staley said. “But it’s going to be a foundation of allowing them to grow and to stand out.”
Staley hopes the certificate will help students once they graduate and begin looking for a job.
“If you have this certificate, you can put it in somebody’s face and it could be the edger,” she said. “You want it to be the differentiator.”
Staley also said she looks forward to building connections with students across campus “who are pounding the pavements and really are paying for their education,” in addition to the athletes on her team.
“For me, I want everybody to win. I want everybody to be successful,” she said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. Senate Majority Leader weighs in on midterm election, skill games and gift ban proposal
description: Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman addressed some of the biggest topics ahead of the final legislative stretch before midterms.
text:
Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) speaks to reporters about skill games and other legislative priorities following a Pennsylvania Press Club luncheon on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)With just five weeks until Election Day, Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) isn’t worried that his party will lose control of the legislature’s upper chamber. Instead, despite warnings of a “blue wave” in November, he believes Senate Republicans will widen their four-seat edge. 
“We have very strong incumbents that know how to reach their constituents and communicate with them,” Pittman told reporters on Monday. “Our incumbents know exactly what we’re doing, and we’re also going to pick up a seat.”
Half of the commonwealth’s senators are on the ballot this year alongside every House member. 
Pa. House lawmakers reintroduce gift ban bill despite decades of legislative inaction

Pittman, speaking at the Pennsylvania Press Club, touched on numerous issues before lawmakers — including a proposal to ban lobbyists from giving gifts to lawmakers, which a House Republican tried to advance later that afternoon.
Near the top of the agenda for Pittman in the coming weeks: skill games and felony murder, two policy areas disrupted by recent Pennsylvania Supreme Court rulings. 
Justices ruled that mandatory life sentences without the possibility of parole for felony murder were unconstitutional in the spring, giving legislators until late July to act. They failed to come to a consensus, leaving judges without any sentencing guidelines for the charge, which is levied when someone dies during the commission of another felony such as robbery — whether the death was intentional or not. 
The General Assembly still has time to meet a court-mandated deadline on skill games, which justices determined should be regulated like other gambling devices. They opted to delay their ruling until Oct. 13 so lawmakers could come to an agreement before Pennsylvania State Police seize the terminals. 
Pittman pointed to a proposal from Senate leadership to tax the gaming terminals at 35%, below the 52% proposed by Gov. Josh Shapiro. Small businesses like laundromats, grocery stores, gas stations and fraternal clubs have come to rely on skill games as a source of revenue, and warn that a high rate will hurt their bottom line.
“Figuring out a regulatory path on them makes sense. Whether we can get there is a very open question,” said Pittman. Stakeholders also disagree whether taxes should be deposited into the state’s general fund or be earmarked for public transit. 
Though he hedged on what bills might move before lawmakers adjourn for the year — including whether there will be any response to grassroots concerns about data centers — Pittman ruled out any action to legalize marijuana in Pennsylvania for recreational use. 
“People tend to forget that recreational marijuana, for better or worse, is a scheduled narcotic at the federal level. And I think we would all be well served to have some more national direction on how to deal with this issue,” he added, also criticizing the state’s handling of its medical marijuana program. 
 Reforming Harrisburg

As one of just four states where the two major parties split control of the legislature, Pittman said the arrangement “puts us in a unique position and oftentimes a very difficult position.” 
“Make no mistake, there are deep philosophical divisions in Harrisburg, and that’s OK. It’s OK to have deep philosophical divisions on policy, but it also requires us to give and take and compromise on issues when the moment arises and requires it,” Pittman said. 
He pointed to budgets that “spent more than I certainly would prefer” as an example of a concession, saying his caucus brought “balance to the conversation.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In response to another question, he said he believed removing cameras from chambers would make Harrisburg more efficient, only adding that “people like to talk in front of cameras.”
Pittman also spoke about proposed “gift bans” that would ban lobbyists from giving gifts to lawmakers, saying he believed the state’s current system works. Current law, as well as chamber rules, are “very clear that we cannot accept anything of value for official action,” he said.
State law requires lawmakers to report gifts over $250 as well as hospitality, such as meals or travel, over the amount of $650 in their yearly ethics disclosure.
“I would be very willing to look at efforts on transparency and figure out where loopholes may or may not be, but I will just further underscore that we have a very robust ethics commission,” Pittman added. “We have an ethics act in place, and I think that does a very good job at shedding light on anything that may occur that shouldn’t.”
Others disagree.
From left, House Republican Reps. Marc Anderson (York), Jamie Walsh (Luzerne), Mike Jones (York) and Scott Barger (Blair) speak in favor of banning lobbyists from giving gifts to legislators on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Pittman’s comments came the same day Rep. Mike Jones (R-York) introduced a discharge petition in order to force a committee vote on House Bill 744. Sponsored by Rep. Jared Solomon (D-Philadelphia), it would prohibit cash gifts in any amount as well as aggregated gifts of more than $50 from one person over the course of a calendar year. 
“For too long, both parties have failed to act on this bipartisan legislation, not even allowing for an up or down vote,” said Jones. “Assuming we get our 25 signatures, which we are confident we will, it at least forces the committee to act.”
Jones said the $133,000 salary and per diem were “more than sufficient” for lawmakers, adding that discharge petitions to force votes on certain issues are one of the few tools available to Republicans in the House, where they are in the minority.
A gift ban has long been a priority for Michael Pollack, who is the co-founder and executive director of March on Harrisburg. The advocacy group pushes to reduce the influence of money on politics and improve government transparency. 
“Because as long as money talks, the voice of the people just is not heard. As long as unlimited gifts are legal, those of who can’t afford to take somebody to Austria or to the Super Bowl just don’t get our point across as effectively,” said Pollack.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Landowner group sues over Wahpeton water sale for large dairy
description: A group of Wahpeton-area residents and the Dakota Resource Council are suing a state agency in a dispute over water for a large dairy farm.  The suit against the North Dakota Department of Water Resources was filed Friday in Burleigh County District Court.  The Department of Water Resources approved the sale of 500,000 gallons of […]
text:
Dairy cows stand on a carousel as they are milked at Riverview’s Campbell Dairy in Wilkin County, Minnesota, on July 10, 2025. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) A group of Wahpeton-area residents and the Dakota Resource Council are suing a state agency in a dispute over water for a large dairy farm. 
The suit against the North Dakota Department of Water Resources was filed Friday in Burleigh County District Court. 
The Department of Water Resources approved the sale of 500,000 gallons of water per day from the city of Wahpeton to the Southeast Water Users District. 
Opponents of giant North Dakota dairy argue for permit reversal

The Southeast Water Users District would be one source of water for the 12,500-cow Abercrombie Dairy, operated by Minnesota-based Riverview. 
The lawsuit seeks to invalidate the water agency’s dismissal of the group’s administrative challenge and to nullify the approval of the water sale. 
The water would come from the Wahpeton Buried Valley Aquifer. The lawsuit argues the residents rely on the same aquifer as the city and the dairy, which is under construction north of Wahpeton.
The lawsuit argues that the Department of Water Resources water sale approval conflicts with the agency’s mission to manage North Dakota’s water resources responsibly. 
“I do not understand why the state is risking the depletion of the only water source for the city of Wahpeton and the surrounding farmsteads,” Richland County resident Mary Sahl, one of the appellants, said in a news release. “There is no backup water supply for Wahpeton or for those of us who rely on this groundwater.”  
On July 30, an administrative law judge dismissed the residents’ claims, saying the residents lacked standing because they do not live in Wahpeton and had not yet been harmed. The residents asked Water Resources to reconsider in August, but the agency denied that request. 
Mary Sahl of Richland County speaks July 1, 2025 in Fargo, about the planned Riverview dairy operation near Wahpeton, North Dakota. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Water Resources said Monday it does not comment on pending litigation. 
Large dairy farms like those proposed by Riverview near Wahpeton and Hillsboro require 28 to 30 gallons of water per cow each day, according to Riverview. That would equal at least 350,000 gallons per day for the Abercrombie Dairy and double that for the Herberg Dairy southeast of Hillsboro in Traill County.  
Riverview says it tries to recycle as much water as possible. Capturing rainwater from the roofs of barns and other buildings provides the Campbell Dairy in Minnesota’s Wilkin County with about half the water that it needs for its 10,000 cows. The company has similar plans for the North Dakota operations. 
Dakota Resource Council, a North Dakota based environmental group, is pursuing another lawsuit against a different state agency and Riverview.
The group has filed a lawsuit against the Department of Environmental Quality and Riverview in Traill County where Riverview plans to build the 25,000-cow Herberg Dairy near the Red River. A judge heard arguments on that case in July but has yet to rule.
